#5625. Crypto and Midterm Election: 3 Risks From Trump’s $5,000 Stimulus to Iran

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Crypto is facing a major political test as Americans head to the polls on November 3, with the US midterm election potentially reshaping regulation, stimulus expectations, and investor risk appetite.

Republicans are fighting to retain control of Congress, while Democrats are seeking to regain power in at least one chamber. The outcome could determine if President Donald Trump advances his economic agenda or faces a tougher legislative road ahead.

For crypto, the midterm election comes with three major risks: Trump’s proposed $5,000 stimulus dividend, the future of stalled crypto legislation, and escalating tensions with Iran.

The election itself may not immediately change Crypto’s fundamentals. However, it could shift expectations around liquidity, regulation, and the financial markets.

Trump has promised a $5,000 dividend payment to adult US citizens if Republicans retain control of both the House and Senate. The proposal would cover 240 million adults, potentially costing around $1.2 trillion, and Trump has also suggested that tariff revenue could help fund the payments.

Trump may have just sealed the deal on stage in Dallas.He's promising a $5,000 dividend to every American adult if Republicans win the midterms — only condition is the money has to be spent in the U.S.I've never seen anything like this. pic.twitter.com/ypJP2fYsLj

A Republican victory could then strengthen expectations for additional household spending and potentially inject fresh liquidity into financial markets. We, in the crypto market, have historical reasons to watch stimulus closely.

During the COVID-19 pandemic, US stimulus checks coincided with extraordinary monetary easing and a powerful crypto rally. A Federal Reserve Bank of Cleveland study found that the 2020 payments increased Bitcoin buy volume by 3.8%, while the associated price effect was modest.

The 2020–2021 rally also benefited from low interest rates, institutional adoption, and abundant liquidity. Hence, a new stimulus program could encourage retail investors to allocate more money toward Bitcoin and other risk assets.

However, the proposed dividend is not approved, and higher inflation expectations or Treasury yields could offset some of the bullish impact. If Democrats win control of Congress, Trump’s proposal could face a much tougher path toward approval.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The Midterm election could also determine whether lawmakers make progress on the most-awaited crypto regulation, the Digital Asset Market CLARITY Act. It aims to establish clearer rules governing digital assets and the division of responsibilities between US regulators.

The bill remains stalled after failing to advance through a Senate procedural vote in September. A Republican victory could improve its chances, although bipartisan support would still be necessary to overcome legislative hurdles.

A Democratic victory, particularly if the party takes control of the House, could bring increased scrutiny of Trump’s crypto-related ventures and campaign connections. That could delay legislation as lawmakers focus on investigations and oversight.

Still, a Democratic win would not automatically mean tougher crypto regulation. Bipartisan support for clearer digital asset rules remains possible, although the final legislation could look different from the current proposal.

The Midterm election presents a mixed outlook for crypto. A Republican victory combined with stimulus optimism, progress on crypto legislation, and Iran de-escalation would create a potentially bullish environment.

A Democratic victory could introduce regulatory uncertainty, while renewed conflict in the Middle East could pressure crypto regardless of the midterm election result. For us, the key question is whether political optimism can outweigh geopolitical risk.

Trump’s stimulus promise may offer a powerful bullish narrative, but crypto’s next major move could ultimately depend on improving liquidity or another inflationary shock.

The biggest immediate threat to crypto is not the midterm election, and it may come from outside Washington. The US carried out limited strikes on Iran’s Qeshm islands near the Strait of Hormuz. This revived concerns about escalation, even as diplomatic contacts continued.

#5624. Open Real Estate: We’re almost there, but not quite

OPINION: The Open Real Estate options give sellers just two choices: market or participant view. Darryl Davis makes the case for a third door.

Picture a homeowner at the kitchen table. She likes you. She trusts you. And she says something agents hear every week: “I want you to sell my house. Just you. I don’t want a parade of strangers walking through my bedroom with agents I have never met. But I don’t want to hide it either. Advertise it. Get the word out. I want the best price.”

That is not a strange request. Some homeowners would happily give up a few dollars on the sale price for less stress, more convenience, and the peace of working with one agent and one office. And right now, the newest system in real estate has no way to say yes to it.

On October 26, Keller Williams, AGNT (the parent of eXp and NextHome), HomeServices of America and Real REMAX Group launched Open Real Estate (ORE). Four competitors came together to stop listings from disappearing into company silos. They deserve real credit. But read the FAQ, and you will see the system gives a seller only two doors.

Now go back to our homeowner. Door one sends strangers through her bedroom. Door two gives her one agent but forbids anyone to advertise her house, the last thing she asked for. She wants one agent and full marketing. ORE makes her pick one.

That is not seller choice. That is a choice between two things she did not ask for.

Here is the option that is missing, and it is simple.

I can already hear the objection. “Darryl, isn’t this just a pocket listing with a nicer name?”

No. A pocket listing is hidden. A Coming Soon tease builds buzz while keeping other agents out, and nobody, not even the listing agent, can show it. The true exclusive is the opposite of both. The house is actively marketed to the public, and every member company knows it is available. The only thing exclusive is who walks through her front door.

Think of a restaurant that only takes reservations. Everybody sees the menu and knows where it is. You call first, and the owner decides who gets a table. Nobody calls that a secret restaurant.

Let’s say it out loud. In a true exclusive, the listing agent may well sell the house to their own buyer and get paid on both sides. For some sellers, that is exactly why they choose it. They understand that one cook in the kitchen managing the whole process beats two, especially when the second one is an untrained buyer’s agent.

ORE already has what it needs to offer this, and technology can make the fiduciary piece stronger than ever.

CCP had the right intentions. NAR wanted to stop listings from disappearing. But it was the wrong strategy, and it did the opposite. Once a listing is publicly marketed, it must go into the MLS within one business day.

Keep it quiet, though, and it falls under the office exclusive exemption. That does not tell agents to share. It tells them to stop advertising and keep the listing inside their own company. The brokerage itself became the pocket.

A rule meant to bring listings into the open pushed many further underground. As I wrote earlier this year, a Redfin analysis found pocket listings rose 67 percent after CCP passed. NAR leaves enforcement to local MLSs, and in a lot of markets, they have quietly stopped enforcing it or issuing penalties. A rule on the books but not enforced protects no one. It only confuses the agents trying to follow it.

For newer agents: Before CCP, a seller could hire one brokerage to market and show her home exclusively. But those exclusives usually stayed out of the MLS, so other agents often never knew the house existed. The true exclusive keeps what sellers liked about the old way and adds what was always missing: every agent knowing the house is for sale. That is the replacement.

Let’s give our homeowner the third door: one agent, full marketing and a way for the right buyer to find her. That is real seller choice.

Until a model like this is in place, we are still hurting buyers and sellers. Period.

The views and opinions expressed here are those of the contributor and separate from the Inman newsroom.

Darryl Davis is the CEO of Darryl Davis Seminars. Get connected on Facebook or YouTube.

#5623. Block shares rise after third-quarter beat and a third straight guidance raise

Shares of Block Inc. rose more than 7% in late trading today after the payments and financial services company beat third-quarter expectations and raised its full-year guidance for the third straight time.

For the quarter that ended on Sept. 30, Block reported adjusted earnings of $1.13 per share, up from 54 cents in the same quarter of the previous year, on revenue of $6.72 billion, up nearly 10% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting $1.03 per share on revenue of $6.58 billion.

Gross profit grew 22%, to $3.24 billion, and finished ahead of the company’s own guidance. Adjusted operating income almost doubled, to a record $923 million, and the adjusted operating margin rose to 29% of gross profit. Product development spending fell 11% from a year earlier, reflecting the workforce cut Block made in February.

Operating income on an unadjusted basis rose a more modest 5%, to $428 million, held back by $435 million in contingencies, restructuring and other charges. Net income attributable to common stockholders came to $566 million, compared with $462 million a year earlier.

Cash App gross profit grew 27% to $2.07 billion. Monthly transacting actives reached 60 million in September, and Block named Neighborhoods as a key driver after the loyalty network auto-enrolled more than 30,000 Square seller locations in August. Consumer lending originations rose 40% to $19 billion, led by Cash App Borrow and Afterpay Post-Purchase. Transaction, loan and consumer receivable losses climbed 66% as that lending grew.

Square gross payment volume grew 14%, to $76.4 billion, the fastest rate since the first quarter of 2023, with U.S. growth accelerating to 10.4%. Square’s gross profit kept pace at $1.16 billion. Block’s bitcoin business shrank again, as gross profit there halved to $52 million after the company cut fees on certain bitcoin transactions in Cash App.

Business highlights in the quarter included the July alpha release of Buzz, an open-source workspace for people and AI agents that has since had more than two dozen updates. General availability of Cash App Tags tap-to-pay hardware followed in August. In September, Block said it would open Cash App Score, its in-house credit score, to outside lenders through Nova Credit Inc.

Much of Chief Executive Jack Dorsey’s shareholder letter dealt with AI. Block, he wrote, has “meaningfully crossed the chasm” in turning itself into a company that “streams intelligence as people need it.”

Pilots of Buzz with prospective customers began in October, and Block expects to book its first machine intelligence revenue in the fourth quarter. Builderlab, the ecosystem Block created to sell Buzz and related tools to other companies, will be formally introduced at a San Francisco event on Nov. 10.

Fourth-quarter guidance calls for gross profit to grow 15%, to $3.32 billion. Adjusted earnings are forecast at $1.15 per share, a cent below the $1.16 analysts had expected. For the full year, Block now projects gross profit of $12.63 billion, up from the $12.51 billion it forecast in August, and adjusted earnings of $4.15 per share, up from $4.02. The consensus estimate was $4.06.

A preliminary outlook for 2027 calls for gross profit to grow at least 15%, to $14.52 billion. Adjusted operating income is expected to rise 30% next year, to $4.58 billion, well above the $3.51 billion target Block set at its investor day in November 2025.

#5622. Amazon’s ‘Fallout’ Filmed Inside This Rare Norman Jaffe Estate—and It Was Just Listed for $4.25 Million

A stunning five-bedroom Long Island estate, designed by Norman Jaffe in 1977 and featured in the popular post-apocalyptic Amazon Prime series “Fallout,” has just hit the market for $4.25 million.

Located in Old Westbury, the 5,291-square-foot home has a well-preserved midcentury modern interior, including a foyer with a 30-foot ceiling and an open floor plan with oversized windows, glass walls, stone and hardwood floors, pine ceilings, and three fireplaces. The sculptural structure has climbed its way to the top of the week’s most popular homes list.

The inviting living room has a dual-sided fireplace and glass doors that open to the rear deck and pool grounds. The industrial-style kitchen has a center island, counter seating, and an eat-in area overlooking the pristine grounds. There is also a home theater for entertaining and relaxing.

The 2.02-acre, resort-inspired lot is surrounded by mature landscaping and has expansive decks and patios with serene views. An in-ground pool with a spa and a two-car garage are also on the property.

Other properties grabbing attention this week include Red Hot Chili Peppers founding member Flea’s California compound, which is returning to the market with a price chop; a Tudor-style estate in Ohio; and two lighthouses in Michigan offered for one low price.

Why it’s here: This affordably priced, 1,800-square-foot “shouse” (shop/house) is designed for a collector, hobbyist, or outdoor enthusiast.

The front of the engineered wood-frame building houses a one-bedroom residence, and the back has a two-car garage. Built in 2012, the building, known as The Roost, even has a cold equipment storage area. The home includes a living room, a kitchen with oak cabinetry, and a bathroom with a walk-in tub/shower. A walk-up loft over the living quarters could be used for extra storage or turned into an entertainment room.

A covered patio overlooks the 3.2-acre lot and its wide open views.

Wes Well of Re/Max Advantage is the listing agent.

Why it’s here: This 40-acre farm has a renovated 1900s farmhouse, equestrian facilities, a cellar house, and two ponds.

The rural four-bedroom home has a country kitchen with new countertops, wood cabinetry, updated appliances, and pantry space. The cozy living room has a gas fireplace, and a modern bathroom has a claw-foot tub with a shower system.

The property also has fenced and cross-fenced pastures, newly constructed gates, a tack room/shed, and a garage with a partly finished loft that could become future living or recreation space.

Jimmy Galusky of Railey WV Properties is the listing agent.

Why it’s here: Here’s a reasonably priced chance to buy an intact Bruce Goff-designed midcentury home with a stunning double-height octagonal great room and a two-car carport.

Built in 1960, the charming two-bedroom home, known as the Howard and Lucille Jones House, has many original details. Highlights include a four-sided brick fireplace tower in the living room, a sunken conversation pit, exposed beams, wood-plank ceilings, original accordion blinds, signature geometric pendant lighting, custom millwork, and built-ins. Twin cantilevered staircases lead to the upstairs sleeping area, which overlooks the main living space. A “continuous floor of irregular marble stone design” runs throughout the lower level and into the screened-in porch.

An “atrium-like” porch overlooks a stone terrace and reflecting pond.

Why it’s here: It's a modestly priced, 2,929-square-foot, midcentury modern home that comes with an extra lot overlooking an adjacent pond.

Nestled in the Homewood Acres neighborhood, the three-bedroom brick residence, built in 1954, has a spacious kitchen with custom wood cabinetry, breakfast bar, and wall oven. A sunroom surrounded by glass walls and skylights overlooks the serene setting. The primary suite offers dual walk-in closets. A finished basement features a bar, fireplace, and walk-out access to a patio.

With applicable permitting, the 2.3-acre property offers the potential to build or sell the additional lot.

Chelsey C Hudson of York Realty is the listing agent.

Sue Wilkerson of Re/Max Crossroads is the listing agent.

Why it’s here: Two lighthouses are up for sale as a package: Gravelly Shoal Lighthouse in Saginaw Bay and Skillagalee Lighthouse in Lake Michigan.

Gravelly Shoal Lighthouse is fully operational and includes a bunker-style structure. Skillagalee Lighthouse sits in the northeast corner of Lake Michigan, between Beaver Island and the mainland. This historic light is also fully operational and has been carefully maintained and updated. The sellers are looking for a buyer who will keep caring for it so future generations can enjoy it.

The four-bedroom "architectural masterpiece" boasts 8,586 square feet of eye-popping living space with sculptural "cube-like forms" boasting glass walls and dramatic ceilings. A glass great room was inspired by I.M. Pei's iconic Louvre Pyramid. Designed for grand-scale entertaining, the residence is equipped with a chef's kitchen, a scullery kitchen with walk-in pantry, a lower-level kitchenette, a fitness center, an executive office, and a library with private entry. The primary suite with a soaking tub opens up to a meditation garden with a hot tub.

The 15.57-acre property, with four deeded parcels, also has an industrial-style art studio, a lighted tennis court, two cascading waterfalls, and a "nationally recognized" koi sanctuary with a glass-covered interior viewing corridor.

Bill Martin of Douglas Elliman CT is the listing agent.

Why it’s here: This Norman Jaffe–designed estate was featured in Amazon Prime Video’s hit series “Fallout.”

Built in 1977, the five-bedroom Long Island home has a foyer with a 30-foot ceiling and a skylight. It opens to a jaw-dropping interior of curved walls, dramatic angles, pine ceilings, and walls of glass. The living room has a dual-sided fireplace and glass doors that open to the back deck and pool area. Other highlights of the 5,291-square-foot interior include an industrial-style kitchen, a dining room overlooking the pool, and a home theater for entertaining.

The beautifully landscaped 2.02-acre lot also has an in-ground pool, a spa, a sun deck, and multiple patios with picturesque views.

Michael Misiti of Compass is the listing agent.

#5621. Americans cling to homeownership as affordability gap widens

New ACS data shows incomes up 3.9 percent, but buyers still need $110,700 to comfortably afford a median-priced home.

Americans are clinging to the dream of homeownership — even though their incomes are barely enough to sustain it.

The U.S. Census Bureau released its 2025 American Community Survey 1-Year data on Thursday, which includes statistics on 40-plus topics, including housing. The national homeownership rate held steady at 65.3 percent, only 0.1 percentage points below the 5-year high of 65.4 percent. The majority of homeowners carry a mortgage (59 percent), with the real median mortgage payment increasing 2.4 percent year over year to $1,598.

Total housing costs, which may include expenses like homeowners association (HOA) fees, maintenance and repairs, increased 3.5 percent year over year from $2,090 to $2,163. Households now spend 21.9 percent of income on these costs, up 0.5 percentage points and just 8.1 points below the widely recognized 30 percent affordability threshold.

Median household incomes are edging up (+1.2 percent yoy after inflation), but Realtor.com Senior Economist Hannah Jones said it’s not enough to keep up with median home value growth.

“New 2025 American Community Survey data show median household income rose 3.9 percent to $84,780, with incomes up nominally in 49 of 50 states,” she said in an emailed statement. “But housing remained out of reach for many households. With a median listing price near $424,000 in 2025, mortgage rates averaging 6.6 percent, a 20 percent down payment, and taxes and insurance at roughly 1.7 percent of home value, a buyer needed about $110,700 to afford a median-priced home, roughly $26,000 more than the typical household earned.”

“Closing that gap would have required incomes to be 30.5 percent higher, prices about $99,000 lower or mortgage rates near 3.5 percent,” she added. “That affordability challenge has persisted, even as the year started with a promise.”

Jones said the market was primed in homebuyers’ favor at the beginning of the year, with sub-6 percent mortgage rates. However, macroeconomic and geopolitical conflicts have pushed mortgage rates up — now in the 7.30 percent range — leaving most homebuyers unable to take advantage of better inventory levels and falling list prices.

“Even assuming incomes have grown in line with recent wage gains of 3 percent to 4 percent since 2025, the typical household income would still be roughly $28,000 short,” she said. “Demand has cooled in response to higher rates, and pending sales fell 4.1 percent year over year in September, the steepest annual drop since March 2025, even as inventory approached pre-pandemic levels and prices softened.”

Realtor.com has released several reports on how homebuyers can attempt to make the math work, even as rates fluctuate. They can improve their credit scores, increase their down payments, shop lenders and build a budget buffer to help them absorb a 0.50 percent rate increase or decrease.

As for what lies ahead this year, homebuyers aren’t expected to receive mortgage rate relief.

The Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate steady (at 3.75 to 4 percent) at its Oct. 28 Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) meeting. The federal funds rate affects how banks and financial institutions set rates, including mortgage rates, but a change doesn’t guarantee mortgage rates will move in tandem.

The 10-Year Treasury Yield has the greatest impact on mortgage rates as lenders add a spread — or percentage markup — on top of it. The spread reflects the effects of monetary and fiscal policies, economic growth, inflation, higher origination costs and the gap between mortgage-backed securities (MBS) and Treasury yields.

“Whether the Fed hikes or holds this month, homebuyers shouldn’t expect a big change in mortgage rates,” First American Senior Economist Sam Williamson told Inman on Wednesday after the Fed’s FOMC meeting. “With another hike widely expected in December and further increases possible next year, borrowing costs are likely to remain elevated, keeping many buyers and sellers on the sidelines. But not everyone has the luxury of waiting. New jobs, growing families and other life events will keep some buyers moving forward, even as higher rates delay moves that can wait.”

Jones said mortgage rates will remain “the swing factor” and will shape next year’s American Community Survey results.

“For rates to trend lower, inflation has to cool, and the latest data shows it is moving the wrong way,” she said. “Annual inflation rose to 3.7 percent in September as energy prices surged amid the conflict in the Middle East, and core inflation edged up to 2.6 percent.”

“With the Fed focused on bringing inflation back under control while protecting the labor market, a significant drop in mortgage rates is unlikely in the near term,” she added. “For buyers on the fence, though, today’s mix of more inventory, more price cuts and more room to negotiate is the best they’ve had in years.”

#5619. Amid ‘tough market,’ Rocket revenues are up

Rocket’s Q3 earnings, explained: Revenue, market share, Redfin metrics and the questions agents should be asking about the integrated model.

Detroit-based Rocket Companies on Thursday announced its third-quarter 2026 earnings, and despite being in what CEO Varun Krishna said “might be the toughest mortgage market in 30 years,” revenues increased.

The company generated net revenue of $3.28 billion and adjusted revenue of $2.57 billion; net income was $709 million and adjusted net income was $419 million. The company’s Q3 adjusted EBITDA was $748 million (a 29 percent margin, up from 28 percent from last quarter).

Rocket also reported $11.4 billion in liquidity (a record), including $2.7 billion in cash and cash equivalents.

“Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance, quarter over quarter and year over year, and delivered our highest profitability margin in nearly five years, even as mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high,” Krishna said in a statement. “We didn’t spend the last three years waiting for rates to fall. We acquired distribution, connected real estate and mortgage, and invested heavily in technology.”

The company’s third-quarter net income compares with a $124 million loss in the same period of 2025.

“The market is literally testing every single lender,” Krishna said during the company’s earnings call Thursday. “If you have a strong business model, it’s gonna shine through, but if you have a flaw, it’s gonna get exposed.”

He pointed to Redfin as a source of new mortgage clients. “Redfin is the doorway to Rocket,” Krishna said. According to the company, the number of Redfin visitors who started a purchase mortgage from a listing rose 50 percent year over year. Cumulative unique listings displayed through Rocket’s partnership with Compass reached nearly 40,000, up from about 25,000 in the prior quarter.

Brian Brown, Rocket’s president, chief financial officer and treasurer, said the fourth quarter will come in well below the third, with refinance volume falling as much as 50 percent. Rocket expects adjusted revenue between $2.1 billion and $2.3 billion for the period. “The fourth quarter will be harder still,” Brown said. “We’re ready for it.”

In Q2 2026 earnings, Rocket Companies reported $2.78 billion in revenue for a $229 million profit, up from $34 million year over year. Company executives credited its broker partners with more than $2 billion in net rate lock volume through its Compass partnership, a three-year collaboration undertaken in February.

In March, Rocket and Redfin joined Compass International Holdings in writing an open letter to multiple listing service leaders, urging them to support phased listing distribution and stop fining agents for what they called “seller-directed marketing plans.”

Rocket Companies now encompasses Rocket Mortgage, the U.S.’s largest lender, which includes Mr. Cooper, the country’s largest mortgage servicer, acquired just over a year ago; Redfin’s brokerage and home search portal; Rocket Close, its title and closing company; and Rocket Money and Rocket Loans, its consumer finance brands.

Christy Murdock and Lucy Cohen Blatter contributed to this story.

#5618. CrowdStrike to acquire cybersecurity startups Fiddler AI, Dreadnode for reported $495M

CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. today disclosed plans to buy Fiddler AI Inc. and Dreadnode Inc., two startups that specialize in securing artificial intelligence agents.

The company announced the deals alongside an update to its Falcon Guardian product.

The Wall Street Journal reported that CrowdStrike will spend $495 million on the acquisitions. Fiddler is believed to account for about four-fifths of that sum. The Palo Alto, California-based startup sells a platform that developers use to test their AI agents for risks before launching them. The software spots issues such as malicious AI-generated code and training data leaks.

Fiddler can try different model and configuration combinations to find the one that minimizes an agent’s risk level. If the agent still generates prompts that breach cybersecurity rules, developers can use the platform to study the reasoning workflow that produced them. Fiddler says that its software makes it easier to identify the specific processing step that went wrong and fix it.

Once an agent is in production, Fiddler uses a series of custom models called Centor to block threats. It filters malicious prompts and blocks harmful output. According to the company, Centor adds less than 80 milliseconds of latency to the requests it reviews.

“As AI security and observability converge, enterprises need to understand their agents’ actions, intervene when they go off course, and explain why,” said Fiddler co-founder and Chief Executive Officer Krishna Gade.

Dreadnode, the other startup that CrowdStrike is acquiring, takes a different approach to securing AI agents. Whereas Fiddler analyzes agents’ prompt processing workflows to identify erroneous steps, Dreadnode launches simulated cyberattacks to reveal vulnerabilities. The company says that its platform uses more than 100 breach tactics to identify weak points.

Dreadnode also looks for vulnerabilities in the MCP servers that an AI agent uses to carry out its work. The platform ranks the issues that it finds by severity, which enables administrators to fix the most urgent ones first.

CrowdStrike plans to integrate Dreadnode’s technology into its Falcon Guardian product. The latter tool can map out the AI agents in a company’s technology environment and ensure that they meet cybersecurity standards. According to CrowdStrike, Falcon Guardian will use vulnerability data from Dreadnode to generate cybersecurity improvement recommendations.

The product is also receiving a second new feature that CrowdStrike revealed in conjunction with the two acquisitions. The AI Kill Switch, as it’s called, enables administrators to manually shut down an AI agent that is exhibiting risky behavior. The feature can also be used to remove the agent’s network access and prevent it from relaunching.

“CrowdStrike introduces a decisive new way to rapidly disrupt dangerous AI activity when risk emerges,” Michael Devins, a director of product marketing at CrowdStrike, explained in a blog post. “This is the first step toward broader enforcement to coordinate containment across the endpoints, identities, cloud environments, SaaS applications, and browsers where agents operate.”

#5617. I analyzed 1,133 Instagram posts with Meta’s new AI

Meta Muse for Small Business connects to your Instagram analytics. Here are five prompts to analyze your past posts before asking AI to create more.

Meta quietly released something at the end of September that I think a lot of real estate agents are going to want to play with.

It’s called Meta Muse for Small Business, and while there are plenty of AI tools that can help you brainstorm a Reel or write a caption, what is massive about Muse is that it can connect directly to your Instagram professional account analytics, along with your Facebook Pages, Meta ad accounts and other business tools.

I connected mine and started playing with it, but instead of asking it to make more content, which is how I use AI most of the time, I wanted to see what would happen if I used it to understand all the content I had already made.

Eventually, we analyzed 1,133 of my Instagram posts. It helped me understand why my rolling views had fallen from roughly 4 million to 2.46 million, showed me that at least 27 of my 98 newest followers were real estate professionals, and identified patterns in the topics and formats that have historically performed best for me.

That was when I realized I had probably been using AI backward. If you have been consistently creating content for a few years, you already have your own data set of what works and what doesn’t, so before asking AI for another 10 Reel ideas, there may be more value in asking it to help you understand what your audience has already told you.

Here are five prompts I’m using to do that.

“Analyze my Instagram performance over the past 90 days. Don’t give me content recommendations yet. First tell me where the biggest weakness is between reach, engagement, profile visits, follower growth and conversion, and show me the data that led you to that conclusion.”

A few months ago, my Instagram analytics showed roughly 4 million views in a 30-day window, and more recently that number had fallen to about 2.46 million, so naturally my first reaction was that something wasn’t working.

The story was a little different once I dug into the data. Some of my biggest posts, including videos with more than 1 million views, had simply aged out of the rolling reporting period. I would love to tell you I publish a million-view video every week, and I’m working on it, but I don’t.

My views were down, but roughly 84 percent were still coming from non-followers, and my content had reached more than 1.4 million accounts. The point wasn’t to ignore the decline; it was to understand what was causing it before changing a strategy that might not actually be broken.

“Analyze my most recent followers, and group them into the most common audience types you can identify. Don’t assume who my target audience is. Tell me what the data shows.”

We pulled roughly 100 of my newest followers, and of the 98 we could analyze, at least 27 had Realtor, real estate, broker or realty directly in their name or username.

Initially, I wondered whether that was a problem because I sell houses and still want consumers seeing my content, but last year we closed roughly $12 million in sales volume from referrals, and relationships with other agents have also created speaking opportunities, partnerships and other revenue. Trying to get rid of an audience already producing real business made very little sense.

Instead, I’m leaning into it while becoming more intentional about building consumer-focused lead pillars through my local Dana Point Daddy page and YouTube.

I’m also still making consumer-focused and humorous content on my main account because my past clients, database, sphere, friends and family are seeing and engaging with it. We’re still marketing directly to our database, hosting client events and doing the things that generate real estate business outside social media.

Your unexpected audience might be completely different from mine, but you probably shouldn’t decide whether the audience you’re building is good or bad until you know who is in it and what that audience is worth to your business.

“Analyze my highest-performing posts from the last year and group them by topic, format and hook. Tell me what patterns repeat among my winners and which patterns I seem to be underusing.”

I spend an embarrassing amount of time studying other creators, saving their posts and trying to understand why something went viral, while apparently not spending nearly enough time studying the years of content I already had telling me what my own audience responds to.

We analyzed 447 of my carousel and single graphic posts and isolated 103 that used headline-style hooks. The winners repeatedly included income statistics that create sticker shock, local rankings people want to agree or disagree with, surprising changes in the Southern California housing market and California housing policies translated into something useful for homeowners.

This October, Inman turns its focus to AI and its rapid rise in real estate. During Artificial Intelligence Month, we’re digging into the startups shaking things up and the established players folding AI into their offerings.

I don’t need to make variations of those posts forever, but I can look for new topics that share the DNA of things my own audience has already told me it wants instead of constantly trying to recreate somebody else’s viral post.

“Compare how frequently I publish each content format with how those formats actually perform. Where is my time allocation inconsistent with my results?”

At the time of the analysis, I had published 66 times over 28 days, and Reels were the format I was publishing most frequently even though they weren’t my best-performing format. Carousels were.

I’m not going to stop making Reels because different content has different jobs, but if I’m deciding where to spend another hour this week, I should probably know whether the format consuming most of my time is producing my best results.

“Based only on the patterns you identified in my historically best-performing content, give me 10 new content ideas. For each one, tell me which past pattern it is based on and why you think it fits my audience.”

This is where the first four prompts become useful instead of just interesting because I can ask any AI tool for 10 content ideas and it will happily give them to me, but without context it is essentially making an educated guess.

Once it understands what my audience has historically responded to, I can ask a much better question: What should I make next based on what has already worked for me?

I’m still going to experiment, tell personal stories and make something weird because I think it’s funny, but now my own history gets a vote.

Meta Muse for Small Business has only been out for about a month, so I am sure I’m barely scratching the surface of what I can do with it, but this experiment has already changed the way I’m using AI.

If you’ve been consistently posting for a few years, you may already have hundreds or thousands of experiments sitting inside your Instagram, so before asking AI for another hook, caption or content idea, ask it to help you understand those experiments first.

For me, the most interesting thing AI has done for my content lately isn’t helping me create more of it. It’s helping me make better decisions about what I create next.

Krys Benyamein is a Realtor with Allstars Realty in Southern California. Get connected on Instagram or LinkedIn.

#5616. Housing Market Feels the Chill as Buyers Pull Back—but Sellers Are Not Panicking Yet

The national housing market is feeling the chill as high borrowing costs are forcing frustrated buyers to throw in the towel, yet sellers are largely digging in to wait out the slump.

Two key metrics—price cuts and delistings—tell the story of American home sellers' resilience in the face of adversity this fall.

Across the U.S., about 4.4% of active listings were pulled off the market in October, down from 4.6% a year ago, according to the latest Realtor.com® monthly housing market trends report released on Wednesday.

On a monthly basis, the delisting rate has ticked up slightly from 4% in September, in line with typical seasonal trends, but no more than that, even with mortgage rates well exceeding 7% and buyer demand waning.

According to Realtor.com senior economist Jake Krimmel, delistings matter because they act as a canary in the coal mine. A jump in the delistings rate could be a sign of a housing market in distress.

However, the October findings show that sellers are not ready to take their ball and go home yet.

"Job relocations, family circumstances, and financial challenges are among the top reasons I am seeing sellers stay on the market rather than withdraw and wait until spring," Josh Stimpson, a real estate agent at The Realtive Group of Reliant Realty in Nashville, TN, tells Realtor.com. "The rising cost of living is also a major factor, prompting many sellers to seek more affordable housing."

The other key data point used to assess the strength of the U.S. housing market is price cuts.

According to the latest housing market data, much like with delistings, there has not been a dramatic change up or down in the share of listings offering discounts, although it remained elevated.

For the fourth consecutive month, more than 1 in 5 active listings (20.5%) saw a price cut, marking the highest October reading since 2022 and the second highest this year, trailing only September, which set a four-year record.

However, Krimmel points out that the national price cut rate actually retreated 0.3 percentage points month over month, snapping a nine-month streak of monthly gains. Annually, the share of active listings with price cuts ticked up by just 0.2 percentage points.

Sellers "are getting used to not everything selling quickly," Learka Bosnak, an agent with of Heather & Learka Team at Douglas Elliman in Beverly Hills, CA, tells Realtor.com. "They aren’t seeing compelling evidence that a slightly lower price will lead to a quick sale. Plus, they aren't feeling a lot of pressure monthly because so many have low-interest-rate mortgages."

Taken together, the October delisting and price cut readouts lead to one conclusion concerning the present state of the market.

"Right now, it looks more like a seller pause than an exodus," says Krimmel. "Sellers are disengaging rather than showing signs of distress."

Regionally, price reductions remained least common in the systemically undersupplied Northeast (16.8% of listings) and most common in the West (21.9%), with the Midwest and South falling in between at 21% each.

Across the 50 largest metro markets, 12 saw price cuts on a quarter or more of the listings, unchanged from September. Thirty-four of the metros are running above their year-ago cut rate, down from 36 in September.

At the local level, price discounts in October were most common in Indianapolis (31.8%), Denver (31.3%), and Portland, OR (31.1%).

While the delisting and price cut numbers stop short of signaling a panic among sellers, October trends do point to a noticeable pullback.

New listings—a measure of homeowners putting their properties on the market—dropped 9.5% from September and 7.5% from a year ago, marking the steepest decline in more than three years.

"Sellers know this is a poor time to list, and you do not list into weak demand unless you need to," notes Krimmel.

At the same time, pending sales plunged 10.5% year over year—the biggest annual drop since October 2023.

However, active listings jumped 7.4% year over year, topping 1.18 million homes for sale—the fourth consecutive month of accelerated growth. This reflects properties piling up on the market as buyers see their purchasing power diminished by surging 30-year mortgage rates, which averaged 7.33% in October.

For context, that is a staggering 107 basis points above October 2025 levels and 53 basis points higher than at the start of September.

"Elevated interest rates and ongoing affordability challenges have caused many buyers to pause, and the midterm election may be adding to that hesitation," notes Stimpson. "As a result, showing activity has declined and days on market are rising, particularly in Nashville and the surrounding areas."

However, patient buyers willing to stick it out can still find attractive deals and see their negotiating position strengthened.

"Buyers can often retain their inspection, appraisal, and financing contingencies while also requesting additional repairs, a longer closing period, or a home warranty," says Stimpson. "Properties with extended market exposure may offer even greater leverage, including opportunities to negotiate a lower purchase price or secure seller concessions."

Looking ahead to late fall and winter, the Nashville agent says there are some encouraging signs on the horizon, including gradually easing mortgage rates, closings holding steady in Middle Tennessee, and premium listings continuing to attract multiple offers.

Yet, both Stimpson and Bosnak agree that what the market sorely lacks is a sense of certainty.

"No one is sure what the market or the world will look like in a year, so it doesn’t feel weird to lean into that wait-and-see part of human nature," says the Beverly Hills agent.

Snejana Farberov is a reporter at Realtor.com covering the U.S. housing market and the latest domestic real estate trends. She has worked as a general assignment journalist in New York City and Long Island for 16 years, writing for New York Post, Daily Mail, and News 12. Snejana earned bachelor's degrees in journalism and Italian from St. John's University, followed by a master’s degree from Columbia University School of Journalism.

#5615. A Halloween tale: Spooky events and a haunted house sale

Author and trainer Bernice Ross shares a spooky tale of unusual home happenings and a sale process plagued by tragedy.

When you’re in the real estate business, sooner or later there will be a house that someone says is haunted. The story below is true. Were these events just coincidence, or were they something else?

When I was working on my doctorate, my closest friend and study partner was living in a new house in Orange County. She was in the antique business. Her home was like a showcase, every last inch of it beautifully decorated. When I met her, she was in the process of getting a divorce.

Although her house was a little over a year old, it already had the makings of a strange history. While the house was being built, a little girl was sexually assaulted in it. A few months after she and her husband moved in, he became manic-depressive.

Over the next few months, he had numerous confrontations with the police. He refused to take his meds. Unbeknownst to his wife, he placed a warranty deed on the property to access part of the equity. He then took off to Hawaii, where he was reportedly living in the bush outside the Honolulu airport.

We would normally study together at her house about twice per month. The lights would flicker periodically. If we went out for dinner, it was common for pieces of the furniture to be moved away from the wall.

Since my friend had changed the locks and placed a security system on the house, there was no one who had access to move the furniture. There was also a window in the family room overlooking the canyon that would vibrate for no apparent reason. You could put your hand on the window and tell it to stop vibrating, and it did.

After spending the afternoon preparing for our upcoming qualifying exams, we decided to go out to dinner to take a break. When we returned, the lights were flickering, and a number of pieces of furniture were moved again.

As we sat back down to hit the books again, there was a loud rustling in the garage where she refinished her antiques. Her German shepherd, a very mellow dog who never barked, started barking and scratching crazily at the door to the garage.

Although this didn’t disturb my friend, I made sure the dog was between me and whatever was in the garage. As soon as she opened the door, the dog broke away from me and raced into the garage. The dog raced to the other side of the garage, sat down and acted as if nothing had happened.

After consuming a carton of chocolate ice cream to soothe our jangled nerves, we decided to watch a movie — The Ghost of Flight 401. This probably wasn’t the smartest movie choice, but that was the best of the evening’s shows back in the days of seven TV channels and no cable.

As I was getting ready to leave, we were standing by the front door adjacent to the stairway. Her stairs had beautiful wrought iron work topped with a heavy oak banister.

As we were standing there talking, the banister and the wrought iron started to vibrate. Everything else in the house was still. I turned and asked her, “Do you see what I see?” She did.

We were both mesmerized because nothing else was moving. This went on for about five minutes, and then it stopped. At that point, I was out of there, and there was no way I was going back.

My friend wanted out of the house. Needless to say, there were numerous challenges that had to be addressed before she could legally sell the property. California law allowed her to list the property, but both she and her husband had to sign the grant deed to close the transaction.

The lender who held the warranty deed was demanding payment as per the terms of the note. Normally, their option would have been to foreclose. The challenge was that the police reports documented the fact that the husband was probably not legally competent at the time he signed the deed.

Since he was nowhere to be found, my friend and the lender petitioned the court to order the sale as part of the divorce proceedings. The court granted her request.

The house was listed and finally went under contract. The buyer was a deputy sheriff. Two days after opening escrow on the property, the escrow officer had a heart attack and died. The title officer handling the file also had a heart attack but recovered.

About four weeks into the transaction, the deputy sheriff’s right arm became mysteriously paralyzed. He saw several specialists, but no one could find a cause for the problem. He was forced to take disability leave from his job. This meant he didn’t have sufficient income to qualify for the loan. The transaction was canceled. Within a few days after he canceled, the paralysis disappeared.

After almost a year, the house finally sold. The buyer was a psychiatrist.

Fortunately, this transaction took place prior to California passing its disclosure laws. I have to wonder how you would make those disclosures today. Much of what happened could be coincidence. I still don’t have an explanation for the moved furniture, the strange window and, most of all, the vibrating staircase. Perhaps it’s just as well that I don’t.

Bernice Ross is president and CEO of BrokerageUP and RealEstateCoach.com, the founder of Profit.RealEstate and a national speaker, author and trainer with over 1,500 published articles.

#5614. AI cloud startup Applied Compute raises $350M after reaching key revenue milestone

Applied Compute Inc., a fast-growing provider of artificial intelligence infrastructure, has raised $350 million in funding at a $3.25 billion valuation.

The startup announced the deal on Monday. Prominent angel investor Elad Gil led the round with participation from Nvidia Corp., Shopify Ventures, HubSpot Ventures and more than a dozen others.

Applied Compute operates a cloud platform that developers use to train large language models and perform inference, the process of running the models to provide responses to queries. Additionally, it has a team of machine learning researchers that can lend customers a hand with their projects. The group takes on tasks such as creating quality evaluations for newly developed models.

The software stack that AI researchers use to train LLMs usually comprises two main components. One creates multiple copies of the model, assigns a different task to each one and turns the results into training data. The other component uses that training data to refine the LLM’s weights. The two components usually run synchronously, which means that each one has to wait for the other to complete its work before launching.

Applied Compute’s platform uses a more efficient training approach called asynchronous reinforcement learning. It enables a training stack’s data generation and weight adjustment components to run at the same time, which speeds up LLM development. Additionally, the platform supports a second optimization method called self-distillation. It removes the need for teacher models, specialized neural networks that researchers use to supervise LLM training runs.

A built-in AI assistant automates repetitive aspects of customers’ work. It can, for example, summarize what new skills an LLM learned during a training run. Uncovering that information usually requires researchers to review lengthy reasoning logs.

Applied Computing’s platform also lends itself to running inference workloads. An autoscaling engine automatically adjusts the amount of hardware allocated to a model based on user traffic. A so-called online RL feature uses the prompts that the LLM receives to fine-tune its weights periodically, which keeps it aligned with customer requirements.

The company offers its training and inference features alongside a model router called Shift-1. It enables coding agents to send each user request to the LLM that can fulfill it in the most cost-efficient manner. Furthermore, it can split complex tasks among multiple LLMs.

Applied Computing disclosed in its funding announcement that its annualized recurring revenue has topped $100 million. The company, which launched less than 18 months ago, counts Microsoft Corp., DoorDash Inc. and other major tech firms as customers. It will use the newly raised capital to grow its market presence and buy more infrastructure.

“Training, inference, and routing are the first pieces of a much larger stack,” Applied Compute founders Rhythm Garg, Yash Patil and Linden Li wrote in a blog post. “We’re building the AI infrastructure every company will need to fully own their intelligence, from the models themselves to the systems that run, monitor and secure them.”

#5613. EXCLUSIVE: Food Network Star Alex Guarnaschelli Reveals Her Secrets To Turning Any Home Into a Holiday Entertaining Hub

Turning your home into a welcoming holiday gathering spot doesn’t have to mean buying new decorations or finding room for a formal dining setup.

For Alex Guarnaschelli, a few thoughtful touches—and some planning before the doorbell rings—can help hosts make the most of their space and enjoy the celebration themselves.

In an exclusive interview with Realtor.com®, the celebrity chef shared her advice for entertaining on a budget, organizing a busy kitchen, and keeping guests comfortable in smaller homes.

“I always think a welcoming home is about the little details, not how much money you spend," she said.Her first suggestion is to adjust the lighting before guests arrive.

"A few candles or lamps instead of bright overhead lighting can completely change the feeling of a room," she explained.

When it comes to decorations, Guarnaschelli recommends looking for items that can serve another purpose once the party ends.

“Second, bring something natural into the space," she said. "I love the idea of filling a bowl with beautiful oranges, pomegranates, or even fresh herbs from the grocery store. They're inexpensive, they look festive, and you can actually use them afterward.”

Making guests comfortable from the moment they enter is another priority.

“And third, think about what your guests experience when they arrive. Have a place for coats and bags, put on some music, and make sure there's something to eat or drink right away,” she advised.

“You don't need a house that looks like a magazine. You just want people to walk in and feel like they're in the right place.”

That thoughtful approach extends to the kitchen, where Guarnaschelli starts by considering how each dish fits into the cooking schedule.

“I like to think of my kitchen almost like a restaurant kitchen before service. Everything should have a purpose and a place,” she explained. “I start by looking at what I'm making and working backward. What needs the oven? What needs the stove? What can stay in the refrigerator until the last minute? You don't want three dishes competing for the same burner when everyone's ready to eat.”

She also recommends deciding how food will be presented before it is ready to leave the kitchen.

“I also pull out the serving dishes ahead of time and decide what goes where. Sometimes I'll even put a little note in each platter so I don't have to think about it later. And clear your counters!” she added.

Choosing equipment that handles several tasks can also help keep the cooking area manageable.

Guarnaschelli points to a piece from her new HSN collection as an example.

“That's also why I love versatile tools, like the sauté pan from my new HSN collection. You can use it for everything from searing chicken to sautéing vegetables or making a quick sauce, without having to pull out a different pan for every dish,” she says. “A little organization and the right tools can make the whole evening feel easier.”

For those entertaining in an apartment or smaller home, Guarnaschelli suggests spreading refreshments across different areas to prevent guests from gathering around the stove.

“The trick to entertaining in a small space is to give people a reason to spread out. If you put the drinks, appetizers, and main course all next to the stove, you're going to end up with a crowd exactly where you’re cooking!”

A side table can become a drink station, while appetizers can encourage guests to mingle elsewhere.

“I would put drinks in the living room, maybe on a bar cart or even a cleared-off side table, and keep a few appetizers somewhere else. A cheese board is great because people can help themselves without needing you to do anything,” she explained.

Guarnaschelli also recommends making use of vertical space when arranging the food.

“I also love using different heights when setting out food. A cake stand or a raised platter can give you more room without taking over the entire table," she added.

And hosts needn’t feel pressured to create a traditional seated dinner.

“Don't feel like everyone needs a formal seat at the same time. Sometimes a more relaxed, casual setup makes for the best party," the chef noted.

Preparing ahead can further reduce the number of tasks competing for a host’s attention. For Guarnaschelli, the day before a gathering is an opportunity to work through smaller jobs.

“The day before a party is when I like to tackle all the little jobs that have a way of piling up. Wash your herbs, measure out ingredients, make your salad dressing, and get your serving dishes ready.”

She also uses equipment from her collection to help with ingredient preparation.

“This is also where a tool like the cordless chopper from my new HSN collection really comes in handy," she added. "You can get through chopping onions, herbs, and other ingredients for your recipes without spending the entire afternoon doing prep work.”

Depending on the menu, some cooking can be completed ahead of time, too.

“You can even prepare things like a soup or a braised dish that will taste better the next day because the flavors have had time to come together," the food guru revealed.

Before filling the kitchen with prepared dishes, however, Guarnaschelli recommended checking that there is somewhere to store them.

“I also like to make sure the refrigerator has enough room for everything before I start cooking. That's one of those things nobody thinks about until they're trying to squeeze a giant platter onto a shelf that's already full.”

On the day of the gathering, she focuses on dishes that need to be finished close to serving.

“For the day of, save the things that really need your attention, like roasting meat, crisping up potatoes, or finishing vegetables. Anything that needs to be hot and fresh should get that last bit of care," the chef said.

Her final suggestion is to leave enough time to welcome guests without simultaneously scrambling to finish the meal.

“Give yourself a little buffer before guests arrive," she said. "You don't want to be pulling something out of the oven with one hand while answering the door with the other.”

Kelsi Karruli is a senior celebrity reporter who joined Realtor.com in 2025. She writes about trends encompassing real estate and celebrity properties. She previously wrote for Daily Mail, True Urban Culture, and JMedia Corporation, where she specialized in covering celebrities, relationships, psychology, and gender issues. She has a bachelor's degree in journalism from Pace University, where she received the James Rose Award for excellence in journalism. When she isn’t updating readers on A-listers' moves, she is spending time with her cat, Mary, and cheering on the Albanian soccer team.

#5612. ‘Haunted as a matter of law’: How real estate agents handle stigmatized listings in 2026

Stigmatized homes have long sold at a steep discount. Agents and attorneys say an unaffordable, low-inventory 2026 market may be shrinking it.

Many may assume that the rule of thumb on stigmatized homes is simple: A murder, suicide or infamous ghost story knocks a big chunk off the price. Real estate agents who’ve sold these homes say it’s more complicated, and today’s unaffordable, short-on-inventory market may be shrinking the discount.

A “stigmatized” property can mean many things. It can be a home tied to a violent crime, a suicide, a notorious former owner or an alleged haunting.

Would you live in the Amityville Horror house, where Ronald DeFeo Jr. killed six members of his family in 1974?

Or what about the Menendez mansion in Beverly Hills, where Lyle and Erik Menendez killed their parents, José and Kitty, in 1989, a case that has stayed in the headlines for more than three decades?

These gruesome crimes may not always change the bedroom count or the square footage. But they can change who’s willing to buy, and for how much.

Ahead of Halloween, Inman asked real estate agents and attorneys how they handle stigmatized listings in 2026.

Their answers suggest the discount is real but uneven. It often depends less on the stigma itself than on how many buyers it drives away. And in a market with increasingly few affordable options, fewer buyers may be walking away.

The best-known estimate for stigmatized listings comes from real estate economist Randall Bell, who has put the typical “murder-house” discount at 10 to 25 percent. Bell has also said he’s seen some stigmatized homes sell at full value — usually smaller, more affordable homes — while others sit unsold for a long time.

Bell is an expert on real estate damage, earning the nickname “Master of Disaster,” and he runs the advisory firm Landmark Research. He has consulted on some of the most notorious crime-linked properties in history, from the Rancho Santa Fe mansions where the bodies of 39 Heaven’s Gate cult members were found to the home of Sandy Hook shooter Adam Lanza.

While Bell’s estimates are frequently cited, academic research suggests the price discount effect on stigmatized properties may fade over time.

A 2020 study of Tokyo apartment buildings by economist Taisuke Sadayuki found that a homicide in one unit initially cut rents on other units in the same building by about 10 percent, with the effect disappearing after roughly seven to eight years.

Survey data suggests buyers may also be less squeamish than agents assume. In a 2023 Zillow survey, 67 percent of prospective buyers said they could be persuaded to buy a “haunted” house with the right features, location or price.

When Inman covered stigmatized homes more than a decade ago, we framed them as bargains. The market has changed a lot since then.

Rebecca Chambliss, an agent with Carmody Real Estate in the Santa Monica, California, area, recently sold a home in a gated community where the previous owner had died by suicide only a few months before it was listed. All of the neighbors knew.

Chambliss disclosed the death to serious buyers who were discussing an offer. In her experience, buyers don’t spread out along a spectrum of tolerance. They split into two groups.

“Some people will never buy a home where a suicide or other non-natural death occurred no matter what, and then there are people who it doesn’t bother,” Chambliss told Inman. “There aren’t people in between.”

One interested buyer made an unexpected offer. When Chambliss disclosed the death, he demanded to know exactly where in the house it happened and how. Chambliss had chosen not to learn those details herself and told him as much. He wouldn’t move forward without them and withdrew the offer.

The home did eventually sell at a discount because of the suicide, Chambliss said. The buyer understood that he’d have to disclose the death if he ever sold. He relisted it about a year later, asking $1 million more than he paid, and the home still hasn’t sold.

Chambliss also brought in an energy clearer before marketing the home. It’s a reminder that for some agents, handling a stigmatized listing takes more than paperwork.

The discount doesn’t always stay with the property. Sometimes a savvy investor who knows about it collects it.

Jonathan Carcone, principal of 4 Brothers Buy Houses and a licensed agent in Washington state, bought a home in Poulsbo, Washington, with local ghost stories attached.

He said the home was listed at $640,000, while comparable homes were selling for about $650,000. Carcone said the listing didn’t mention ghost stories, but neighbors told him about them.

Carcone used the ghost stories in negotiations and bought the house for $585,000, about 9 percent below list and roughly 10 percent below comps.

Carcone’s company buys, renovates and sells dozens of houses every year, including “challenging properties.” After renovating the house in Poulsbo, he sold it for $660,000 about two months later.

“The ghost stories had no influence on the sale, and we made a good profit,” Carcone told Inman.

He said Washington law doesn’t require agents to disclose a home’s reputation, including ghost stories, so he didn’t. No buyer asked about it during showings, either. So, in this case, Carcone used the stigma to his advantage.

Because the resale price reflects a renovation, it isn’t a clean before-and-after comparison. Still, the pattern is worth noting. The seller absorbed a 10 percent discount for the stigma, and the next buyer paid none.

What agents must disclose for stigmatized properties varies widely by state.

California sets a three-year line. Under California Civil Code Section 1710.2, sellers and agents aren’t required to disclose a death that occurred on the property more than three years before a buyer’s offer. They also can’t be sued for staying silent. Whether it must be disclosed depends on whether it’s material, and the common practice is to disclose to be safe.

Answering a direct question is a separate matter. The law doesn’t protect anyone who lies when asked.

“The main point of contention between sellers and buyers is whether answering questions truthfully violates the seller’s wishes,” Nick Heimlich, founder and attorney of San Jose, California-based Nick Heimlich Law, told Inman. “Under California Civil Code, a seller’s agent cannot refuse to answer questions about the property’s history.”

Texas Property Code Section 5.008(c) says a seller or seller’s agent has no duty to disclose a death on the property from natural causes, suicide or an accident unrelated to the property’s condition. But not homicide, which may still be a material fact that must be disclosed.

Tennessee goes further. Tenn. Code Ann. § 66-5-207 lists a homicide, felony or suicide on the property among the things sellers don’t have to disclose. It also covers any act or occurrence that didn’t affect the property’s physical structure.

Ghost stories bring their own risk. In the famous case of Stambovsky v. Ackley (1991), a New York appellate court let a buyer back out of buying an allegedly haunted home in Nyack, New York.

The seller had publicized the ghost stories herself in Reader’s Digest and the local press, then didn’t tell the out-of-town buyer. In effect, the court held that because she’d told everyone else the house was haunted, it was haunted as a matter of law.

Donald Leeth, managing partner at Leeth & Gaglione, has spent 27 years as a criminal defense attorney and former prosecutor in Monroe County, Pennsylvania, and the Poconos. During that time, he’s encountered many homes where crimes took place. He advises disclosing rather than gambling on the legal minimum.

“It’s always best to be honest up front so you’re not dealing with misrepresentation claims once your transaction has closed,” Leeth said.

The more interesting question for 2026 is whether affordability is eroding the discount stigmatized listings usually have.

Median prices for new and existing homes now both top $400,000, according to Harvard University’s Joint Center for Housing Studies. Existing-home prices have climbed 54 percent nationwide since 2020 and sit at nearly five times median income, well above the 3-to-1 ratio that held in the 1990s.

Leeth thinks the affordability crisis is negating the discount effect on stigmatized listings.

“Many buyers won’t care if there’s an infamous story behind a house because they simply don’t have other options,” he said. “Stigma isn’t as much of a factor as it once was because the price will determine what someone buys.”

That fits with Chambliss’s two-camp theory. If the buyers who’ll never consider a stigmatized home stay out no matter what, the discount depends on how many buyers are left in the other camp. In a tight, low-inventory market, more buyers are in that camp, and they may have fewer alternatives.

Heimlich said the type of event still matters. Buyers might shrug at a home that sat empty for a long time, he said, but something like a murder “can severely influence the property value.”

Still, he added, it likely depends on the market. And if stigma leads to a bargain, that helps, too.

“Some buyers may be willing to invest in stigmatized real estate if it falls within an affordable price range,” Heimlich said.

For agents, the practical takeaway is that a stigmatized listing’s real challenge is finding the buyers who don’t care, not pricing in a fixed discount, and disclosing in a way that doesn’t create legal exposure after closing.

Sometimes the stigma bothers the buyer’s friends and family more than the buyer themselves.

Years ago, Chambliss, the California-based agent, sold a home where a murder had taken place in the front yard. The buyer was a young single father whose Italian immigrant parents were involved in the buying process and may have been helping with the purchase. Chambliss took him outside and told him what had happened there.

He became very concerned, then immediately asked, “Do you have to tell my parents?”

His whole body relaxed, and he laughed. Then he said, “OK, I have no issue with it. But my parents would never let me buy this house if they knew.”

He bought the house, and Chambliss assumed he never told them.

#5611. This 83-Acre Blue Ridge Mountain Wedding Estate Is Heading to Auction With No Reserve

Imagine hosting a wedding or lavish event for 150 friends and family right on your very own Blue Ridge Mountain farm.

That could become a reality as an 83.56-acre property with a 5,000-square-foot event barn in Franklin, NC, heads to auction with no reserve on Nov. 7.

Created in 2010, Tessentee Farm has multiple structures, including an eight-bedroom primary residence, three two-bedroom guest cabins, and plenty of space to entertain.

"It has a nice big spread of land, so the duality of it also being an income-generating asset is pretty impressive," says Trayor Lesnock, founder and president of Platinum Luxury Auctions, who will host the auction. The listing is held by Isaiah Thomas Johns of Mountain Pro Real Estate Professionals.

The property last changed hands for $2,500,000 in 2013 and had hit the market for $6.9 million in November 2025.

“You have this large house with all the bells and whistles where you could live, an event barn, and three separate cabins where you could host events,” Lesnock says. “There is a good record of the farm being used for weddings and events.”

The luxury event barn, which can be heated and cooled, has hosted everything from destination weddings and rehearsal dinners to milestone celebrations and corporate retreats.

“We have had large families from the Blue Ridge Mountain region look at it and are wanting to use it for multigenerational living,” he notes. “About 50% were looking to use it as a private property and the other 50% were looking at it for the income generation.”

The primary residence has arched doorways, built-ins, French doors, a spacious dining room, a chef's kitchen with a breakfast bar, and a primary suite with a fireplace, soaking tub, and walk-in shower.

Covered terraces overlook the pool, which has a water slide and a swim-up bar, as well as an outdoor kitchen and a hot tub.

“It will probably go to someone who wants to use it privately,” Lesnock adds. “There are no outright restrictions, so you could develop it further.”

The rustic barn has exposed beams, wood-paneled walls, string lighting, and an open field ideal for photos. A ceremony could be held in the pasture, followed by cocktails under the stars, and dinner and dancing inside the barn, with guests retreating to cabins for an overnight stay.

Lesnock says the countryside setting could lend itself to an equestrian estate.

“You could make it more of a farm and add an arena if you wanted,” he says. “Franklin is not an area that pops up on a lot of people’s maps, but it’s in the southern foothills of the Blue Ridge Mountains. Asheville is only an hour away. There is also a creek that borders the property that is excellent for trout fishing.”

Kellie Speed is a contributor to Realtor.com. As a writer and editor, she has worked for a variety of online and print publications, including Inked magazine, Jetset, Westchester magazine, JustLuxe, The Boston Globe, and U.S. Veterans Magazine. A Massachusetts native, Kellie attended Northeastern University for journalism, was previously the Boston editor for Haute Living, and contributed to Avalon Publishing's Moon Metro Boston guidebook. Kellie writes celebrity profiles and covers restaurants, travel, and lifestyle.
