#5594. 7 ways to breathe new life into a listing that isn’t selling

Don’t jump straight to a price cut when you have a listing not selling. These seven strategies refresh your marketing and put it in front of new buyers.

Listing not selling? If I had a listing that had been sitting on the market for 30, 60 or even 90 days, and I needed to get it sold in the next 60 days, I wouldn’t simply keep doing the same things and hope a buyer eventually showed up. I also wouldn’t immediately call the seller and ask for a price reduction.

I’d start by developing a specific plan to create new interest in the home. These are the seven strategies I’d use.

The first thing I’d do is give the listing a completely fresh look. I want someone who has already seen the property online to notice something different when it shows up again.

I’d start with the MLS description. I’d use AI to help me rewrite it to highlight the most compelling features of the property, tell a better story and give potential buyers a reason to schedule a showing.

Act as an expert real estate MLS copywriter. Rewrite the following MLS description in a fresh, creative and compelling way that helps potential buyers imagine living in this home and encourages them to schedule a showing. Avoid generic real estate language, highlight what makes this property unique and naturally include relevant location and property keywords for SEO and AEO optimization. Ask me any questions needed before writing the new description.

Next, I’d also take a close look at the photos and videos. If the property has been on the market for several months, it may be time for new photography, updated staging or a different approach to showcasing the home.

I’d consider whether an accurately represented twilight photo or a newly staged room could make the property more appealing. If AI-assisted photo editing is involved, I’d make sure any alterations are properly disclosed in accordance with MLS rules and accurately represent the property and its surroundings.

One of the simplest changes you can make is updating the primary listing photo. I’d take five or six of the strongest photos and ask other agents which one would most likely make them stop scrolling. Sometimes it’s the front elevation, but sometimes it’s a beautiful outdoor living area, an incredible kitchen or a view that immediately captures someone’s attention.

I’d also refresh the social media posts promoting the home. Instead of recycling the same graphics and captions, I’d create fresh content tailored to each platform where I’m marketing the property.

The goal is simple. Before doing anything else, make the listing look fresh to give people who may have previously overlooked it a reason to take another look.

The next thing I’d do is identify exactly who the most likely buyers are for this property. Instead of marketing the home to everybody, I’d identify two or three distinct buyer groups who might align with its features and benefits.

For example, a home with a first-floor primary suite, a dedicated office and a low-maintenance yard might appeal to several types of buyers for different reasons. One buyer may be focused on working from home. Another may be interested in reducing the amount of exterior maintenance required. A third may value the floor plan and flexibility of the living spaces.

Once I identified the potential buyer groups, I’d use AI to help me understand which property features, lifestyle benefits and potential concerns might matter most to each group. Then I’d ask AI to help me create separate marketing campaigns that speak to those different priorities.

The key is to focus on the property’s features and the benefits they provide, rather than making assumptions about who should live there. That helps keep the marketing inclusive and aligned with fair housing requirements.

This is a different approach from simply posting the same listing description repeatedly and hoping someone responds. We’re identifying what makes the property attractive to different buyers and creating marketing that helps them recognize those benefits.

When you understand what someone is looking for, you can do a much better job of showing them why a particular property deserves their attention.

The third strategy I’d use is a focused, 10-day campaign to make sure the agents most likely to have a buyer for the property know about it.

I’d start by reviewing MLS data to identify agents who have recently sold comparable homes in the area. I’d also look for agents who have active listings or, where available, buyer activity that suggests they’re working with people interested in similar properties.

Then I’d create a list of the agents most likely to have relationships with buyers who might be interested in my listing. Over the next 10 business days, I’d personally call two of those agents every day.

I’d say something like, “Hey, I know you do a lot of business in this neighborhood and price range. I’ve got a listing I wanted to make sure was on your radar. I’d love to get your feedback on it and see if you might have someone who’s looking for something similar.”

That’s 20 personal conversations with agents who have demonstrated experience selling the type of property I’m trying to get sold. I’d also create an email campaign to share the property’s most compelling features with a broader group of agents, using appropriate contact information and respecting communication preferences.

Another opportunity is reaching out to agents who have competing listings. I’d ask what kind of activity they’re seeing and what feedback they’re receiving. I’d also offer to share information about my listing so that if one of their buyers doesn’t find the right fit in their property, they know about mine. And I’d do the same for them.

The goal isn’t simply to promote my listing. It’s to build relationships with agents who are actively working with the buyers I’m trying to reach. Sometimes the best opportunity to sell a home isn’t through another social media post. It’s through a conversation with the agent who already has the right buyer.

One of my favorite ways to generate new interest in a listing is to stop focusing exclusively on the house and start showing what it might feel like to live there. I’d create videos that help potential buyers imagine the experiences the property and its location make possible.

For instance, I might create a video titled, “Here’s what a Saturday could look like living in this home.” The video could start with coffee on the back porch, move to a nearby farmers’ market, showcase a local restaurant for lunch and end with an evening enjoying the outdoor living space.

Another idea might be, “Here’s what date night could look like if you lived here.” The video could highlight nearby restaurants, entertainment or a relaxing evening at home. If the property is close to a park, I’d show the actual route and how convenient it is to get there. If it’s within walking distance of restaurants or shopping, I’d create a short video showcasing that experience.

I’d also think about the lifestyle opportunities inside the home. Maybe there’s a great outdoor kitchen for entertaining, a flexible bonus room or a covered porch that creates a natural gathering place. The key is to help people see something they may have missed when they first looked at the listing photos.

A buyer may not remember that a home has a 12-by-20-foot covered porch. But they may remember the video showing what a Saturday evening with friends could look like in that space.

Features tell people what a home has. Lifestyle marketing helps them imagine what living there could feel like.

The fifth strategy I’d use is finding ways to make the property more financially attractive than competing homes. We hear a lot about affordability, and for many buyers, the challenge isn’t simply the purchase price. It’s the monthly payment, closing costs or the amount of cash required to purchase the home.

That’s why I’d evaluate potential incentives before assuming that a price reduction is the only option. Maybe the seller could offer a closing-cost credit. Maybe a mortgage rate buydown would make the monthly payment more attractive. Maybe covering a portion of the HOA dues or offering an allowable allowance for improvements could help the property stand out.

I’d approach this the way a new-home builder might. Builders don’t always compete exclusively on price. They often use incentives to create a more attractive financial opportunity for buyers. I’d work with the seller and a qualified lender to determine which incentives are appropriate, what they would actually cost and how they compare with a price reduction.

For example, if a seller is considering a $10,000 price reduction, I’d want to know whether a properly structured $10,000 concession could provide greater value to the right buyer. The answer will depend on the buyer’s financing, the property, lender requirements and the local market. But it’s a conversation worth having.

Then I’d make sure those incentives were clearly communicated in the listing and marketing materials, including any important terms or limitations. Sometimes the opportunity isn’t simply making the house less expensive. It’s finding a way to make purchasing the house more attractive.

Once I’ve refreshed the listing, identified ideal buyer groups, connected with active agents and evaluated potential incentives, I’d launch a 21-day marketing blitz. This is where I’d get creative.

The mistake I see agents make is posting the same property photo and listing information over and over again. They may think they’re marketing the property 10 different times, but in reality, they’re often repeating the same message 10 times. I’d rather create 21 different pieces of content that give people different reasons to take notice.

For example, if the home is listed at $450,000, I’d create a video titled, “What does $450,000 buy you in this neighborhood?” Another video might be, “What the listing photos don’t tell you about this home.” I’d create content about the history of the neighborhood, the builder, nearby amenities and what makes the location unique. I’d showcase individual features that deserve more attention and answer questions buyers might have about the property.

I’d also create content comparing the home with other available options in the same price range. The goal would be to help buyers understand the value and opportunities the property offers. Some content would be short-form video. Some might be photo carousels. Some would be longer walkthroughs, neighborhood videos or educational posts.

I’d also use AI to brainstorm additional angles. I’d ask it to develop a 21-day content campaign that highlights the property from different perspectives without simply repeating the same sales message. The goal is to create enough variety that someone who wasn’t interested in the original listing post might see something new that changes their perspective.

One piece of content might attract someone because of the price point. Another might attract someone because of the neighborhood. Another might reveal a feature a buyer didn’t realize the home offered.

That’s a marketing campaign. Not simply posting the same listing over and over again.

If I’ve done everything I can to refresh the marketing, identify potential buyers, communicate with agents, highlight the lifestyle, create financial incentives and execute a 21-day content campaign, but the property still isn’t generating the activity we need, it’s time to have the conversation most agents dread: the price reduction conversation.

But here’s the difference. I don’t want this to be the first time the seller has heard that a price adjustment might become necessary. I’d communicate with them throughout the entire process. Before launching the marketing blitz, I’d explain exactly what we’re going to do and why. I’d also let them know what happens if those efforts don’t generate the results we’re looking for.

“I want you to know we’re going to make a significant push over the next 21 days to create new interest in your home. We’re going to refresh the marketing, reach out to agents who are active in this price range and launch a series of new campaigns. But if we get through that process and still aren’t seeing the activity we need, my responsibility is to bring you the most current market information so you can make the best decision for you and your family.”

That conversation sets the expectation before the difficult decision arrives. I’d actually recommend having a version of this conversation when you first take the listing. I’d explain that we have a comprehensive listing launch program designed to generate exposure and buyer interest. But if the market doesn’t respond the way we expect, we need to be willing to evaluate what it’s telling us.

Then, when the time comes, I’d bring the seller updated comparable sales, competing listings, properties that have gone under contract, showing activity and buyer feedback. I’d explain what the information suggests and present a specific recommendation.

But I wouldn’t simply ask for a price reduction. I’d show the seller what a strategic price improvement could allow us to do. Maybe it means reaching buyers searching in a different price range. Maybe it creates an opportunity to reconnect with agents who previously showed the property. Maybe it gives us a reason to host another open house, relaunch the marketing and communicate the new value proposition. I’d create a list of the specific activities we would execute following the adjustment.

I’d also be strategic about the timing. Depending on the market, I’d consider making the adjustment before the period when buyers are most actively scheduling weekend showings. I’d review the local data and how the major real estate portals display price changes rather than assuming every market or platform behaves the same way.

The important thing is that we’re not simply changing a number in the MLS. We’re using the new price as an opportunity to create renewed interest through a coordinated marketing plan. And ultimately, I’d remind the seller that the decision is theirs. It’s their home, and my responsibility is to give them the best market knowledge, professional guidance and clear recommendations they need to make an informed decision.

When a listing isn’t selling, continuing to do the same things and hoping for a different result isn’t a strategy. Neither is immediately asking the seller for a price reduction without first evaluating what else can be done.

The most important part of this entire process is communication. Your sellers should never wonder what you’re doing to get their home sold or be surprised when you recommend an adjustment. They should know you’re working on their behalf, evaluating the market and doing everything possible to help them achieve their goal.

This is a market that rewards professionals who are willing to think differently, market more creatively and communicate more effectively. Remember, your sellers didn’t hire you simply to market their home. They hired you to help them get it sold. Our job is to bring the creativity, strategy and professional advice necessary to give them the best opportunity to make that happen.

Jimmy Burgess is the Chief Coaching Officer for HomeServices of America and President of Berkshire Hathaway HomeServices. Get connected on Instagram and LinkedIn.

#5593. Jeff Glover goes indie after 17 years with Keller Williams (EXCLUSIVE)

Jeff Glover, founder of Live Unreal Companies |

Jeff Glover takes Glover Agency independent after 17 years with Keller Williams, telling Inman the move is about keeping Glover U broker-agnostic.

Glover Agency, the Michigan team Jeff Glover founded in 2008, became fully independent on Nov. 1, ending a 17-year run with Keller Williams. The move comes roughly three months after Glover sold his three Keller Williams market centers.

The team says it has been Michigan’s top homeselling team across all brands in 11 of the past 13 years and has sold more than 10,000 homes. It operates out of four offices in Birmingham, Plymouth, Fenton and Grand Rapids.

Glover Agency will now operate only in Michigan and isn’t affiliated with any franchise or national brand.

With Glover Agency out of the franchise system, none of Glover’s Live Unreal Companies are tied to a single brand, which Glover says frees Glover U to work with agents and leaders at every brokerage in the U.S. and Canada.

In an exclusive interview with Inman, Glover said the decision had a lot to do with Glover U, the coaching and training company where he now spends most of his time. Glover U has long pitched itself as broker-agnostic, but Glover said his KW ties kept closing doors, even after the market center sale.

In August, Glover sold his ownership stakes in three Keller Williams market centers across Michigan, where he served as majority owner and operating principal. He said the sale supported Glover U’s broker-agnostic approach to serving agents across the U.S. and Canada. The three market centers combined closed nearly $1 billion in sales volume in 2025.

“Most of [the potential Glover U clients], if they don’t know me and their agents don’t know me, they’re not going to return my call,” Glover said of leaders at rival brands. “I had leaders of large companies — I mean, the largest that exist today — say, ‘Hey, Jeff, that’s great you sold your franchises, and we’re definitely open to you helping our agents, but I’m sorry, I can’t put a Keller Williams guy on our stage.'”

Joining another brand would have recreated the same problem. Going independent, Glover says, removes it.

“This move furthers the brand-agnostic approach we’ve been working toward, and now there should be little to no objection to somebody trusting me with their agents, because I don’t have a dog in the fight,” Glover said. “They don’t have to worry about me pushing their agents to go to any one company when I’m independent.”

The second driver is marketing. Glover Agency has advertised under its own name for years on TV, radio and billboards, and Glover said most Michigan consumers already assumed the team was independent.

Franchise rules on how the team could advertise, down to how large its name could appear, made it harder for individual agents to build their own brands.

“It’s very hard for them to create a brand within a brand within a brand,” Glover said. “It’s confusing to consumers. It’s confusing to other agents and other companies.”

Glover said top teams that understand marketing already know where consumer loyalty sits.

“The everyday seller and everyday buyer generally doesn’t say, ‘ We’re listing our home with Keller Williams or with Coldwell Banker,'” Glover said. “They say, ‘We’re listing our home with ‘Joe Smith’ or ‘Amy Duncan.'”

For the consumer, Glover said that the brand is “just the gravy on top.” “The brand helps, but today’s consumer resonates more with an agent’s or a team’s brand than with the company’s brand,” he said.

Day-to-day operations at Glover Agency are run by CEO Taylor Kerrigan. Glover remains involved and still lists and sells. He said he was prospecting in front of the team’s agents just before speaking with Inman on Friday.

“For our clients, nothing changes about how we serve them, other than a more personalized approach,” Kerrigan said in a statement. “What does change is that the name on the door is entirely ours.”

Glover joined Keller Williams in 2009, and the company says the team climbed as high as No. 3 nationally among all groups and No. 1 among expansion teams for homes sold. Asked what would be hardest about leaving, Glover didn’t hesitate.

“Without question, my relationship with Gary Keller,” he said, pointing to Keller’s early top 100 mastermind and a smaller circle of about a dozen agents, the Pirate Group, who got regular access to the KW co-founder. “I wouldn’t be where I am today if it weren’t for him.”

Glover said he still considers Keller a mentor and expects to keep speaking at KW events “so long as I’m welcome.”

The timing puts Glover on the opposite side of an industry trend. Consolidation has dominated brokerage headlines this year, including Compass–Anywhere and Real–REMAX, and independents face growing pressure to align with a larger platform.

Glover doesn’t think independence is right for everyone. He said it works for owners who know what agents need today, such as database growth, leverage and help building personal brands, and who have the energy to deliver it.

“For the person who somewhat wants the easy button, and maybe they’re at a point in their life where they don’t have the energy or time to pour into their company,” he said, joining a franchise or a company like Real, eXp or LPT “makes a lot of sense for that individual.”

For Glover, the bigger bet is on Glover U.

“The biggest thing is neutralizing Glover U so that it will be the No. 1 training and coaching company on the planet for real estate agents at the rate we’re growing,” he told Inman. “And I can’t do that if I’m affiliated with any one brand. So that’s a big part of it. The other part is the freedom and flexibility this gives us to help our agents grow their brands even bigger.”

SAN FRANCISCO, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Doppel, the Frontier AI Social Engineering Defense (SED) platform, today announced its acquisition of PropRise, a Y Combinator-backed technology company. Doppel was recently named to Fast Company's 2026 Best Workplaces for Innovators list, as well as the 2026â2027 Fortune Cyber 60 for the second consecutive year. To learn more about open roles and opportunities to join Doppel, visit our careers page.

Digital Risk Protection (DRP) sees attacks forming, mapping attacker infrastructure across channels and dismantling it before launch. Email Security defends the inbox, judging every message by the infrastructure behind it and taking that infrastructure down so the campaign can't retarget. Human Risk Management (HRM) hardens the people attackers target, turning live threats into simulations and training and measuring risk by user and team. Every signal flows through a shared Threat Graph, so a threat seen anywhere strengthens defenses everywhere, and self-healing agents patch every missed detection. Together, they break the social engineering attack chain, advancing Doppel's mission to protect the world from social engineering attacks every day.

#5591. Autonomous site reliability engineering startup Traversal bags $120M in funding at a $1B valuation

Traversal Inc., a startup that’s trying to automate site reliability engineering tasks with artificial intelligence agents, seems to be closing in on that goal after raising $120 million in fresh funding, bringing its valuation to $1 billion.

The newly minted unicorn’s round was led by Kleiner Perkins, Redpoint Ventures and Khosla Ventures, three of Silicon Valley’s highest-profile venture capital firms, whose names should give it the credibility it needs to accelerate its growth plans. Sequoia Capital – another big VC name – also participated in the round, alongside Battery Ventures and Amex Ventures.

AI might have made the job of software developers much easier than it used to be, but for the site reliability engineers tasked with maintaining the infrastructure to run that code, it has only made life much more difficult. The influx of AI-generated code has put infrastructure engineers under intense pressure, and they’re struggling to keep up.

According to a report earlier this year by Splunk Inc. and Oxford Economics, enterprise downtime costs have risen more than 50% in the last two years, draining up to $600 billion annually from businesses worldwide. That’s because software developers have increased their code output by around 180% over the same timeframe, which means those poor infrastructure engineers are forced to work harder than ever to match their growing output.

Enter Traversal, which is coming to the rescue with a highly promising autonomous site reliability engineer that’s designed to assist human specialists by diagnosing, remediating and preventing information technology infrastructure problems. Instead of just keeping watch and firing off alerts to human engineers when an outage occurs, Traversal actively investigates any issues that pop up and does its best to fix them so as to ease their ungodly workload.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Anish Agarwal said there’s an urgent need for a specialized AI site reliability engineer, because not even the best general-purpose large language models have been able to show they’re up to the task. He points to the ORCA-bench benchmark that his company co-developed alongside researchers from Cornell Tech and Columbia University. It reveals that even the most advanced frontier models barely achieve 25% accuracy on medium-difficulty SRE tasks, with their hallucination rates often exceeding 40%.

“Site reliability engineering is one of the hardest problems in applied AI because every company’s software environment is different, and with downtime costing companies as much as $600 billion a year, the stakes are clearly enormous,” Agarwal said.

Traversal’s AI far surpasses what the best frontier models can do. It’s designed to be deployed in enterprises’ IT environments, where it sits and analyzes massive volumes of operational telemetry, including logs, metrics and traces, so as to establish a baseline for normal behavior. When problems occur, it uses causal machine learning to identify the root cause of the issue, and then works out a solution so all the human engineer has to do is accept its recommendation to restore normal service.

Agarwal’s background in causal machine learning is the key to Traversal’s AI SRE’s much higher accuracy. It’s an AI discipline that combines causal inference with machine learning to identify cause-and-effect relationships, rather than relying on statistical correlations. In essence, it enables Traversal’s models to simulate the effects of various actions, interventions and policy changes have on IT infrastructure, so it can quickly work out what the likely cause of a problem is.

Agarwal said the company is striving to build a “superintelligent AI SRE” that can finally help enterprises to keep pace with the rapid velocity of their AI-enabled developer teams. And he believes it’s well on the way to achieving that goal. “After two years refining our technology, we’re seeing customers expand how they use Traversal across increasingly complex production environments,” he said.

In the last year, Traversal has grown its revenue more than nine-fold and its number of monthly active users has multiplied by 20. Some of its best-known customers include Pepsi Co., DigitalOcean Holdings Inc., Nubank and Harvey AI Corp.

Traversal’s momentum is impressive, but Agarwal said the company is only just getting started. With $120 million in the bank, it’s going to accelerate hiring within its engineering, go-to-market and research and development teams so it can get closer to its goal of building a superintelligent AI SRE.

Kleiner Perkins’ Aditya Naganath said Traversal is the first company he has seen that brings “real intelligence” into complex production environments, and he’s confident there’s going to be enormous demand for it. “As AI dramatically accelerates the pace at which software is written and shipped, the complexity of managing production will only grow,” he predicted. “Traversal gives engineering teams the intelligence they need to understand their systems, resolve incidents faster and operate with confidence at scales that simply weren’t possible before.”

#5590. Zcash Upgrade Could Triple Transaction Speed as ZEC Faces Crypto Governance Turmoil

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

Zcash is preparing to triple transaction speed as its NU7 network upgrade approaches November 5, but governance tensions and falling prices are testing investor confidence.

The Zcash upgrade will reduce target block times from 75 seconds to 25 seconds, making transaction confirmations significantly faster. The activation is planned for block height 3,543,405, according to the network’s deployment schedule.

Zcash Network Upgrade 7 mainnet activation height is being set for Block 3,543,405 (~November 5th 2026) pic.twitter.com/C4D5Dch61l

The technical changes arrive as Zcash faces a separate debate over its community-grants funding system. ZEC has also suffered recent price weakness, leaving traders weighing network improvements against growing uncertainty over its future direction.

The upcoming Zcash upgrade introduces several changes beyond faster block production. Under ZIP 218, the network will target a new block every 25 seconds, down from 75 seconds. That could reduce the waiting time for three transaction confirmations from nearly four minutes to around 75 seconds.

The upgrade also introduces limits on shielded transaction activity, designed to improve network efficiency and protect wallets against spam.

Meanwhile, ZIP 235 will remove 60% of transaction fees from circulation and place them into a reserve. The mechanism is intended to support future mining rewards as block subsidies decline.

Node operators must also upgrade their software to remain on the network’s consensus chain. at present, Zcash Foundation has released Zebra 7.0.0, which supports NU7 on mainnet and includes additional synchronization and security improvements.

The Zcash Upgrade comes as the project faces renewed debate over how its development ecosystem should be funded. Zcash co-founder Sean Bowe recently proposed ending the automatic allocation of 8% of newly issued ZEC to the Zcash Community Grants program.

Bowe said that the program already holds approximately $125 million after existing commitments, enough to fund years of development without continuing automatic inflows.

His proposal would redirect the allocation toward a reserve supporting future mining rewards. The committee would retain its existing funds and continue distributing grants.

The proposal does not directly cite that controversy, instead focusing on the size of the grants treasury and long-term funding sustainability.

ZEC has also faced selling pressure ahead of the upgrade. Recent market coverage placed the token near $1,135 after an approximately 11% decline, highlighting the disconnect between improving network fundamentals and short-term price performance.

#5587. Mortgage rates have a quiet week as markets digest Fed comments, Trump’s directive

Mortgage rates were mostly flat week over week, with the 30-year fixed averaging 7.38%. Jumbo and FHA rates fell modestly, while markets are still pricing a likely 25-bps Fed hike in December.  AI Summary

Mortgage rate movement was largely flat in the past week, with the downward momentum of previous weeks cooling off even as more potential homebuyers have been incentivized to seek financing.

At HousingWire’s Mortgage Rates Center on Tuesday, rates for 30-year loans averaged 7.38% — the same as one week ago. Rates for 30-year jumbo loans averaged 7.62%, down 7 bps in a week, while 30-year rates for Federal Housing Administration (FHA) loans stood at 7.16%, down 8 bps.

The small declines in rates come a week after the Federal Reserve held the federal funds rate at a range of 3.75% of 4% in a widely expected decision. But after policymakers hiked rates in September, further increases are anticipated, with the CME Group’s FedWatch tool showing that 77% of interest rate traders predict a 25-basis-point increase in December.

HousingWire Lead Analyst Logan Mohtashami wrote this week that tighter monetary policy “has created financial pain for some AI companies.” With the Fed focusing on the inflationary aspects of AI and associated debt-financing issues, the 10-year Treasury yield has been dropping, which has placed downward pressure on mortgage rates.

Hector Amendola, president of Las Vegas-based mortgage lender SimplyPMG, told HousingWire in an interview that he believes a December hike is already baked into current rates and that drastic movement, up or down, is unlikely to happen for the rest of this year.

“It’s kind of been par for the course now for a while, that rates are continuing to rise based on the expectation that the Fed will go up a little bit more until there’s a way to figure out how to tame inflation a little bit,” Amendola said.

Fed Chair Kevin Warsh announced last week that the central bank would be shifting to fewer policy votes in each of the next two years. The Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC) currently meets eight times a year, with a vote scheduled after each, but the number of votes will be reduced to seven in 2027 and potentially to six in 2028.

“I think it puts a little bit more weight on each of the meetings,” he said. “I also think it’s interesting, because as Warsh kicks over, you’re kind of wondering if it’ll be like, ‘Let’s break everything and see what happens and figure it out later,’ or are we going to continue to really look at the data and do what the data tells us?

“I think what I’ve seen so far is, it’s still a wait-and-see approach. Let’s see what the data says, and that’s kind of why I think this particular decision that came out [last week] was expected, because the data is saying, ‘Slow down.’”

Last month, President Donald Trump signed an executive order that targets lower costs in multiple areas of housing finance. These include proactive mortgage insurance cancellations for conventional loan servicers, an expanded title waiver program through the Federal Housing Finance Agency (FHFA), reduced rates on some government-backed loans and the creation of a manufactured housing task force.

Mat Ishbia, president and CEO of United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM), said this week in his monthly “3 Points” video that “housing affordability continues to be front and center in Washington D.C. There’s a real focus right now on finding ways to lower the cost of homeownership, reduce friction in the mortgage process and make financing more accessible.”

He pointed specifically to the proposal to make the title insurance waiver pilot a permanent program, saying that prior waivers on some low-risk refinances have been “saving consumers thousands of dollars.”

“Some of these ideas will help; some of them won’t help,” Ishbia said of the executive order. “We’ll see how it all shakes out. But I think these are good things they’re looking at doing.”

Amendola said his company has “always been big proponents” of waiving title insurance on refi transactions with loan-to-value ratios below 80%. “Like, what are we really doing? It’s the same consumer. You know, all that stuff is still coming up,” he remarked.

He also said that allowing servicers of Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac loans to help borrowers cancel their mortgage insurance premiums when they reach the statutory threshold “is a bigger deal than people think.” U.S. Mortgage Insurers have expressed their support for the move, while some analysts label it as “fairly benign” for the financial performance of mortgage insurers.

“That’s extra revenue that they’re making right now that they, honestly, probably shouldn’t be making — and suddenly they’re going to have an impact on their end,” Amendola said. “But it’s going to be really good for the homeowner to free up some of that cash that can then turn into something else for them.”

#5586. Jupiter's Q3 Staking Rewards For All Wallets Opens Today, See Who Clears the 50 JUP Bar

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

50 JUP sounds like a threshold almost anyone can meet. It isn't, and today is when many stakers will find that out.

Jupiter's Active Staking Rewards (ASR) for July to September 2026 are now open to every wallet. That means a 50 million JUP pool can be claimed by anyone who qualified. The problem is that "qualified" doesn't mean what most people think. The rule isn't "have 50 JUP staked." It's "average 50 JUP across the whole quarter." Running the numbers this morning and a lot of wallets that look eligible at a glance aren't.

The round started quietly. According to the official Q3 campaign page, the campaign ran from July 1 until earning closed on September 30, and claims opened on October 12. That first week was reserved for Jupiter's own apps. Early access was limited to Jupiter Wallet and the Jupiter Mobile app, and other wallets can claim from 20 October 2026.

So if you stake from Phantom, Solflare, Backpack or a hardware wallet, today is your first real opportunity. Jupiter's documentation explains why the wallet matters. Rewards are linked to the wallet you staked from. If that wallet lives in another app, you either wait for the general opening or import the same recovery phrase into Jupiter Wallet or Jupiter Mobile.

There's no rush to the finish line yet. Reports put the claim deadline at January 12, 2027. Still, I wouldn't leave it to the holidays.

The campaign page states the rules plainly. 50M JUP will be distributed to stakers this period, ASR is calculated on a time-weighted average of your stake, and an average of 50 JUP or more staked during the quarter qualifies.

The words that matter are "time-weighted average." A wallet that held 50 JUP for all 92 days of Q3 averages exactly 50. A wallet that held 500 JUP for only a few days might average less than that. Jupiter designed it this way on purpose. The 7-day unstaking cooldown stops users from staking briefly around distribution periods to collect rewards without sustained participation.

One more detail surprised me, given the program's name. Voting has no effect on ASR, and you do not need to vote to be eligible. The "Active" in Active Staking Rewards now refers to keeping tokens staked, not to governance turnout.

Here's the simple math. It assumes the average is weighted day by day across the 92 days from July 1 to September 30. Jupiter hasn't published its exact snapshot schedule, so treat these figures as close estimates, not guarantees.

The edge cases are where people get caught. Suppose a wallet held 60 JUP from July 1 but started unstaking at the end of August. Its average comes to only about 40 JUP, so it misses. Another wallet held 40 JUP all quarter and added 30 more on September 1. It ends up at roughly 49.8 JUP, just under the line. Adding 31 instead of 30 would have qualified it.

The simplest check is to connect your wallet at Jupiter Rewards. The page will show the amount of ASR you're eligible to claim. If it shows nothing for an older address, the time-weighting is the most likely reason.

Now for the payout. As of mid-October 2026, total staked JUP topped 1.1 billion tokens, roughly 33% of circulating supply, spread across more than 357,000 wallets.

If you divide 50 million JUP by about 1.1 billion staked, you get roughly 4.5% for the quarter. A wallet that just clears the 50 JUP average would receive about 2.3 JUP. An average of 1,000 JUP works out to about 45, and 10,000 to around 455. The quarter's average total stake may have been a bit below the October figure, so actual allocations could come in slightly higher. Your campaign page shows the real number.

Don't expect the tokens to show up as spendable JUP. ASR is paid in JUP and added to your staked balance, which increases your governance power over time.

Three problems come up again and again in Jupiter's support notes:

Squads multisig users have a more manual process. The ASR documentation covers it in detail, including checking that the claim uses the Jupiter Merkle Distributor program, DiS3nNjFVMieMgmiQFm6wgJL7nevk4NrhXKLbtEH1Z2R before you approve anything.

Missing the deadline has real consequences. According to the Jupiter DAO portal, unclaimed ASR goes back to the community treasury once the claim period ends. Jupiter also says that no transfer is made on your behalf after the support deadline.

The bigger picture is a pool that's getting more crowded. Every quarter, 50M JUP goes to eligible stakers, and that figure doesn't change. With staked JUP now above 1.1 billion, each new staker gets a smaller slice of the same pie.

ASR is also the main reward Jupiter is still paying out. The Jupiter DAO voted in February 2026 to postpone Jupuary and send its 700 million JUP back to a community multisig. That leaves this quarterly distribution as the core reason to keep JUP staked.

My advice is to claim this round now and then look ahead. The October to December period is already more than halfway through. The same math applies, and each week you wait raises how much JUP you need to reach a 50 JUP average.

#5585. Sentra raises $150M to control what AI agents can reach in corporate data

Data security startup Sentra Inc. today revealed it has raised $150 million in new funding to expand its platform for controlling what artificial intelligence agents can reach inside corporate data stores.

Sentra, which provides data security software, says its business grew more than 300% over the past year. The platform works on data at rest, wherever an enterprise happens to keep it.

Each customer gets classification tuned to its own business. Alongside that sits an identity map of which people, service accounts and AI agents can reach a given dataset, inherited permissions included.

Every AI agent a company switches on is another identity reading its data, often around the clock, with no central control plane overseeing it. Sentra expects agent counts at large enterprises to climb steeply over the next few years. Only a small minority of organizations have governance in place to control what those agents touch, according to the company.

Sentra co-founder and Chief Executive Yoav Regev called agents “the busiest consumers of enterprise data.” In Regev’s view, many of them inherit access to data that has never been fully classified or governed, and traditional perimeter controls were not built for agents moving at machine speed. “What organizations can do is make sure the data those agents reach is already secured,” he said.

To get there, Sentra removes stale and high-risk data that no agent has any reason to see, and service accounts and agents get only the minimum access their work calls for. An agent that later reaches for sensitive data it does not normally touch gets flagged. The platform can then strip the permissions or sharing involved on its own, and the worst cases are passed to whoever owns the data.

After an incident, legal and compliance teams get a record from Sentra of everything the agent could have reached, including business context on each dataset.

The analysis behind all of this happens inside the customer’s own environment, so sensitive data never leaves it. Sentra contends that tools that copy customer data into a vendor’s environment leave buyers with a second data estate to protect, adding retention and residency risk in regulated industries.

Product spending from the round will focus on visibility into the agents, copilots and models touching sensitive data. Faster containment is another priority, for cases where an agent behaves unexpectedly. Commercially, Sentra plans to scale its field and channel programs and push into new geographies.

Capital One Financial Corp.’s venture arm, Capital One Ventures, led the Series C round and will place a representative on Sentra’s board of directors. Existing investors Bessemer Venture Partners LP, Zeev Ventures, Standard Investments Inc., Munich Re Ventures and Key1 Capital also participated. Key1 led a $50 million Series B round for the company in April 2025. Sentra did not disclose a valuation.

Regev started Sentra in 2021 with Asaf Kochan, Ron Reiter and Yair Cohen. Kochan is a former commander of the Israeli military’s Unit 8200, where Regev once headed the cyber department. Including the new round, investors have put more than $250 million into the company since its launch.

#5584. Copado Acquires Valo.ai to Extend AI-Powered Governance from Release to Runtime

Acquisition connects governed software delivery with production intelligence to help Salesforce teams manage access, identify risk and simplify operations.

NEW ORLEANS, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Copado, a leader in AI-powered AgentOps for business applications, today announced that it has acquired Valo.ai, an AI-powered operational intelligence and governance platform for Salesforce environments.

The acquisition advances Copado's vision of Governance Done Right by extending governance beyond software releases into the ongoing operation of enterprise applications. Together, Copado and Valo.ai aim to help teams understand application connections, manage access and identify operational risks, while building a foundation for AI-agent governance. Over time, planned integration will help teams move from identifying those risks to resolving them through governed, tested and auditable workflows.

For years, enterprises have invested in release management and DevOps to control how changes enter production. Yet once those changes are live, understanding what is connected, who has access, what has changed and where risks are emerging can remain difficult and time-consuming. Valo.ai gives Salesforce administrators and operations teams practical intelligence to address those challenges.

"Governance shouldn't stop when software goes live," said Ted Elliott, CEO of Copado. "For years, we've helped customers control how changes reach production. But once those changes are live, teams still need to understand what's connected, who has access, and where risks are emerging. As AI agents become part of everyday operations, that visibility becomes even more important. Bringing Valo into Copado is how we begin connecting governed delivery with governed operations."

What Valo.ai brings today Valo.ai helps Salesforce administrators and operations teams identify connected applications, dormant integrations, excessive permissions and unused accounts. It also surfaces opportunities to optimize license usage and reduce administrative effort. Designed for minimal setup, the platform prioritizes findings so teams can focus on the issues that matter most. For example, an administrator can identify an integration that no longer serves a business purpose but retains access to Salesforce, review its permissions and determine whether that access should be removed.

Valo.ai was founded by leaders with deep experience building Salesforce security and platform technologies, including Salesforce Shield.

Connecting production intelligence with governed delivery The acquisition builds on Copado's introduction of AgentiaÂ®, which uses context-aware AI agents to automate software planning, development, testing and releases while maintaining enterprise governance and control. With Valo.ai, Copado plans to connect that delivery foundation with operational intelligence from production.

Copado plans to progressively integrate Valo.ai's production intelligence into its development, testing and release workflows. The goal is to help teams turn identified risks into recommended changes, validate those changes through testing and deploy them through governed processes, with human approval and auditability throughout. Integrated capabilities will be introduced through a phased roadmap.

The acquisition brings operational visibility today and creates a foundation for broader governance capabilities over time:

"Joining Copado gives us the opportunity to bring governance and visibility to every stage of the AI and software lifecycle," said Jari Salomaa, CEO and co-founder of Valo.ai. "As enterprises introduce more AI agents and applications into their business systems, they need to understand what has access to their data and how it's being used. Together with Copado, we can help customers innovate with greater speed and confidence, while maintaining the control and visibility they need."

Together, Copado and Valo.ai are working toward a future in which enterprises can move from identifying operational risks to resolving them through governed, tested, and auditable workflows.

Availability Valo.ai will remain available as a standalone product, with continued service and support for existing customers. Copado plans to introduce additional capabilities through a phased integration roadmap, with details on availability and timing to be announced. For more information, visit copado.com.

About CopadoCopado is a leader in AI-powered AgentOps for business applications, helping organizations plan, build, test, release and operate software with greater speed, quality and control. Its platform combines DevOps automation, continuous testing, governance and context-aware AI agents to help enterprises accelerate innovation across complex Salesforce environments. Learn more at copado.com.

About Valo.aiValo.ai provides security and operational intelligence for Salesforce environments, helping enterprises understand connected applications, integrations, access permissions and potential risks. Its platform delivers actionable insights to strengthen governance, optimize costs and protect sensitive business data. Learn more at valo.ai.

#5583. Real Brokerage expands in Midwest with Iowa-based The Team

The Real Brokerage announced that Cody Burger and Dennis Buchheit moved their 30-agent group, The Team, to Real. The Dubuque, Iowa-based brokerage covers Iowa, Illinois and Wisconsin, with reported volume of $1.2B since 2020.  AI Summary

The Real Brokerage announced that real estate leaders Cody Burger and Dennis Buchheit have moved their 30-agent brokerage to Real under the name The Team. The group, based in Dubuque, Iowa, previously operated as an independent brokerage known as Unlimited.

The Team serves buyers and sellers across Dubuque; Galena, Illinois; and southern Wisconsin. Since 2020, the brokerage has closed about 5,000 transactions totaling $1.2 billion in volume, according to the company announcement.

The move gives Real, a top-ranked firm by RealTrends Verified, a larger foothold in a smaller but active Midwest market as national brokerages continue to compete for productive teams rather than individual agents. For brokers and team leaders, these platform moves can signal shifting economics around splits, stock incentives, technology stacks and administrative support.

Buchheit brings more than 30 years of real estate experience to Real and also co-owns multiple complementary businesses in property management, insurance, HVAC, cleaning and construction. That ecosystem can create cross-sales and referral opportunities while helping to stabilize revenue through market cycles.

Buchheit recruited Burger to Unlimited in 2020 to run the company, a partnership that preceded Unlimited’s merger with the region’s largest brokerage. Together they grew Unlimited into a local market leader by both agent count and production, the announcement explained.

Burger has balanced ownership responsibilities with active production. He is on track to generate about $15 million in personal sales volume in 2026, according to the announcement.

At Real, Burger and Buchheit plan to leverage the firm’s cloud-based brokerage platform to streamline operations, recruit additional agents and expand into new Midwest markets.

“Cody and Dennis have built a business with a strong regional presence and a clear vision for growth,” Joel Kirsch, senior vice president of growth at Real and a 2024 HousingWire Insider, said in the announcement. “They bring valuable operational experience, production success and an entrepreneurial mindset.”

Buchheit said the switch was driven largely by technology and long-term positioning.

“Real is light-years ahead when it comes to technology and where the industry is going,” he said, noting that the platform and community provide tools and relationships to “build a business that’s positioned for the future.”

Burger said the move will allow him to spend less time on day-to-day management and more time on production, agent development and geographic expansion. “I’ve spent years running every aspect of the business while still producing, and Real gives me an opportunity to take a lot off my plate,” he said.

#5582. Social Security COLA, tax break could narrow spending gap for older consumers in 2027

A Bank of America Institute report finds baby boomer and traditionalist households have weaker discretionary spending growth than other generations despite large wealth gains among the richest older households. Because many retirees rely on fixed income sources and benefit less from recent wage growth, their budgets have been under pressure. A temporary federal tax deduction for those 65 and older and a 3.6% Social Security cost-of-living adjustment for 2027 could modestly improve real incomes, particularly if inflation cools as forecast.   AI Summary

The spending growth of older consumers has trailed other age groups for the past year despite sizable wealth gains at the top. But a 2027 cost-of-living adjustment for Social Security recipients and temporary tax break could modestly improve their purchasing power, according to a Bank of America Institute report released last week.

Bank of America aggregated credit and debit card data to show that baby boomer and traditionalist households have posted weaker discretionary spending growth than other Americans for roughly a year. That marks a reversal from 2022 and 2023, when older households were outpacing others. Boomers were defined as those born between 1946 and 1964, while traditionalists are those born before 1946.

The report ties part of this slowdown to how wealth is distributed within the older cohorts. Using 2025 data from the Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances, the bank found that about two-thirds of net wealth among households headed by someone older than 65 is held by the top 10% of these households. This concentration means that stock market and asset gains may do little to support spending for most older consumers.

Overall consumer spending strength in 2026 appears to be driven primarily by wage and salary growth, particularly among lower- and middle-income working households. Older households, by contrast, depend on a broader mix of income sources and are less exposed to accelerating wages.

Fed survey data shows that as households age, a smaller share of income comes from wages or self-employment and more from pensions, Social Security, and interest, dividends or rental income. Bank of America’s internal data highlight the resulting divergence within older cohorts: Households over 62 that rely only on Social Security have average income and discretionary spending close to half that of their peers who drawing from Social Security, pensions and employment combined.

Discretionary spending is also more uneven across income tiers for older generations than for all households. Retirees are the least likely group to expect their finances to improve over the next six months, according to the study, reflecting the challenges of living on largely fixed income sources.

The report points to two policy levers that could support older consumers’ budgets in the near term:

COLAs are based on the year-over-year change in the third quarter for the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers (CPI-W). While these increases are designed to preserve purchasing power, they can be more or less generous depending on the inflation path in the year that follows.

In 2022, for example, inflation slowed sharply after a large COLA took effect, effectively boosting real benefits and helping older generations outspend other age cohorts in 2022 and 2023.

Consensus forecasts cited in the Bank of America report anticipate that overall inflation will cool in 2027, largely as the impact of higher gasoline prices fades. If that occurs, the 3.6% COLA could outpace actual price increases next year, delivering a more meaningful real income gain for households heavily reliant on Social Security.

The survey data shows that the largest spending growth gaps between older generations and all households are concentrated in discretionary categories like electronics, lodging, restaurants, clothing, furniture and airlines. In many of these areas, older cohorts’ year-over-year spending growth lags the overall population by several percentage points.

Some of this pattern likely reflects differences in preferences and life stages. But if Social Security benefits rise faster than prices in 2027 and the tax deduction continues to support middle-income seniors, the report suggests there may be room for older households’ discretionary spending growth to narrow the gap with other age groups.

Slower discretionary spending among older Americans, combined with highly concentrated wealth, underscores the financial pressures on many households that are past their peak earning years. For housing professionals, this has several implications:

Bank of America stresses that its findings are based on anonymized, aggregated transaction and survey data and should be considered alongside broader economic indicators.

The decision reaffirms the approach taken to establish Canton. #5580. Why homebuilders and lot sellers no longer price risk the same way

As slower sales and shrinking margins test homebuilders' financial flexibility, land developers and capital providers face different economic pressures. Builder Advisor Group CEO Tony Avila sees an industry adapting to a longer period of difficult conditions, even as investment interest persists.  AI Summary

Stagflation is an economic rule-breaker. It delivers the double whammy of a market downturn and high prices, both at once. The U.S. homebuilding industry’s mounting financial pressures have similarly coalesced into a riptide that grows harder to paddle against with each passing quarter.

Builders are selling homes more slowly, sacrificing margins to maintain sales volume, and finding that many of the land deals needed to replenish their pipelines no longer deliver acceptable returns and, in an increasing number of cases, barely yield positive net margins.

Yet the land developers supplying finished lots to builders have not faced the same level of financial pressure. Tony Avila, CEO of Builder Advisor Group and Avila Real Estate Capital, says that developers borrowing from his firm generally continue to earn higher margins than the homebuilders who buy their lots, and that the scarcity of finished lots in many markets continues to give sellers room to resist price cuts.

“Today there are more homebuilders than there are vacant developed lots in most markets,” Avila said in a November 2 interview with HousingWire TBD. “That makes it a lot sellers’ market as opposed to a lot buyers’ market.”

The imbalance reflects a growing fault line in the economics of U.S. homebuilding, and the risks on either side of that chasm. Builders must underwrite land based on current home prices, construction costs, incentives, and slower absorption rates, whereas developers with sufficient financial flexibility can wait for multiple bidders willing to meet their lot-price expectations, allowing some give-and-take on terms.

The result is a difficult alignment of interests among homebuilders, land sellers, lenders and investors, each of whom earns a bigger or smaller share of the return from the same ultimate source: the price a household can afford to pay for a new home.

Avila believes the industry is preparing for an indefinitely prolonged period of constrained homebuyer purchasing power rather than counting on a near-term return to the conditions that supported record profitability earlier this decade. His perspective draws on his firms’ work with homebuilders, land developers, capital providers and prospective acquirers, as well as discussions at the October 13 Forum for Housing Executives in Lafayette Hill, Pennsylvania.

“I think that everyone is getting prepared for a different landscape, a more challenging selling environment, and an environment where we are higher-for-longer on interest rates,” Avila said.

The adjustment extends beyond pricing and sales incentives. Builders are reassessing how much land they control, how quickly they can convert their investments into cash, which customers they can serve profitably, and how much financial leverage they can carry while waiting for demand to improve.

Avila compares the current environment more closely to the high-interest-rate housing market of 1981 than to the 2007 financial crisis. Appreciating the contrast and its after-effects may give those who do so a competitive jumpstart on a playbook. The GFC followed years of excessive construction, speculative investment and aggressive bank lending for residential development assets.

Today’s pressures differ markedly. The industry faces an affordability problem exacerbated by mortgage rates, inflation, household expenses and construction costs, while conventional bank financing for acquisition, development and construction remains well below the levels Avila recalls from the previous housing boom.

By his estimate, banks had more than $200 billion committed to AD&C lending around 2006, compared with about $90 billion today. Those figures are Avila’s historical comparison rather than a standardized statistical series, but they illustrate his view that the financing structure supporting residential development has changed substantially.

Private lenders and institutional land-capital providers have filled part of the gap. However, their participation does not eliminate the cost of financing land and construction, particularly when slower absorption extends the time between an initial investment and the eventual closing of a home.

Avila says his firm is seeing strong demand for private development financing, even as builders become more selective about new commitments.

“We are being deluged with loan requests right now across the board,” he said.

Financing availability is not the same as the ability to put it to profitable use. Higher borrowing costs, slower inventory turnover, and reduced homebuilding margins can make a project economically unattractive even when a lender is willing to provide capital.

The financial pressure is evident in the industry benchmarks presented at the October Forum, which brought together executives from major public, private, and internationally owned homebuilders, as well as developers and capital providers.

According to the Forum’s survey findings, public-builder gross margins have declined from about 26% at their fourth-quarter 2022 peak to about 20%, while EBITDA margins have fallen from about 18% to 9%. Sales incentives, which accounted for roughly 2% to 3% of home prices in 2021, have risen to about 8% to 12% in the current environment.

The private-builder survey data tell a similar story. Median gross margins declined from about 20% in 2024 to 18% in 2025, while returns on equity fell from about 17% to 6% and debt-to-capital ratios rose from about 52% to 62%.

These figures describe an industry in which builders have considerably less room to absorb adverse changes in selling prices, construction costs and land acquisition economics. They also help explain why capital allocation decisions that were relatively forgiving during periods of rapid sales and rising home prices now carry greater financial risk.

The differences between homebuilders’ and land developers’ financial positions have become increasingly evident in negotiations over finished lots. As builders revise their assumptions about selling prices, incentives, and absorption rates, the prices they can justify paying for land are moving further from what some developers are prepared to accept.

For developers backed by patient capital, slower lot sales may be preferable to accepting prices that do not meet their investment objectives. That financial agility can sustain land values even as builders who purchase those lots face declining returns.

“If you’re patient capital and you’re a lot seller, you just wait,” Avila said.

The resulting disagreement over land values is constraining transactions. Avila says the gap between what sellers expect and what builders can justify has become a primary obstacle to closing deals.

The difficulty is compounded when slower sales force builders to revise their expectations about how quickly a community will generate revenue. A parcel that penciled attractively when homes were selling faster may no longer produce acceptable returns if the same investment must be carried for longer.

Avila also sees signs that builders are recognizing some of those changed economics through land impairments and the write-off of deposits on transactions they no longer intend to complete. He characterizes impairments to date as relatively modest compared with the land and work-in-process assets on builders’ balance sheets, though he expects additional charges if margins continue to contract.

That does not necessarily mean a broad land-price correction is imminent. The availability of finished lots, the number of competing builders, the strength of local buyer demand, and the patience of land sellers’ financial backers can lead to very different outcomes across markets.

The customer segments a property can serve factor into the calculation. Builders targeting move-up, second move-up, and active-adult buyers may have different underwriting opportunities than competitors focused on entry-level households, which face more severe down-payment, monthly-payment, and cost-of-living constraints.

The underlying question is how much of the industry’s deteriorating economics will eventually be reflected in land prices, how much builders will continue to absorb, and how long the current disagreement between buyers and sellers can persist.

According to Avila, the challenges have not eliminated investor interest in U.S. homebuilding. Avila’s advisory firm has identified 60 prospective strategic, financial, and hybrid acquirers of homebuilding businesses.

That number represents a pool of potential buyers, not completed or pending acquisitions. Still, it suggests that investors continue to evaluate opportunities even as homebuilding profitability has weakened and valuations have become harder to reconcile.

Avila recently returned from meetings in Japan, South Korea, and Singapore, where he says interest in U.S. for-sale housing remained strong. In his assessment, the sector continues to compare favorably with several other real estate investment categories, including segments of the office, retail, and multifamily markets.

That view reflects both his capital markets experience and his firms’ commercial activities. Builder Advisor Group advises homebuilding companies on mergers, acquisitions, and strategic transactions, while Avila Real Estate Capital provides private real estate financing and investment opportunities in a market that also includes institutional land banks, global asset managers, and other specialized capital providers.

Avila therefore has direct visibility into investor inquiries and financing demand, and a business interest in expanding private capital’s role in residential development. His observations offer a useful perspective on investment activity, although the number of interested investors does not indicate how much capital will ultimately be deployed or on what terms.

When prospective buyers and sellers disagree on the value of a homebuilding company, the difference between the number of would-be investors and their ultimate motivation to put capital to work tends to come clearer.

“If your earnings are down, that’ll obviously adversely affect your valuation,” Avila said.

For owners of private homebuilding companies, this creates difficult choices about whether to pursue a sale, seek additional capital, bring in a strategic partner, or continue operating independently while waiting for stronger financial results.

The major Japanese-backed homebuilding companies have been among the most prominent acquirers in recent years. Daiwa House, Sekisui House and Sumitomo Forestry have expanded their U.S. operations through various ownership and integration strategies, supported by long-term investment horizons that can extend well beyond the planning cycles typical of American homebuilding companies.

Avila believes those three companies are now focusing on digesting, integrating and absorbing earlier acquisitions rather than maintaining the same pace of acquisitions. He says other prospective buyers remain active, though he declined to identify the companies involved in confidential discussions.

The October Forum noted 12 announced homebuilder M&A transactions in 2026, compared with 17 in all of 2025, with Japanese-backed companies accounting for approximately five of the current year’s deals.

Those figures do not telegraph a new wave of imminent acquisitions. They do suggest that the industry’s ownership structure remains in flux as investors assess the relationship among current earnings, future growth potential, land positions and the price required to acquire an operating platform.

Another development Avila describes is homebuilders’ participation in private real estate credit.

He says that approximately 15 public and private homebuilding companies, including U.S. businesses owned by Japanese parents, have invested in AREC’s debt fund. These investments are among several ways financially stronger builders are deploying available cash, alongside share repurchases and acquisitions.

The arrangement shows how some homebuilders are financing residential development beyond their direct construction operations. It also highlights differences in financial flexibility among builders, particularly between companies generating substantial cash and those relying on outside financing to support their existing land and construction commitments.

Private credit, institutional land banking and other financing structures offer different combinations of cost, control, risk and flexibility. Their attractiveness depends on whether they improve a builder’s overall return on invested capital after accounting for the cost of obtaining and using the financing.

In some circumstances, keeping land off a builder’s balance sheet can preserve liquidity and reduce exposure to declining land values. In others, the cost of such flexibility can erode too much of the margin available from selling the completed home.

The upshot is that expanding financing alternatives does not resolve the industry’s underlying economic problem. Capital providers must earn returns, land developers must recover their investment and earn a profit, and homebuilders must deliver houses at prices customers can afford while generating sufficient earnings to sustain their businesses.

Right now, those three root business drivers have gone out of sync.

Avila’s observations on the characteristics of successful builders offer a useful way to connect the capital-market discussion to decisions within homebuilding companies.

He identifies stronger margins, lower leverage, attractive finished-lot positions, higher returns on capital and the ability to serve a broader range of buyers as key indicators of financial strength. Geographic diversification can provide additional protection, although he notes that builders operating in individual markets with favorable supply-and-demand balances and dynamics can also perform well.

The strategic adjustments he describes are already underway among the builders and borrowers his firms serve.

Some companies that historically focused on entry-level buyers are re-platforming products and land positions into higher price points and move-up segments to reach households with greater purchasing flexibility. Others are reducing their reliance on speculative construction and placing greater emphasis on build-to-order sales.

Avila says that the shift toward build-to-order has become increasingly visible among his clients and borrowers.

The appeal is straightforward. When homes take longer to sell, reducing speculative inventory can limit the capital tied up in completed or nearly completed homes without buyers, though it may also require changes to sales operations, construction scheduling and customer expectations.

At the same time, builders are reviewing overhead, direct construction costs and the pace of land acquisition and monetization. The objective is not simply to cut spending but to preserve financial capacity to continue operating and investing when demand remains uncertain. For acquisition candidates, operating capabilities may increasingly shape how investors assess earnings durability and future growth potential.

Avila says prospective homebuilding company acquirers favor operators with growing earnings, strong lot positions, strong margins, and high returns on capital and equity. The ability to control or bank land for future development can also make a target more attractive.

Those criteria reinforce the distinction between having access to capital and having a business that can earn an acceptable return on that capital. Meanwhile, builders must operate within the purchasing power of today’s customers rather than on demand that may emerge under more favorable conditions.

That is the common challenge facing the industry’s capital providers and operators. The long-term need for housing may attract investors, but the immediate economics of building and selling homes determine whether their investments generate acceptable returns.

For homebuilders, the near- and medium-term future may reward companies that can preserve financial flexibility, secure land at workable prices, adapt their product offerings and improve operating performance without relying on a rapid recovery in demand.

For land developers and capital providers, the challenge is related yet distinct. Their opportunities ultimately depend on builders’ ability to convert land and financing into homes that customers can purchase profitably.

The industry has begun adjusting to that reality, Avila suggests, although the process remains spotty across markets and companies. In his view, the next phase of homebuilding’s capital cycle may be shaped as much by the terms on which builders, land sellers and investors agree to do business as by the timing of the next increase in home sales.

#5578. Exclusive: BlueFlag Security expands AI agent governance to cover unapproved coding agents

Software development security startup BlueFlag Security Inc. today expanded the artificial intelligence agent governance tools in its developer risk platform to cover unapproved coding agents, including those running on engineers’ laptops outside the code repository.

The update also brings automated fixes for some of the risks the platform turns up.

BlueFlag is going after a problem that has grown fast as coding assistants have evolved into agents that plan their own work and spin up the environments they need. Many sign in with a developer’s credentials. An agent working that way inherits every permission the developer holds.

Raj Mallempati, BlueFlag’s co-founder and chief executive, described the AI agent as “the most powerful and least governed identity in the development environment.” The company plans to start interrupting attack paths as they form early next year, he said. For now, the platform reports them.

In the current release, the work starts with finding the agents, which BlueFlag does from activity in the code. It picks up each agent through the commits and pull requests it produces, then classifies it by what it does with the code and whose identity it uses. Security teams can trace any agent back to the developers who work with it and the repositories it operates in, with unapproved agents marked as such.

AI tools running locally on a developer’s machine are harder to spot. To catch those, BlueFlag reads data from endpoint detection and response products such as those from CrowdStrike Holdings Inc. and SentinelOne Inc., so nothing new has to be installed on the device.

Human review gets its own checks. BlueFlag now flags pull requests approved by an AI agent, along with commits an agent wrote from start to finish and pipeline runs that went out with no person signing off. Organizations can also require a human review before anything merges or deploys. For any software release, customers can document where a person was in the decision and where one was not.

A separate inventory looks at AI inside the applications a company builds. It records the model providers and agent frameworks each application relies on and scores them against the Open Worldwide Application Security Project’s Top 10 for Agentic Applications.

AI spending is measured as well. BlueFlag ties the tokens and dollars each developer burns through to the commits and accepted code that came out of them, and it points to places where spending keeps climbing with no new commits behind it. Paid seats that sit idle show up in the same report.

Remediation runs through two new tools. AccessGuard targets identity problems such as overpermissioned accounts and stale credentials.

Misconfigured repositories and pipelines are handled by DriftGuard, which corrects settings such as missing branch protections that drift over time. Fixes can be applied by hand from written instructions or run automatically with one click, and automated changes can be rolled back.

Auto parts supplier Marelli Holdings Co. Ltd. is a customer. Kristie Pfosi, its global chief information security officer, said agentic AI made the unknowns inside her company’s own development environment bigger “overnight.”

“Within the first week BlueFlag showed us which AI agents were working in our repositories, which developers they worked with, and where the gaps were in how they were approved, scoped and reviewed,” Pfosi said. “Those are findings we can act on the same day.”

The launch comes a day after BlueFlag published its first research report, “The State of Developer Risk 2026.” Its figures come from metadata the platform collected on tens of thousands of identities and access tokens at a subset of BlueFlag’s enterprise customers, in a snapshot taken in September.

Unapproved coding agents turned up in 83% of the organizations measured, and more than two-thirds of the identities agents operate under carry administrator rights. In 22% of organizations an autonomous agent had already merged code with no human involved.

Older problems have not gone away. Nonhuman identities that can reach code repositories outnumber human developers eight to one, and 99% of access tokens are set never to expire.

The new features are generally available now. BlueFlag says the platform connects through application programming interfaces that are read-only by default and can be running in under five minutes, with automated fixes applied only when a customer opts in.

The company launched in March 2024 with $11.5 million in seed funding. Maverick Ventures and Ten Eleven Ventures led that round and came back to lead a Series A this past March that took total funding to $28 million.
