#5577. NIMBYs cite a 155-year-old law to thwart a San Francisco project

Opponents sued San Francisco over an AB 2011 approval for 848 homes at the Marina Safeway site, invoking Section 1983 of the Civil Rights Act of 1871, a Reconstruction-era law also known as the Ku Klux Klan Act, to keep the case in federal court. The developer argues neighbors have no constitutional right to a hearing and contamination issues can be addressed before occupancy.   AI Summary

California state lawmakers have spent years tilting the rules toward new housing.

Projects that meet fixed standards can skip public hearings, and cities that say no face legal and financial risk. Still, muncipal and local neighborhood opponents never seem to run out of ways to try to scuttle projects. A Northern California federal court is embroiled in one of the latest examples.

In San Francisco, one of the most expensive housing cities in the world, opponents of an 848-unit residential structure above an existing Safeway grocery store have escalated to a new level. They invoked the Civil Rights Act of 1871, a law passed to protect Black Americans from Ku Klux Klan violence, when they sued the city in September.

Assembly Bill 2011 is increasingly at the center of these disputes. The 2022 state law lets qualifying projects on commercially zoned land skip public hearings and environmental review. Lawmakers broadened it last year, while community opposition groups keep probing its edges.

Neighbors and other opponents argue that the Safeway project doesn’t qualify for the shortcut. They claim the city shut them out of the process. Last week, the Marina Safeway developer’s lawyers asked the court to dismiss the suit. The filing called the opposition’s tactic “a deeper perversion” of a law meant to protect Black Americans from Klan violence. They argue that civil rights statutes exist to protect victims of discrimination, not to serve as “a weapon” for one of San Francisco’s “most well-resourced communities” to block new home development.

The developers’ plan would replace the Safeway at 15 Marina Blvd. and its parking lot with 848 homes. Eighty-six would be for lower-income households. The homes would rise in towers of 22 and 18 stories above a newly built grocery store at ground level. The site is zoned for 40 feet.

California AB 2011 instructs city planners to check only that the plans meet fixed rules. San Francisco declared the project eligible Aug. 13.

In response, YesAnd Foundation, Neighborhoods United SF and four residents sued Sept. 11 in federal court in San Francisco. The defendants named are the city, its planning and public health directors, and PG&E. PG&E once operated a power plant on the site.

Align Real Estate and Marina Property Owner LLC are named as real parties in interest.

The complaint says the plaintiffs “support the creation of housing generally.” It accuses city planners of “rubber-stamping” a project that doesn’t qualify.

The neighbors’ only federal claim says the permitting and approval shortcut denied them a public hearing, violating their due process rights. They filed the case under Section 1983, part of a 1871 law. It is the only claim that qualifies the case for federal court.

Their other six claims arise under California law. Holland & Knight, the developer’s firm, argues that civil rights laws have long been “powerless” to undo the effects of the housing shortage. The state’s own housing law says the crisis has caused “discrimination against low-income and minority households.”

The brief says California has finally moved to end its pattern of privileging existing homeowners over people who need housing. The neighbors, it argues, want to use civil rights law “not to protect the victims of discrimination.” It says Section 1983 targeted a Klan “campaign of violence and deception,” quoting a 1985 Supreme Court ruling.

The brief also cites a 2008 Ninth Circuit ruling that rejected a similar claim from neighbors in Spokane. That court held neighbors have no constitutional right to a hearing on someone else’s permit. The brief argues that accepting the claim would turn every ministerial approval into a potential federal lawsuit.

But the plaintiffs also turned to a more common approach in fighting projects. They argue there are environmental dangers.

The Safeway sits on the site of an old PG&E steam plant, next to a former coal-gas plant. A state toxics official told city planners in December 2025 she didn’t expect the site “to qualify for streamlined approval.” She cited 2023 petroleum readings 10 times the residential screening level.

In 2024, the regional Water Board, the lead regulator, closed the cleanup of petroleum from the steam plant. It found “no unacceptable public health risks for the current land use.” That finding rested on the store’s commercial use, and the board said it “may reconsider” if the use changes.

The neighbors say the city approved the project before anyone sampled soil beneath the store. In February, the complaint says, the developer’s consultant acknowledged “a data gap.” The consultant said Safeway would not allow drilling while the store operates.

The developer’s lawyers say AB 2011 requires cleanup only before the city issues a certificate of occupancy. The neighbors argue that full contamination assessment must come first.

The brief says state law now strongly favors housing. It cites the Housing Accountability Act, which it says requires courts to give “the fullest possible weight” to approving homes. Under that law, it argues, a city’s finding can be overturned only if no reasonable person could have reached it.

The developer’s attorneys target the lawsuit’s placement in federal court. Federal courts can’t issue the California-style court orders the neighbors want, they argue. If the federal claim fails, they contend, the case belongs in state court. Their brief notes no California court has yet interpreted AB 2011. U.S. District Judge Araceli Martínez-Olguín will hear the motion Feb. 4, 2027.

#5575. CertiK Verified 40.68M TPS for Sui, Here Is What It Means

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

The biggest throughput figure a blockchain security firm has ever signed off on is sitting on CertiK's homepage right now: 40.68 million transactions per second.

It isn't CertiK's own number, and it isn't an on-chain number either. If you read the 2,000-word report behind it, you'll come to become more interested in what CertiK chose not to verify than in what it did.

Scroll past the client logos and media mentions on CertiK and you'll find it in the "Latest Research And Market Insights" strip. One card says CertiK independently verified Sui's Mainnet Tunnel performance campaign, which recorded more than 15.2 billion off-chain transactions across 7,680 tunnels at a peak of 40.68 million TPS.

Most readers will see "CertiK" next to "40.68 million TPS" and stop there. Crypto social media mostly did the same. Sui's own post described the figure as set live on stage at Sui Basecamp 2026 and certified by CertiK, and added that the network now clears in under 20 seconds what Visa processes in a day.Walking through CertiK's verification method when the report first came out. Now that the number has been promoted to CertiK's front page, it's worth looking at exactly what it represents.

According to CertiK's announcement, Sui ran a live Mainnet performance campaign on October 7, 2026, during Sui Basecamp Day. It recorded 15,241,348,297 tunnel transactions across 7,680 tunnels, and every tunnel was opened and settled on chain.

A Sui Tunnel works roughly like a private room. A small group of participants carries out many application actions without sending each one to the blockchain. Sui records the starting terms when the tunnel opens and the final result when it closes. Everything in between happens off-chain as signed receipts. CertiK compares the design to Bitcoin's Lightning Network but notes that tunnels can handle more than payments.

The test was more varied than a single payment loop. The campaign ran 10 runs across five workload types: simple payments, flash, blackjack, tic-tac-toe and battleship. Payments still made up most of the activity. Its 6,144 tunnels committed more than 12 billion transactions, or 78.98% of the total.

This is the part of the report I respect most. The peak came from the busiest complete second, between 08:46:17 and 08:46:18 UTC, when 40,682,328 qualifying tunnel transactions were committed. The highest 60-second rolling average was 40,339,143.65 TPS.

Doing the math on the gap between those two figures. It's about 343,000 transactions, or roughly 0.84%. In other words, the network held near-peak throughput for a full minute rather than spiking for one second.

CertiK also avoided the easiest way to inflate a number like this. For concurrent tunnels sharing the same time window, it added up their transaction counts once and divided by a single shared duration. It did not add individual per-tunnel rates together or multiply one tunnel's rate by the number of tunnels.

The checking itself was thorough. All 7,680 executions and all 960 slots reached VERIFIED status, and the 15.24 billion committed transactions matched the full-history admitted receipts exactly. The work ran on dedicated AWS infrastructure with 128 vCPUs and 247 GiB of RAM.

There's also a small correction in the story. Sui's first announcement reported 40,614,180 TPS. CertiK's audited peak came in about 68,000 higher, a 0.17% difference. A verifier landing slightly above the project's own claim is unusual, and I think it reflects well on the method.

The homepage card doesn't mention any of this, but the full report is clear about its limits.

First, this isn't on-chain throughput. CertiK states that Tunnel TPS measures off-chain tunnel transactions and is not a measurement of Sui's on-chain capacity.

Second, the data came from the project being tested. The Sui team supplied the campaign data and executed all test scenarios, and CertiK examined the retained evidence and recalculated the totals.

Third, the cryptographic checks were not exhaustive. CertiK reconciled the arithmetic, receipt counts and timestamps, but it did not re-run individual signatures or do a fresh cryptographic replay of every receipt.

Fourth, the report can't speak to how the system would behave in normal use. The records don't establish clock accuracy, failure rates, latency percentiles or results across repeated runs. The sustained figure is the best 60-second window observed, not a guaranteed minimum.

Put simply, CertiK verified that the accounting is correct. It did not verify that Sui can handle 40 million real users' actions every second.

The number that's most telling isn't the TPS figure. More than 15.2 billion off-chain transactions were anchored to Sui through just 1,920 on-chain lifecycle transactions: 960 openings and 960 settlements.

By simple calculation, that's about 7.9 million off-chain actions for every on-chain transaction. That ratio is what the tunnel design is built to achieve. It's an impressive engineering result, but it measures how well Sui compresses activity, not how fast its base layer runs.

This isn't the first speed record CertiK has signed off on, and the earlier ones show why comparisons are tricky. In its earlier TON verification, CertiK worked from per-minute transaction count data and arrived at 104,715 TPS for TON's testnet. In April 2025, Qubic announced 15.52 million TPS verified by CertiK, measured over 10 peak ticks on its Layer 1 mainnet.

On paper, Sui's tunnel figure is about 2.6 times Qubic's and nearly 390 times TON's. But these were three different kinds of tests: a sharded testnet, a base-layer burst and an off-chain channel network. They don't belong on the same leaderboard.

My view is that the 40.68 million figure is real, well documented and carefully bounded. It's also a measure of what an off-chain system can process, not what Sui's blockchain itself handles. CertiK's report is honest about that, even if the one-line homepage card isn't.

#5574. MSRs trade at richest levels in decades as lenders, funds pile in

Mortgage servicing rights are trading at their richest levels in decades, with pristine MSR multiples nearing 7x as more lenders choose to retain servicing and build recapture platforms.  AI Summary

Chicago-based Rate has recently changed its servicing strategy, retaining mortgage servicing rights (MSRs) instead of selling.

“We’ve been retaining all of our MSRs for the last 12 months, so we’re over $50 billion in MSR retention,” CEO Victor Ciardelli said in an exclusive interview with HousingWire. “We really believe in retaining the MSRs, staying close to the customer.”

Rate’s approach reflects a broader trend of mortgage lenders holding onto their portfolios or seeking to add MSRs as a way to recapture borrowers when rates eventually fall.

John Sullivan, managing director of MSR advisory services at Milliman, has seen that shift firsthand. Speaking during IMN’s Mortgage Servicing Rights Conference in New York on Monday, he said he’s having more conversations with clients about retaining their portfolios “unless liquidity is an issue,” and about monetizing them if they are not hedging.

Higher demand for MSRs is not limited to independent mortgage banks (IMBs). Depository institutions are also showing more interest, executives told HousingWire during the conference.

“Banks historically are not great at recapture, but we think that given some changes on the Basel capital front, we’re going to see more bank participation in this space on a go-forward basis, and I think banks will think about just customer acquisition in general, cross-selling in general,” said Larry Goldstone, president of capital markets and lending at BSI Financial Services.

Strategic investors are also willing to grow their portfolios. Rob Williams, co-founder and CEO at Grander Investment Management, a specialized asset manager focused on MSRs, said he’s tactical but sees MSRs as a “spectacular asset” that can reach double-digit returns.

“I can probably be more patient,” he said during the conference, when comparing his approach to the other buyers. “I can be more tactical.”

The buyer base views MSRs through different lenses.

Rich McRedmond, managing director at CrossCountry Mortgage, said that while banks see MSRs as part of their consumer banking strategy, real estate investment trusts (REITs) see them as a pure investment. And mortgage companies see them as a borrower recapture tool “from when they get the mortgage to when they get the next mortgage.”

Conventional, pristine MSRs are seeing 7x multiples amid high demand, a level not reached in more than two decades.

“We’ve seen some pretty extraordinary multiples of late,” Goldstone said. “This is usually an inexpensive asset, and therefore an asset that people want to be able to own. I think you could hedge MSR pretty effectively and still get low-double digits, high-single digit returns up until about the last year. That’s pretty attractive for an asset that really doesn’t have a whole lot of credit risk associated with it.”

Simon Aldrich, senior executive vice president at Freedom Mortgage, believes that at this point, “it’s very difficult to be in this market if you don’t have recapture.”

“In our model, we don’t hedge, so I’m not worried about rates going up or rates going down. Rates go up, I get the pickup at slower speeds. Rates go down, our call center kicks into gear.”

Bayview Asset Management, which acquires MSRs from the bulk and flow markets and uses five different subservicers, has also built out a full recapture strategy, including through its acquisition of Guild Mortgage. Managing director Michael Lau said Bayview has partnered with investors, including sovereign wealth funds and pension funds, that have long-duration strategies.

“MSRs are great because they’re not correlated to the equity or the bond market, and gives them something alternative that also, because we hedge out all the interest rate risk for them, delivers a very consistent return on their money, net of our fees,” Lau said.

Some companies have taken advantage of current pricing to sell MSRs for different reasons, including to pay back debt or raise funds.

In the third quarter, Rocket Companies sold $23 billion of unpaid principal balance (UPB) for $379 million in cash proceeds, retaining the subservicing and recapture services on nearly 70% of the MSRs sold. Analysts told HousingWire the company usually sells production in the wholesale channel due to lower recapture possibility.

Pennymac Financial Services entered into an agreement to sell $29 billion in UPB of low-coupon conventional MSRs, with $490 million of proceeds expected to pay down debt. The transaction is expected to close in the fourth quarter.

Meanwhile United Wholesale Mortgage (UWM) sold about $60 billion — at a roughly 6x multiple — to JPMorgan Chase, sources told HousingWire. The companies declined to comment. This is part of a plan to bring up to $80 billion of MSRs to market in the fourth quarter, with the expectation of being paid more than $1.8 billion in an attempt to reduce leverage.

Newrez President Baron Silverstein said his company is taking a disciplined approach. Across the Newrez portfolio, 60% of loans were originated before or during the COVID-19 pandemic.

“In today’s market, given where we are from a rate perspective, there’s pressure in a competitive environment where MSRs get created — where that gain on sale is from an all-in gain-on-sale perspective on loans that we originate or buy. And when we think about that, we get very selective and stay very disciplined about how we put that capital to work,” Silverstein said.

“When you think about hedging in a market like this, that also requires a lot of capital, and it’s very challenging in these markets today, regardless of the interest rate environment. This has been the case for the last year to year and a half.”

Looking ahead, servicing executives believe that multiples can stay higher as elevated mortgage rates reduce prepayment risks, which supports MSR cash flows. Some of them said multiples could move lower if there’s a liquidity issue due to large bulk sales hitting the market.

Regulation could also play a role. “If Basel III goes through and the banks decide to get back into the space, I think the high-six multiples could be relatively inexpensive,” Goldstone said. “You could see multiples in the 7x-8x category.”

The CryptoNews editorial team is composed of seasoned writers specializing in cryptocurrency and blockchain technology. Their expertise ensures comprehensive, accurate, and insightful content for...

MetaMask is facing fresh questions about its future after Consensys launched a new institutional settlement network targeting banks, asset managers and financial market infrastructure providers.

The announcement puts Consensys’ institutional ambitions in the spotlight just weeks before its planned separation from MetaMask. The move could also leave the popular wallet competing independently while its former parent pursues Wall Street.

Introducing Sovereign Network Interoperability by Consensys.State-of-the-art interoperability that enables institutions to do business freely, settling securities, exchanging currencies and posting collateral across ledgers, without bridges or moving assets onto a shared…

Consensys unveiled Sovereign Network Interoperability at Devcon, introducing infrastructure designed to coordinate transactions across independently operated financial networks. Can MetaMask maintain its position as institutional blockchain adoption accelerates?

The new Sovereign Network Interoperability platform aims to help institutions settle securities, exchange currencies, and move collateral across separate blockchain networks.

Its bridgeless design keeps assets on their original ledgers while coordinating transactions between approved counterparties. Consensys says the system uses cryptographic verification to reduce reliance on additional trusted intermediaries.

The platform targets four major financial workflows, including securities settlement, wholesale payments, collateral mobility, and tokenized fund transactions.

Consensys plans to support Ethereum-compatible networks and protocols such as the Ethereum Economic Zone and Inter-Blockchain Communication. Canton connectivity is also planned.

The launch builds on Consensys’ existing institutional infrastructure, including Linea, Hyperledger Besu and Teku. The company is positioning itself as a technology provider for financial institutions seeking private, always-on blockchain settlement.

Discover: The Crypto Presales This Q4 2026

The institutional launch arrives as Consensys prepares to separate its consumer and enterprise operations into two companies.

Under the September restructuring plan, Consensys Software Inc. will rebrand as MetaMask, with Joe Lubin serving as chairman and CEO. The protocols and institutional infrastructure business will move into a newly formed company retaining the Consensys name. The separation is expected to be completed by the end of 2026.

Today, MetaMask begins its next chapter as an independent company.Consensys Software Inc., the company behind MetaMask, is rebranding as MetaMask, fully focused on the consumer platform. The protocols and institutional infrastructure businesses, including Linea, are becoming a…

MetaMask will focus on consumer finance, expanding beyond its traditional wallet functions into payments, savings, trading and access to financial instruments.

The company has reported more than 100 million downloads across approximately 190 countries. Its Money Account product also signals an ambition to become a self-custodial financial platform.

Still, the split creates uncertainty around how resources, intellectual property and shared development capabilities will be allocated.

Consensys has not disclosed separate revenue figures, financing arrangements or detailed asset allocations for the two businesses. This leaves MetaMask facing a strategic challenge. It must continue developing its consumer platform while Consensys builds infrastructure aimed at some of crypto’s largest potential customers.

The institutional settlement push also highlights a potential opportunity for Bitcoin Layer 2 projects seeking to expand beyond payments and decentralized finance.

Bitcoin Hyper is one project positioning itself around this idea, combining a Bitcoin Layer 2 design with a wallet and an execution environment intended to support faster transactions and applications.

Different route. Stronger vision. That's the Hyper way. ⚡️https://t.co/VNG0P4GuDo pic.twitter.com/jyimj70P5J

Its longer-term opportunity could extend into settlement infrastructure if the network develops the security, interoperability, and compliance features institutions require.

The project has raised more than $33.2 million in its presale, with HYPER priced at just $0.0136. It also offers 35% staking rewards, while the planned network uses a canonical BTC bridge, transaction batching, and zero-knowledge proofs to settle Layer 2 activity back to Bitcoin.

Bitcoin Hyper is also developing a wallet and broader application ecosystem. Its testnet explorer is live, with additional wallet, bridge, and staking features listed among upcoming milestones. The token launch has been announced for November 26, and exchange listings and full network rollout are planned.

If Bitcoin Hyper can deliver reliable BTC transfers, secure settlement, and applications suited to financial institutions, its infrastructure could eventually compete for use cases now being developed on Ethereum-compatible networks.

That would put Bitcoin Layer 2 projects in a different conversation, not simply as faster payment rails for retail users, but as potential infrastructure for tokenized assets and cross-network settlement.

#5571. Finance of America grows origination volume but reports $110M loss in Q3

Finance of America reported a $110M net loss in Q3 2026, driven mainly by $125M in noncash fair value adjustments. Funded volume rose 24% year over year to $748M, while adjusted net income was $6M and adjusted EBITDA was $17M.   AI Summary

Finance of America (FOA) reported a net loss of $110 million in the third quarter of 2026, as noncash fair value adjustments weighed on results despite growth in the company’s home equity lending business.

The Plano, Texas-based company on Tuesday reported $748 million in funded volume for the quarter ending Sept. 30, up 24% from $603 million during the same period last year. Year-to-date funded volume reached $2.07 billion, a 17% increase from the first nine months of 2025.

FOA recorded a basic loss of $5.24 per share, compared with a loss of 98 cents per share in the third quarter of 2025. The quarterly net loss was primarily driven by $125 million in noncash fair value adjustments.

On an adjusted basis, FOA reported net income of $6 million, or 28 cents per share, compared with $33 million, or $1.33 per share, a year earlier. Adjusted EBITDA totaled $17 million, down from $55 million in the third quarter of 2025.

“The third quarter of 2026 demonstrated the continued strength of our platform, with funded origination volume growing 24% year over year. While higher interest rates drove near-term pressure on earnings, we believe this impact is temporary,” CEO Graham Fleming said in a statement. “We have already taken steps to improve margins.”

During the company’s earnings call, Fleming said the company remains focused on production growth, operational efficiency and cash generation, and explained that margins compressed after the Federal Reserve shifted from cutting to raising interest rates.

“We have already made the necessary changes to product pricing, and we expect margins to return to historical levels in the first half of 2027,” Fleming told investors.

“Finance of America has grown volumes on average by 20% each year since 2023. The third quarter was a challenging rate environment, with the 10-year Treasury yields increasing over 75 basis points during the quarter, a reaction to the Fed’s pivot to raising rates and elevated inflation,” he added.

FOA’s retirement solutions segment, which originates home equity-based financing products, including reverse mortgages, recorded $748 million in funded volume during the quarter, up 24% year over year.

“Our retirement solutions revenue margin was impacted in the third quarter, decreasing to 9%, compared with 11.3% in the third quarter of 2025, and a historical average since the start of 2024 of 10.7%,” Fleming said during the call. “We believe these impacts are temporary and do not change the underlying fundamentals of our business.”

Revenue for the segment totaled $67 million, down 1% from the prior-year period and a decrease from Q2 2026‘s $74 million. Pretax income fell to $3 million, down from $10 million a year earlier, while adjusted net income declined to $9 million, down from $20 million.

The company attributed the decline in profitability primarily to pressure on origination margins as benchmark interest rates increased during the quarter. It said it implemented product and pricing adjustments to address the impact and expects margins to return to historical levels.

For the first nine months of 2026, the retirement solutions segment generated $2.07 billion in funded volume, up 17% year over year. Revenue increased 14% to $208 million.

“Since 2023, our submission volumes have increased by 21% annually, while our funded volume has grown by 20% annually. This is across our product suite, as HECM volume is up 14% year over year, HomeSafe first liens are up 15%, and HomeSafe seconds are up 63%,” FOA President Kristen Sieffert said during the call.

FOA’s portfolio management segment, which generates revenue through net interest income and fair value changes on portfolio assets, reported a pretax loss of $138 million, compared with an $11 million loss in the third quarter of 2025.

The company attributed the loss primarily to negative non-cash fair value adjustments on retained interests in securitizations. Portfolio management reported adjusted net income of $11 million, down from $30 million a year earlier.

Assets under management in the segment increased 23% year over year to $37.4 billion. The growth reflected new originations and the acquisition of Onity Mortgage Corp.‘s HECM servicing portfolio on July 1.

For the first nine months of 2026, portfolio management recorded a pretax loss of $128 million, compared with pretax income of $202 million in the same period last year. Adjusted net income totaled $57 million, down from $66 million.

FOA ended the third quarter with $118 million in cash and cash equivalents, up from $85 million at the end of June. The company attributed the increase to cash generation from originations and capital markets activity.

Total equity stood at $307 million as of Sept. 30, including $259 million attributable to common stock. Book value was $28.08 per common share.

The company said it expects to complete a $60 million paydown of senior secured notes in November. Looking ahead to the final quarter of 2026, chief financial officer Matt Engel said the company expects funded volume to reach $3.1 billion to $3.4 billion, a range “supported by consumer demographics, our product breadth, and ongoing conversion improvements.”

#5570. Google fine-tunes its Agentic Data Cloud to support highly scalable autonomous AI workers

Artificial intelligence is no longer just about conversational assistants that tell people what to do. These days, it’s all about work automation, and Google Cloud is making sure it’s right at the forefront of that trend with its revamped Agentic Data Cloud platform, which received a host of new updates today.

The Agentic Data Cloud was launched earlier this year at Google Cloud Next. It’s meant to be the architectural “system of action” for AI agents, replacing the brittle extract, transform and load-based data pipelines, or ETL, that feed legacy software applications. The key advantage of Agentic Data Cloud is that it meets customers where their data is, so rather than forcing them to squeeze all of their information in a large, centralized data warehouse, it enables AI agents to access it wherever it lives.

In a blog post, Sirish Chandrasekaran, Google’s vice president of product management for data analytics, outlined the company’s belief that autonomous agents rather than humans will soon become the primary consumers of data. As such, it makes sense to build a purpose-built infrastructure stack specifically for them, prioritizing low latency, zero data movement and automated governance. “That is why we built the Agentic Data Cloud — a system of action designed to activate all your data by breaking down walled gardens, deliver high accuracy and trust, and operate proactively at low cost,” Chandrasekaran said.

The flagship new feature in Agentic Data Cloud is borderless Lakehouse, a special version of Google’s “cross-border Lakehouse” product that also debuted at Cloud Next. Chandrasekaran said borderless Lakehouse is built upon the open-source Apache Iceberg table format and designed to eliminate multicloud friction with new caching capabilities for Amazon Web Services and Microsoft Azure. This allows companies to query remote data held in those cloud platforms over a secure private link, without having to pay egress fees.

Chandrasekaran detailed how it works, saying that it automatically caches retrieved data blocks within Google Cloud to accelerate subsequent queries. There’s also a new AlloyDB integration that allows users to query external Iceberg tables with standard PostgreSQL queries without having to copy data. In this way, it bridges real-time transactional data with historical lakehouse records.

One of the big problems with autonomous agents is that they can be prone to hallucinations without proper guardrails in place, which is why Google has overhauled another capability within Agentic Data Cloud. The Knowledge Catalog, which is a kind of map of business meaning that’s meant to inform AI agents of the peculiarities of the organization they work for, is getting a new self-learning enrichment capability in preview.

According to Chandrasekaran, it works by continuously scanning unstructured data in Google Workspace, Jira, SharePoint and GitHub to translate operational knowledge into Open Knowledge Format context sets. These can be used to ground AI agents in organizational knowledge, and the results from early adopters shows that it can help make the average agent four-times more accurate, while reducing token consumption by up to 75%.

Knowledge Catalog is seen as so important to Google’s agentic future that it’s also being enabled by default in the Gemini application starting today. Because it’s so tightly integrated, it can resolve issues around business metric definitions and access controls before it translates user’s prompts into Structured Query Language queries. Companies can also choose to ground agents in semantic models for specific data platforms, including Google BigQuery, Snowflake, SAP, Looker and dbt.

“Agents are only as accurate as the business context they’re grounded in,” Chandrasekaran said. “Whether an agent is calculating net revenue for finance or customer churn for operations, it applies the exact same governed formulas your business teams rely on.”

Gemini is also getting new autonomous machine learning capabilities that can help to streamline everyday work for both technical teams and business workers. For instance, data engineers can now tell Gemini a specific business outcome they want to achieve in natural language, and Gemini will generate the PySpark code, run the notebooks and fix any data pipeline errors as it works toward that goal. Meanwhile, business users will be able to generate reliable, real-time operational reports in Gemini simply by asking for them.

“Gemini uses operational reporting skills integrated with BigQuery and the Knowledge Catalog to construct and save the query,” Chandrasekaran explained. “Once saved, teams can run reports on demand without incurring token costs, guaranteeing consistent and verified answers every time.”

Google also has a few gifts for software developers, starting with the new Data Agent Kit, which is generally available from today, bringing Model Context Protocol tooling into integrated development environments such as VS Code, Claude Code and Antigravity. This means that developers can now just define their business intent in natural language and have agents automatically create, fine-tune and test the associated data pipelines.

Developers can also take advantage of infrastructure updates that are designed to facilitate “high-concurrency agent interactions,” so that thousands of AI agents can query the same database simultaneously without swamping it and causing problems. These include the broader preview of AlloyDB Express, a highly scalable database that supports sub-two-second provisioning for rapid agent prototyping. There’s also PostgreSQL for agents in AlloyDB, which provides an isolated workload environment that can handle three million queries per second.

Finally, Google said BigQuery Graph is now generally available, bringing petabyte-scale graph analytics into relational database tables with zero ETL. It’s joined by previews of the TimesFM 3.0 forecasting model and TabFM predictive analytics model.

#5569. The mortgage operating model after AI

AI could move mortgage origination from role-based handoffs to a persistent, evidence-backed borrower profile. Lenders and agencies could apply different risk models to the same underlying data while AI agents manage conditions and document work with human oversight.   AI Summary

In my previous two articles, I explored why the mortgage industry’s biggest AI challenge is structural and how the traditional brokerage operating model creates complexity as businesses grow. That brings us to a more fundamental question: If we could redesign mortgage origination around what AI now makes possible, what would we build?

Today, the process is organized around a series of narrowly defined roles and handoffs, with loan officers, assistants, processors, underwriters and others each responsible for moving the file to the next stage. Every handoff creates another opportunity for information to get lost and responsibility to be pushed downstream.

I believe the mortgage operating model of the future will be organized around a persistent, provable understanding of the borrower and the lifecycle of the loan, rather than the people, systems and handoffs that define the process today.

At its core, a mortgage involves building an evidence-based profile of an individual and applying a risk model to it. Today, that profile is repeatedly reconstructed or revalidated by originators, lenders, underwriters and other participants because each has limited visibility into, or confidence in, the work that came before.

Imagine instead a persistent, evidence-backed borrower profile that brings together information from pay stubs, tax returns, credit reports and other sources, with each data point retaining a verifiable connection to its original evidence. That includes where the information came from and how it was calculated, interpreted or reconciled with other information.

The result would be a more complete and transparent understanding of the borrower that persists throughout the loan lifecycle. Rather than reconstructing that information each time another party needs to assess the loan, participants could trace the underlying evidence, understand how previous conclusions were reached and build on the work already performed, while still conducting their own necessary evaluations and verifications.

To be sure, understanding the borrower is only part of the equation. Every lender, agency and mortgage product has its own requirements and risk criteria. Today, those requirements are translated into guidelines, matrices and documents that must be interpreted and applied by people across multiple stages of the origination process.

With a common, verifiable borrower profile, different risk models could be applied to the same underlying information. A system could evaluate how Fannie Mae, Freddie Mac or a particular lender would assess the borrower, identify missing evidence and determine what needs to happen next.

Specialized AI agents could then coordinate and execute much of that work, from collecting documents and preparing calculations to addressing conditions and identifying exceptions that require human review.

Consider how often a missing document or unresolved discrepancy surfaces late in the process, forcing a loan officer or processor to revisit work that should have been completed weeks earlier. With a more complete understanding of the borrower and the requirements of the loan, those agents could identify many of those issues earlier, coordinate the necessary follow-up and maintain an auditable record of the work performed.

The implications extend beyond making individual tasks faster to changing how information is maintained and how work gets done, creating an opportunity to rethink the organization itself.

When technology maintains the evidence, context and requirements throughout the loan lifecycle, people no longer need to serve as the connective tissue between every task and system. Specialized AI agents can increasingly handle work traditionally distributed across different roles, while experienced mortgage professionals oversee execution, validate results and exercise judgment.

Consider the processor, whose role could evolve from coordinating documents, conditions and handoffs to overseeing the quality and performance of the loan process. Specialized AI agents could collect documents, prepare calculations and track conditions, while the processor sets standards, validates results, resolves exceptions and continuously improves the workflow.

This shift would also change how mortgage organizations define and reward expertise. Rather than measuring success by the number of people someone manages or the tasks they complete, organizations could focus on accurate files, predictable closings, borrower experience and ultimately, a lower cost to originate. By reducing manual handoffs and repetitive work, experienced professionals could oversee more loans without a corresponding increase in staffing.

The result would be a mortgage organization structured around the lifecycle of the loan rather than inherited job descriptions. Instead of scaling by adding more people to manage each stage of origination, companies could build teams around broader accountability for the loan from application to funding, with AI supporting the work required along the way.

Origination is the logical place to prove this model because it is where the borrower’s evidence is first assembled and evaluated. But once a provable, evidence-based profile exists, its usefulness could extend well beyond funding. Other participants across the mortgage value chain, including investors and capital markets firms, could eventually apply their own risk models to the same underlying information, allowing for more granular risk assessment without repeatedly reconstructing the loan.

My prediction is that AI will reshape not only mortgage organizations, but also how they work together. Even as the technology supporting the industry becomes more sophisticated, the underlying operating model could become fundamentally simpler. With evidence and context following the loan, each participant could build on the work already performed while focusing its expertise on the decisions and responsibilities that matter most.

Oren Michaely is the Co-Founder and CEO of Elio Mortgage.This column does not necessarily reflect the opinion of HousingWire’s editorial department and its owners. To contact the editor responsible for this piece: [email protected].

#5568. OneStream Named Leader and Ranked Number One Overall in the 2026 ISG Buyers Guides™ for Record to Report, Financial Close, and Financial Consolidation

OneStream ranks ahead of all evaluated software providers across all three reports, earning the highest overall ranking and ISG's top 'Exemplary' rating

BIRMINGHAM, Mich., Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- OneStream, the AI operating system for modern Finance that unifies core financial and operational processes, embedding the governance, context, and control required to make AI work for Finance, today announced it has been named a Leader and ranked number one overall in the 2026 ISG Buyers Guidesâ¢ for Record to Report, Financial Close, and Financial Consolidation. OneStream ranked ahead of every evaluated provider in each of the three reports, earning an Exemplary ratingâISG Research's top rating tierâand leading more individual evaluation categories than any other participating provider.

The ISG Buyers Guide for Record to Report evaluated 10 software providers on their ability to support financial consolidation, close management, reconciliation, and financial reporting. In the ISG Buyers Guide for Financial Close, ISG evaluated 14 software providers offering products that support close process management, reconciliation, journal management, and financial analysis and reporting. Finally, the ISG Buyers Guide for Financial Consolidation evaluated 19 software providers offering products that support consolidation process management, intercompany management, journals, and auditing.

"Finance teams need software that shortens the close and gives them control and auditability across complex organizations. Our research shows enterprises should look for strength in both product capability and customer experience when they evaluate these tools," commented Robert Kugel, Executive Director, Business Research at ISG Research. "In our 2026 research, OneStream ranked first overall in all three of our Buyers Guides for Record to Report, Financial Close and Financial Consolidation, and was rated Exemplary in each."

"When the market is shifting beneath them, Finance teams need to move fast, but they won't compromise on numbers they can trust," said Tom Shea, Founder and CEO at OneStream. "Ranking as a Leader and rated Exemplary across all three ISG Buyers Guides underscores how a trusted software provider like OneStream gives Finance leaders the control and confidence to report accurately and act decisively, with a platform they can rely on."

This achievement follows OneStream's recent recognition as one of three finalists in the ISG Software Innovation Awards in the Business & Technologies category.

For more information about OneStream's financial close and consolidation capabilities, visit https://www.onestream.com/solutions/financial-close-and-consolidation-software/.

#5567. The deal closed. When do the savings start?

For homebuilders, the timing of acquisition savings often comes down to the systems and Supplier connections already in place

Purchasing synergies can materially improve homebuilder acquisition savings and strengthen the economics of the deal. They can also be overstated when the deal model doesn’t fully reflect the cost and time required to achieve them.

Combining the purchasing volume of two builders should create leverage for better pricing and stronger margins. But before that leverage is real, someone has to determine what each company is buying, how their supplier agreements differ and what it will take to operate under a common set of processes.

That’s where the financial projections meet the realities of running the business.

I’ve worked on acquisition diligence and integration across different industries, and the question I believe deserves more attention isn’t how much a deal can save. It’s when those savings actually show up in the P&L. For homebuilders, technology has a significant role in the solution. Buying power only matters if you can use it Consider a builder acquiring a regional operation with established supplier relationships and a healthy pipeline of homes under construction. The opportunity is clear. The combined company is buying more materials across more communities, which should create leverage to negotiate better terms. Now look at what has to happen to capture those savings. The acquired company may use a different ERP, organize its purchasing data differently or have supplier agreements that don’t align with the parent company’s contracts. Before purchasing leadership can negotiate from a position of combined volume, they need an accurate, combined view of what that volume actually is. Meanwhile, both businesses still have homes to build. Construction schedules can’t be put on hold while systems are reconciled. It’s entirely possible to have a sound purchasing strategy and spend the first several months after closing working through the operational issues that prevent successful execution. As builders know better than anyone, these delays carry real cost. If the acquisition model assumes purchasing savings will start contributing to margin within two quarters and integration takes a year, you won’t get the return you underwrote. The savings may still arrive, but every quarter of delay is value that doesn’t come back. This matters even more when interest rates are high. There’s usually a second cost hiding in the same delay: running two sets of systems, two sets of processes and often two teams doing the same work until integration is complete. Those dual running costs rarely get the same scrutiny as the synergy number. Homebuilder M&A integration is a financial decision Technology deserves a more prominent place in acquisition diligence and homebuilder M&A integration, particularly when operating efficiencies account for a meaningful share of the expected return. Knowing which applications a company runs is a starting point. The more important question is how those systems will work inside the larger organization, and what it will cost to get them there. Can the acquiring builder get reliable purchasing data across both businesses on day one? Can existing systems exchange the information needed to keep construction moving? What will it cost to maintain separate environments while integration is underway, and for how long? These sound like operating questions. They’re also valuation questions. The same applies to proprietary technology. Many builders have invested heavily in systems developed specifically for their businesses, and there can be good reasons for doing so. The challenge arises when those systems must accommodate an organization they weren’t originally designed to support. Custom integrations require people and capital to build. They also require ongoing security and maintenance as the business changes, and that cost doesn’t end when the integration goes live. I want to understand those costs before committing to an acquisition, not discover them in the first integration budget review. The advantage of an established network One factor that is often overlooked in technology discussions is the value of connectivity that already exists. A homebuilding operation depends on relationships with suppliers, manufacturers and trades that extend well beyond its internal systems. Those connections become particularly important when a company expands into new markets or brings another Builder into the organization. At Hyphen Solutions, we’ve spent more than 25 years building a network that connects hundreds of Builders and more than 18,000 suppliers, trades and manufacturers across North America. That matters because a builder operating within an established network isn’t starting from zero. In many acquisitions, the acquired builder’s suppliers are already on the same network as the parent company. When that’s the case, many of the connections the combined company needs exist before the deal closes, and purchasing teams aren’t onboarding suppliers a second time while homes are under construction. Our technology connects construction scheduling, purchasing and supplier communication, and integrates with different ERP and back-office environments. That gives purchasing leadership the combined view of orders, pricing and supplier activity across both businesses that consolidated buying depends on, without replacing every existing system first. We’ve seen this play out over the past year as a number of builders combined operations, and the ones that moved fastest had something in common. Their companies already shared many of the same suppliers and trades on the Hyphen network. Bringing everyone onto a single instance went quicker, and the trades doing the work in the field had a much simpler transition. Nobody was asking a framer to learn a new system in the middle of a build. There will still be work to do following an acquisition. Supplier contracts have to be evaluated, processes aligned and technology decisions made. No platform eliminates those responsibilities. But when connections and integrations are already in place, there’s less to build, and the combined company gets to consolidated purchasing sooner. From a financial standpoint, that shows up in two places: lower cost to achieve, and a shorter path to realized savings. Put a timeline behind the savings Acquisition models typically do a good job of identifying where value can be created. I would encourage builders to apply the same discipline to understanding what it will take to capture the expected value, and how much time and risk stand between the deal and the savings. If the investment thesis depends on consolidated purchasing, define what has to happen before the company can actually operate that way. Put a cost on the technology requirements. Build a realistic integration timeline into the model and align the timing of purchasing synergies with it. And ask these questions before an acquisition is on the table. The same infrastructure that supports integration also determines how efficiently a builder expands into new markets or adds divisions organically. For a CFO, the synergy number is only part of the picture. The timing and the cost to achieve it matter just as much to the investment decision. Before signing off on an expected savings number, I want to understand what has to change in the business for that number to become real. If technology integration is part of the answer, it needs to be part of the financial plan. Learn more about Hyphen Solutions and its connected residential construction network Click Here Related

Those connections become particularly important when a company expands into new markets or brings another Builder into the organization. At Hyphen Solutions, we’ve spent more than 25 years building a network that connects hundreds of Builders and more than 18,000 suppliers, trades and manufacturers across North America. That matters because a builder operating within an established network isn’t starting from zero. In many acquisitions, the acquired builder’s suppliers are already on the same network as the parent company. When that’s the case, many of the connections the combined company needs exist before the deal closes, and purchasing teams aren’t onboarding suppliers a second time while homes are under construction. Our technology connects construction scheduling, purchasing and supplier communication, and integrates with different ERP and back-office environments. That gives purchasing leadership the combined view of orders, pricing and supplier activity across both businesses that consolidated buying depends on, without replacing every existing system first. We’ve seen this play out over the past year as a number of builders combined operations, and the ones that moved fastest had something in common. Their companies already shared many of the same suppliers and trades on the Hyphen network. Bringing everyone onto a single instance went quicker, and the trades doing the work in the field had a much simpler transition. Nobody was asking a framer to learn a new system in the middle of a build. There will still be work to do following an acquisition. Supplier contracts have to be evaluated, processes aligned and technology decisions made. No platform eliminates those responsibilities. But when connections and integrations are already in place, there’s less to build, and the combined company gets to consolidated purchasing sooner. From a financial standpoint, that shows up in two places: lower cost to achieve, and a shorter path to realized savings. Put a timeline behind the savings Acquisition models typically do a good job of identifying where value can be created. I would encourage builders to apply the same discipline to understanding what it will take to capture the expected value, and how much time and risk stand between the deal and the savings. If the investment thesis depends on consolidated purchasing, define what has to happen before the company can actually operate that way. Put a cost on the technology requirements. Build a realistic integration timeline into the model and align the timing of purchasing synergies with it. And ask these questions before an acquisition is on the table. The same infrastructure that supports integration also determines how efficiently a builder expands into new markets or adds divisions organically. For a CFO, the synergy number is only part of the picture. The timing and the cost to achieve it matter just as much to the investment decision. Before signing off on an expected savings number, I want to understand what has to change in the business for that number to become real. If technology integration is part of the answer, it needs to be part of the financial plan. Learn more about Hyphen Solutions and its connected residential construction network Click Here Related

Meanwhile, both businesses still have homes to build. Construction schedules can’t be put on hold while systems are reconciled. It’s entirely possible to have a sound purchasing strategy and spend the first several months after closing working through the operational issues that prevent successful execution. As builders know better than anyone, these delays carry real cost. If the acquisition model assumes purchasing savings will start contributing to margin within two quarters and integration takes a year, you won’t get the return you underwrote. The savings may still arrive, but every quarter of delay is value that doesn’t come back. This matters even more when interest rates are high. There’s usually a second cost hiding in the same delay: running two sets of systems, two sets of processes and often two teams doing the same work until integration is complete. Those dual running costs rarely get the same scrutiny as the synergy number. Homebuilder M&A integration is a financial decision Technology deserves a more prominent place in acquisition diligence and homebuilder M&A integration, particularly when operating efficiencies account for a meaningful share of the expected return. Knowing which applications a company runs is a starting point. The more important question is how those systems will work inside the larger organization, and what it will cost to get them there. Can the acquiring builder get reliable purchasing data across both businesses on day one? Can existing systems exchange the information needed to keep construction moving? What will it cost to maintain separate environments while integration is underway, and for how long? These sound like operating questions. They’re also valuation questions. The same applies to proprietary technology. Many builders have invested heavily in systems developed specifically for their businesses, and there can be good reasons for doing so. The challenge arises when those systems must accommodate an organization they weren’t originally designed to support. Custom integrations require people and capital to build. They also require ongoing security and maintenance as the business changes, and that cost doesn’t end when the integration goes live. I want to understand those costs before committing to an acquisition, not discover them in the first integration budget review. A homebuilding operation depends on relationships with suppliers, manufacturers and trades that extend well beyond its internal systems. Those connections become particularly important when a company expands into new markets or brings another Builder into the organization. At Hyphen Solutions, we’ve spent more than 25 years building a network that connects hundreds of Builders and more than 18,000 suppliers, trades and manufacturers across North America. That matters because a builder operating within an established network isn’t starting from zero. In many acquisitions, the acquired builder’s suppliers are already on the same network as the parent company. When that’s the case, many of the connections the combined company needs exist before the deal closes, and purchasing teams aren’t onboarding suppliers a second time while homes are under construction. Our technology connects construction scheduling, purchasing and supplier communication, and integrates with different ERP and back-office environments. That gives purchasing leadership the combined view of orders, pricing and supplier activity across both businesses that consolidated buying depends on, without replacing every existing system first. We’ve seen this play out over the past year as a number of builders combined operations, and the ones that moved fastest had something in common. Their companies already shared many of the same suppliers and trades on the Hyphen network. Bringing everyone onto a single instance went quicker, and the trades doing the work in the field had a much simpler transition. Nobody was asking a framer to learn a new system in the middle of a build. There will still be work to do following an acquisition. Supplier contracts have to be evaluated, processes aligned and technology decisions made. No platform eliminates those responsibilities. But when connections and integrations are already in place, there’s less to build, and the combined company gets to consolidated purchasing sooner. From a financial standpoint, that shows up in two places: lower cost to achieve, and a shorter path to realized savings. Put a timeline behind the savings Acquisition models typically do a good job of identifying where value can be created. I would encourage builders to apply the same discipline to understanding what it will take to capture the expected value, and how much time and risk stand between the deal and the savings. Build a realistic integration timeline into the model and align the timing of purchasing synergies with it. And ask these questions before an acquisition is on the table. #5566. 21X AG and LayerZero Deliver Institutional-Grade Onchain Trading Pilot on Private-Permissioned Deployment of Zero

Joint pilot ran 21X AG's live central limit order book on a private-permissioned instance of Zero, delivering up to a 45x improvement in performance with no offchain matching

VANCOUVER, BC and FRANKFURT, Germany, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- LayerZero, a leading interoperability protocol behind more than $300 billion in cross-chain volume, today released the results of a joint technical pilot with 21X AG, the first venue licensed under the EU's DLT Pilot Regime to operate both trading and settlement from a single source.

The month-long pilot, which focused on US equity tokens, ran 21X AG's fully onchain central limit order book on a private-permissioned instance of Zero and benchmarked the results against other common public and private EVM networks. The pilot recorded 10,000 matches per second, a 45x improvement compared to the L2 EVM baseline.

"Capital markets are already moving onchain, and throughput across the industry is rising fast. What institutions need next is infrastructure that can carry real order flow at full scale without compromise," said Bryan Pellegrino, Co-Founder and CEO of LayerZero. "We built Zero for exactly that, with a novel architecture designed for the scale and performance institutions require. We're excited to partner with 21X AG to develop one of the world's fastest EVM for high-performance, institutional use cases."

A CLOB pilot on a private-permissioned instance of ZeroA central limit order book is the mechanism that matches buyers and sellers at a trading venue. Running one entirely onchain often hits limitations due to the underlying infrastructure, which typically encounters constraints impacting the number of matches per second to support institutional order flow. Venues that refer to themselves as onchain typically match orders on private servers and post results to a chain afterward.

21X AG's CLOB was built to run onchain with no offchain matching and is live in production in Europe, demonstrating the viability of the approach for trading and settlement of regulated financial instruments, with appropriate regulatory approval. The joint pilot with LayerZero indicates that the same approach can reach materially higher throughput on EVM.

"Our pilot demonstrates that the Zero blockchain architecture enables a regulated venue to run institutional order flow, end to end, entirely onchain," stated Max Heinzle, Founder and CEO of 21X Group. "We're excited to continue exploring how the performance can be improved even further with more tuning."

Built on a private-permissioned instance of ZeroZero is the blockchain LayerZero announced in February in collaboration with Citadel Securities, the DTCC, ARK Invest, and the Intercontinental Exchange. The 21X AG pilot was deployed on a private-permissioned instance of Zero, which gives institutions control over network participation and data visibility, while preserving compatibility with the broader EVM and multi-chain ecosystem. 21X AG continues to operate its live multi-chain infrastructure alongside it.

Performance by the numbersThe pilot set out to quantify Zero's throughput against common EVM networks used in capital markets and to establish a baseline for further optimization. Over a month of continuous testing on a private-permissioned instance of Zero, it recorded 10,000 order matches per second with headroom to go further, up to a 45x improvement over the EVM deployments used as a baseline, with matching and settlement completed in the same transaction.

About LayerZeroLayerZero is the interoperability protocol that allows assets and applications to move across blockchains. LayerZero powers the OFT Standard and has facilitated more than $300 billion in cross-chain volume across 165 blockchains. LayerZero is also the creator of Zero - the high-performance blockchain announced in February 2026 in collaboration with Citadel Securities, DTCC, ARK Invest and the Intercontinental Exchange - and LayerZero ATLAS, a headless exchange built for the future of global markets.

Learn more at https://layerzero.network/.

About 21X Group21X Group is an international financial market infrastructure group building regulated, tokenized capital markets, comprising 21X AG and 21X Service GmbH in Europe; and 21X LLC and 21X USA LLC in the United States.

In September 2025, 21X AG opened the first authorized distributed ledger technology trading and settlement system (DLT TSS) in the EU, positioning the company as a leader in the transition from traditional to tokenized asset-based capital markets. 21X AG operates its trading and settlement venue in the EU under BaFin (Bundesanstalt fÃ¼r Finanzdienstleistungsaufsicht) and ESMA (European Securities and Markets Authority) oversight. In September 2026, 21X Group announced its expansion into the US with the opening of a New York office and the operations of its US subsidiary, 21X LLC.

21X Group's infrastructure is designed to operate across multiple distributed ledger networks, adapted to the regulatory requirements of the markets in which it operates. 21X AG's platform in the EU enables atomic trading without counterparty risk through smart contract-based issuance, trading and settlement of tokenized stocks, bonds and funds.

See the video about 21X Group and our blockchain-based exchange here.

#5565. Beyond the credit report: How lenders can navigate the next era of mortgage credit

Advantage Partners Solutions’ Patrick Tynan explains why new scoring options, rising costs and evolving credit requirements are changing how lenders approach mortgage credit strategy.

New scoring models, evolving credit requirements and persistent cost pressures are forcing mortgage lenders to rethink their mortgage credit strategy. As the industry moves toward more flexible credit scoring, lenders must balance potential savings with risk, operational efficiency and borrower access.

In this conversation, Patrick Tynan, Chief Sales Officer at Advantage Partners Solutions (APS), discusses the impact of VantageScore 4.0, why cost per funded loan matters more than individual credit report pricing and how strategic CRA partnerships can help lenders prepare for what comes next.

HousingWire: Mortgage credit is entering a period of significant change, with new scoring models and continued cost pressure. Which shifts do you believe will have the greatest impact on lenders, and where should they be paying closer attention?

Patrick Tynan: One of the biggest changes I have seen in my career is happening right now, and it is VantageScore 4.0. For decades, lenders had one option. Now they have a real choice. Lenders can use VantageScore 4.0 today on most loans sold to Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac, and FHA begins accepting it on January 1.

I am a big believer in it. VantageScore 4.0 builds trended data into its scoring algorithm, so it can score borrowers who have thin files or who have worked hard to improve their credit. That means more people getting into homes without anyone lowering the bar, and it delivers significant savings compared with what lenders pay today.

Where I would tell lenders to slow down is the push to collect less information on the borrower. There is a lot of talk about pulling fewer bureaus, and I understand the appeal. But saving a few dollars by seeing less of the borrower is not a good trade. My advice is to take advantage of the new score option and keep the tri-merge credit report.

HW: As lenders evaluate adopting VantageScore 4.0 and other changes to the credit landscape, how should they balance potential cost savings with adapting workflows, implementation and borrower experience?

PT: Here is what I tell every lender I sit down with: When it comes to credit, there is no one-size-fits-all. A shop doing heavy purchase business with a lot of preapprovals runs completely differently than one with strong pull-through. Some lenders come out ahead paying per report. Others save a lot more with a bundled approach.

That is why we do not just hand someone a price sheet. We are a partner, not just a company that sells credit reports. We learn how a lender does business and build the pricing structure that saves them the most money and runs the most efficiently. The number I care about is cost per funded loan, not cost per pull, because only about one in five pulls ever closes. From there, make sure your systems, investors and MI partners are ready for VantageScore 4.0 and for FICO 10T down the road.

HW: As credit becomes more complex, how is the relationship between lenders and their credit providers evolving beyond a transactional service? What should lenders expect from a strategic CRA partner today?

PT: I came up on the lending side, managing teams at Wells Fargo and Countrywide, before I ever worked for a vendor. So, I know what it feels like to be the lender waiting on a report with a closing on the line. What has changed is that lenders need a lot more than a fast, accurate report now. They are deciding which score to use, how many bureaus to pull and when to pull them, and the rules keep moving under their feet. That is where a real partner earns their keep.

Tell them what a new rule means for their shop. Deliver the scores they need from all three bureaus without making them rip out their technology. Show them where every credit dollar is going. And answer the phone when a rescore is holding up a closing. If your credit provider only shows up when the invoice does, you do not have a partner. You have a vendor.

HW: Advantage Partners Solutions combines scale with a privately held structure and capabilities beyond credit reporting. How does that position APS to support lenders differently as market and vendor dynamics continue to shift?

PT: Advantage Partners Solutions is one of the top five credit resellers in the country by revenue, but we are one of the rare companies at that level that is privately held rather than owned by private equity or publicly traded. Our job is to bring the three bureaus together for our clients. Because we are not a bureau ourselves, we are not tied to any one source of data, so we can give lenders the complete tri-merge picture with whatever scoring model fits their business best – that independence matters to us. We make decisions based on what our clients need, not on an investor’s timeline or a quarterly earnings call, and that lets us move early.

VantageScore 4.0 is a good example of how we move early and in the best interests of our clients. We believed lenders and borrowers should have options, so we moved quickly to offer it.

Also, bringing Advantage Credit and Partners Credit & Verifications together gave us the scale to keep investing in technology and people, so our clients are not rebuilding workflows every time the rules shift. It also means we are a fully stocked provider of credit, verification services, flood certifications, and a full suite of QC products with the same breadth lenders expect from the largest companies in our industry. Lenders can rely on one partner across more of the loan file instead of managing a long list of vendors.

HW: Looking ahead, what changes do you expect to reshape mortgage credit over the next several years, and what should lenders be doing now to make sure their credit strategy can adapt?

PT: A few years from now, I think having multiple score options will simply be how business gets done. More data, such as rent payments and other nontraditional tradelines, will feed into scoring, but the cost pressure is not going away. The rules are still moving, too.

FHFA has said it is reviewing both the credit report requirement and loan-level pricing, so lenders should expect more change, and likely soon. With that said, our positions is simple: keep the tri-merge. It is the safest and fairest way to evaluate a borrower, and there are smarter ways to save money than pulling less data.

My advice is not to wait for a final rule. We are actively working with our lenders to create a mortgage credit strategy. We are making sure our technology is ready for VantageScore 4.0. The lenders who do that work now will be the ones ahead when the next announcement comes.

#5564. Oumi’s Frontier AI Engineer now builds AI agents and retrains the models behind them

Enterprise artificial intelligence platform company Oumi PBC today extended its Frontier AI Engineer agent so it can build AI agents for customers and retrain the models those agents run on.

The release goes after a problem that tends to surface once agents leave the demo stage. A failing agent might have a bad prompt, a broken tool or a weak underlying model.

Oumi says enterprises have traditionally tried to fix it with prompt and harness engineering because retraining a model’s weights has required skills normally found at frontier AI labs. That approach often stalls before the agent is reliable enough to put to work.

Oumi’s Frontier AI Engineer already sets objectives, designs evaluations and runs training experiments for custom models on its platform. With today’s update, a team can describe in plain language what it wants an agent to accomplish, and FAiE helps define the tools and environments that agent needs before moving on to evaluation and training. Whatever goes wrong once the agent is in production is turned into evaluation sets and training data for the next round.

Co-founder and Chief Executive Manos Koukoumidis said better prompts and bigger generic models will only take agents so far. The ones that succeed will improve “by training the weights of the models powering them, learning from their own work,” he said, pointing to failed tasks and user preferences as the signals that count.

Companies that already run agents elsewhere can keep them there. Under a feature Oumi calls Bring Your Own Harness, the customer’s orchestration, tools and memory stay put and connect to Oumi for evaluation and model training. Models end up tuned in the same environment the agent works in every day.

Oumi is also adding direct preference optimization to the supervised fine-tuning it already supported, so a model can be trained on examples of the behavior users preferred. Reinforcement learning arrives through group relative policy optimization, which grades a model on task outcomes. Several methods can be chained together in a single multistage training run, and FAiE helps choose the strategy, set up rewards and diagnose problems along the way.

The training work feeds Oumi’s broader argument about model ownership. Most enterprise agents run on general-purpose models from frontier AI providers that aren’t optimized for a particular customer’s work. The company’s pitch since launching a commercial platform for custom models in March has been that a specialized model the customer owns outright can do better work at lower cost.

Group relative policy optimization is launching in private preview, and the Seattle company is taking requests for access. Oumi is a venture capital-backed startup that raised a $10 million seed round led by Venrock Management and Obvious Management Services in January 2025. The founding team includes former engineering leaders from Google LLC’s Gemini group.
