#5563. What Solana’s Alpenglow Switch Actually Changes at Slot 459,653,000

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

For about 400 milliseconds this afternoon, Solana will stop landing user transactions. That isn't a failure.

It's the scheduled handoff between two consensus systems, and it's probably the only "400 ms" figure that matters today.

Many people heading into the Alpenglow launch still treat 400 ms block times and 12.8-second finality as the bar to beat. Those are the old chain's numbers. They describe TowerBFT, the system Alpenglow is replacing, so Alpenglow shouldn't be checked against them. If you go through Solana's own documentation, you'll find the right benchmarks before the first post-launch numbers arrive.

According to Solana's official Alpenglow page, the upgrade's feature gate activates at the start of epoch 1064 on Wednesday, October 21, at about 13:20 UTC. The Solana Foundation says to treat that time as an estimate and to watch the epoch instead.

The new consensus doesn't take over the moment the epoch begins. TowerBFT keeps running for the first 5,000 slots, and Alpenglow takes control at slot 459,653,000. Anza, the team behind the main Agave client, put that switch at around 14:00 UTC.

That time isn't fixed. Solana Compass calculated that with about 375,000 slots left before the switch, each millisecond of drift in average slot time moves the boundary by roughly six minutes. Using epoch 1062's pace, it estimated the switch at about 14:02 UTC.

The transition itself has a cost. Solana Compass reports a gap of roughly two slots, about 400 ms, during which blocks carry only votes and user transactions don't land. So the 400 ms everyone is watching for will turn up, just as a pause rather than a block time.

This is where much of today's coverage gets it wrong.

Block time first. Solana's page says slots moved from 400 ms to 200 ms in a separate "reduced slot times" upgrade, which finished this month. That change isn't part of Alpenglow. It was already running before today. Solana Compass measured epoch 1062 averaging 217.7 ms per slot over 26.1 hours. Checking Alpenglow against 400 ms would mean grading it against a number the network had already beaten before the switch.

Then finality. The 12.8 seconds is TowerBFT's figure. Under that system, a block became final only after enough votes built up over 32 slots. Alpenglow's stated target is about 150 ms, which Solana describes as 99% faster than TowerBFT.

Solana is careful about that 150 ms figure, and I think readers should be too. The Foundation calls it an expectation, not a constant, and says one-round finality comes in lower. Galaxy's engineers, quoted by Solana Compass, call it a design target rather than a measured result. As I noted when looking at how CertiK verifies a TPS claim, a target is a claim until someone measures it on the live network.

Alpenglow is Solana's first replacement of its core consensus since TowerBFT, and today's launch only covers part of it.

The first phase, Votor, ships in Agave 4.3. Validators now send votes directly to each other and combine them into certificates, instead of submitting votes as on-chain transactions. Per Solana's page, votes are no longer transactions and no longer appear in blocks. A block can finalize in one round if at least 80% of stake notarizes it. Otherwise, a second round uses 60% thresholds.

Proof of History no longer paces block production. Execution stays the same: the SVM, programs, transactions and fees don't change.

The second phase, Rotor, will replace Turbine, Solana's block propagation layer. Solana lists it as "not yet scheduled." If someone credits today's numbers to "Alpenglow" as a whole, half of the design hasn't shipped yet.

The security trade-off is also worth knowing. TowerBFT needed more than two-thirds of stake for confirmation. Alpenglow tolerates 20% malicious stake plus 20% offline stake. Solana Compass notes that slashing for double voting is defined but not enabled in this first version.

Validators also pay differently. TowerBFT voting cost about 1 SOL per epoch in vote transaction fees. Alpenglow replaces that with a flat 0.8 SOL per epoch Validator Admission Ticket (SIMD-0357), which is burned. A validator that can't pay doesn't vote or produce blocks in the next epoch.

In my view, this is the detail most likely to affect today's real numbers.

Alpenglow's fastest finality depends on the one-round fast path, which needs at least 80% of stake to notarize a block. On the morning of October 20, a tracker run by Pumpkin's Pool, cited by SolanaFloor and reported by Solana Compass, flagged 151 validators holding 20.3% of stake as unprepared. The day before, that figure was 45%.

The math is uncomfortable. If 20.3% of stake really couldn't vote, only 79.7% would be left, which is just short of the fast-path threshold. In that case, blocks would need the slower second round, and finality would land above the headline figure.

I expect that number to drop before the switch, since operators have been upgrading quickly. But it's the main reason I wouldn't trust any finality figure from the first hour without also checking how much stake is actually voting. Validators without a registered BLS key, or that miss the required client version, stop voting entirely. Their delegators also stop earning inflation rewards.

There's already one public reference point. Solana's page links to a community cluster explorer run by Valid Blocks, where Alpenglow has been running on Agave 4.3.2.

When I checked this morning, it showed an average finalization time of 131 ms over the past hour, ranging from 111 ms to 156 ms. Average slot time was 215 ms. That's inside Solana's target range.

That cluster had 62 active validators and about 10.2 million SOL staked. Mainnet is far larger, more spread out geographically, and runs under real load. Test-cluster results are a strong sign, but they aren't proof of how mainnet will perform.

You don't need to wait for a press release to know whether the switch happened. Solana's getAgGenesisCert RPC method returns null while the cluster is still on TowerBFT and returns a genesis certificate once Alpenglow is live. Nodes older than Agave 4.3 return a "Method not found" error, which shouldn't be confused with null.

Once the certificate shows up, here's what I'll be watching over the first few epochs:

One caveat for developers: according to Anza's operator notes, the Clock sysvar's unix_timestamp now estimates when the parent block ended, not when the current block began, and should be treated as approximate. Any timing tool that reads block timestamps may need adjusting.

If Alpenglow delivers, Solana goes from finality you wait for to finality you'd barely notice. I'll believe the 150 ms figure once mainnet consistently shows it.

#5562. Rogervoice Brings Free, Real-Time Captioning to In-Person Conversations

The captioning app for calls and in-person conversations now helps users follow everyday conversations in real time, with saved transcripts and on-device captioning that works offline.

NEW YORK, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Rogervoice, the AI-powered captioning app, today announced the launch of free in-person captioning. The new feature brings real-time captions and saved transcripts to face-to-face conversations, helping users keep up with the moments that matter, from work meetings and doctor's appointments to dinners with friends and family.

Not every conversation happens on the phone. There's the client lunch where someone rattles off a deadline, the pharmacy counter where you need to catch every detail, or catching up with a friend or family member. Rogervoice's new in-person captioning feature lets users read along as conversations happen, so they can stay in the moment and revisit the details afterward.

"I used to rely on two separate apps for phone calls and for meetings or in-person events. Now Rogervoice has everything in one place, which makes it so much simpler. I love that the captions are real-time, just like on my calls, and that they're saved so I can go back to them whenever I need. As someone who is hard of hearing, having real-time captions makes everything easier," said Brittany M., a Rogervoice user.

Available through the new Live tab in the Rogervoice app, in-person captioning is simple to use: open the app, start a session, and let the conversation unfold. Speech appears in real time in an adjustable, full-width caption area designed for readability. Captioning runs directly on the user's phone, works offline and is available in 45 languages on iPhone and 15 on Android. Afterward, users can revisit and export their saved transcripts.

"Earlier this year in our State of the Phone Call Survey, we found that 60% of Americans believe phone calls are not fully accessible to people who are deaf or hard of hearing. But conversations don't stop at the end of a call. People need to keep up at work, at the doctor's office and with the people they love. We built Rogervoice around that reality, and in-person captioning is another way to help people stay connected and keep moving on their own terms," said Olivier Jeannel, founder of Rogervoice, who has been deaf since age two.

The launch builds on Rogervoice's continued growth and recognition in 2026. Founded in 2014, the company has captioned more than 12 million calls in over 100 languages. Over the past few months, Rogervoice won The A.I. Awards (AI for Good) and the Hearing Technology Innovator Award (Captioning Technologies: Mobile Apps), was named as a finalist in The Anthem Awards and ranked No. 3 on TechRound's US50 list of American startups to watch.

Rogervoice brings phone-call and in-person captioning together in one app. Captioned calls are FCC-certified and free for eligible users, while in-person captioning is free. Captioning is AI-only, with no human listener on calls, no ads and no data sold. In-person captioning works offline and on-device, so conversation data never leaves the user's phone.

To download the free app, visit the App Store and Google Play, or go to rogervoice.com/app.

#5560. Assail Introduces Cassandra, a Proactive AI Agent Connecting Threat Modeling with Autonomous Security Testing

New capabilities in Ares identify emerging exposures, prioritize security assessments, and connect attack scenarios to validated findings and remediation verification.

BOSTON, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Assail, Inc., a developer of sovereign AI-powered offensive security platforms, today announced Cassandraâ¢, a proactive AI agent integrated into its Aresâ¢ platform, alongside expanded threat modeling capabilities that connect attack scenarios directly to autonomous security testing and remediation verification.

Cassandra continuously monitors changes across an organization's attack surface, identifies emerging exposures, prioritizes security activities, and prepares assessment and retest plans. Combined with Ares Threat Models, these capabilities help security teams move beyond identifying potential vulnerabilities to understanding which attack paths can be exploited, what requires attention, and whether remediation efforts have been successful.

Unlike traditional security tools that rely on periodic assessments and disconnected reporting, Ares connects threat modeling, autonomous testing, and verification in a coordinated workflow. Cassandra serves as the proactive intelligence layer, identifying changes and recommending next steps while keeping operators in control of testing decisions.

"Security teams need to know what attackers can exploit and whether their fixes work. We built Cassandra and threat modeling into Ares to help them answer those questions and act on the results," said Alissa Knight, CEO of Assail. "We're connecting those two disciplines inside Ares. Cassandra helps teams decide what to test next. Ares tests it, shows what attackers can exploit, and checks whether the fixes work."

Cassandra: Turning Security Intelligence into Action

Cassandra introduces a proactive approach to security operations by bringing critical exposures, attack surface changes, and recommended actions directly into the Ares operator experience.

Using existing assessment findings, asset information, and discovery results, Cassandra identifies newly exposed APIs, critical vulnerabilities, previously remediated issues that have resurfaced, and newly discovered assets. She explains why changes matter, connects findings to supporting evidence, and recommends appropriate next steps.

Security teams can use Cassandra to summarize recent activity, identify outstanding risks, prepare assessment and retest plans, and coordinate follow-up through Ares, email, or Slack. Cassandra also maintains operator-defined restrictions, including excluded targets and deferred testing activities.

Organizations retain operational control through configurable modes: Brief Only, Draft for Me, and Act on Approval. Every assessment initiated through Cassandra requires human approval and remains subject to authorization, permissions, and established scope controls.

Importantly, Cassandra distinguishes completed assessments from interrupted or failed testing, ensuring incomplete results are not mistaken for evidence that a system is secure.

Threat Models: Connecting Attack Scenarios to Evidence

Ares Threat Models extends traditional threat modeling by connecting potential attack scenarios to the results of authorized autonomous security assessments.

Security teams can map application components, system relationships, sensitive data, and potential attack paths, whether evaluating an existing application or a system still in development. Ares then translates relevant scenarios into testing objectives, helping teams determine which threats are exploitable and which remain unverified.

Assessment results feed directly into the threat model, distinguishing successful attacks, unsuccessful attempts, and scenarios requiring additional testing. Findings remain connected to supporting evidence, corrective actions, and subsequent verification.

As environments change, Ares incorporates new assessment evidence while preserving customer-authored scenarios and decisions. Proposed AI-generated changes to system diagrams remain subject to operator review, ensuring teams maintain control over their security models and risk decisions.

A Continuous Cycle of Discovery, Testing, and Verification

Together, Cassandra and Threat Models establish a connected process for identifying exposures, validating attack scenarios, and verifying remediation.

For example, when Ares discovers an undocumented API endpoint, Cassandra can flag the exposure and associate it with an existing authorization threat. Ares can then execute an approved assessment, attach the findings to the relevant threat scenario, and update the model. Following remediation, Cassandra can prepare a retest plan for operator approval.

This integrated approach reduces the disconnect between what security teams believe could happen, what autonomous testing demonstrates, and what remains unresolved.

Cassandra and Threat Models operate within Ares, Assail's expeditionary offensive security platform designed for enterprise and mission-critical environments.

Through Assail Anywhereâ¢, organizations can deploy the platform and its AI model through SaaS, within their own cloud infrastructure, on-premises, or in disconnected and air-gapped environments. This deployment flexibility enables organizations to maintain control over sensitive data, testing operations, and AI infrastructure without sacrificing autonomous security capabilities.

Assail builds sovereign AI-powered offensive security platforms for enterprise, federal, and defense organizations. Its expeditionary-by-design platforms discover attack surfaces, test applications and APIs, validate vulnerabilities and attack paths, and support remediation verification. Through Assail Anywhere, organizations can deploy the platform and its AI model through SaaS, in their own cloud, on-premises, or in isolated and air-gapped environments.

#5559. Descope launches Envoy to let consumer apps accept personal AI agents as users

Customer and agentic identity platform company Descope Inc. today launched Envoy, a service that lets consumer websites and apps accept personal artificial intelligence agents acting for their customers without rebuilding how people sign in.

Agents arriving through Envoy get an identity of their own, separate from the customer’s. The launch goes after a choice consumer businesses have been stuck with since agents such as Meta Platforms Inc.’s Muse started shopping and paying for things on people’s behalf.

Amazon.com Inc. blocked Muse from its store in September, saying the agent did not identify itself as one when placing orders, and JPMorgan Chase & Co. moved a month later to keep outside agents away from customer bank accounts. Descope expects blocking will get harder to maintain as more customers do their shopping through an agent.

The alternative, in Descope’s telling, is an agent that signs in as the customer with the person’s own password and one-time code. Nothing in that session shows software was involved, so when a fraud rule fires the logs point at the person. The business ends up absorbing the cost in disputed orders and returns.

Envoy is built around a proposed standard that offers a third option. Meta and Sierra Technologies Inc. published a 0.1 draft of the Personal Agent Protocol in October to set rules for how an agent signs in for someone without posing as them. Under Poppy, as the draft is known, a business publishes the endpoints agents should use and verifies which agent is calling. The business then issues a session bound cryptographically to that agent until the interaction ends.

Developers who adopt Envoy do not have to implement Poppy themselves or keep pace with revisions to it. Descope runs discovery and agent identification, and agents need no advance registration because each one presents a published client metadata document. Session tokens are tied to a key the agent holds through the Demonstrating Proof of Possession standard. Envoy supports all three of the draft’s sign-in types.

Inside Envoy, businesses spell out what an agent is allowed to do on a customer’s account through the Rich Authorization Requests extension to OAuth. In the example Descope gives, a retailer could let a shopping agent place orders for a customer and still keep it away from the payment methods on file. How long any elevated access lasts is left to the retailer as well.

Sensitive actions can go back to the customer for approval on a separate channel, using Client-Initiated Backchannel Authentication. Another example from Descope has an agent booking travel hold a fare it found overnight and send the details to the customer’s phone for approval the next morning.

Every token and log entry records the customer and the agent as separate parties, so a company can revoke an agent’s access without signing the customer out. Envoy runs alongside whatever customer identity system a business already has.

Descope co-founder and Chief Executive Slavik Markovich said every login page on the internet was built for a person on the other side, and “that assumption no longer holds true.” In his view, the Personal Agent Protocol is doing for consumer agents what the Model Context Protocol did for enterprise tools.

GoFundMe Inc. and GoodRx Holdings Inc. are among the launch and design partners working with Descope on Envoy over the coming months. Each donation on GoFundMe is “an act of trust,” according to Arnie Katz, the fundraising platform’s chief product and technology officer. He said Envoy will keep the donor and the agent distinct in every session and ask users to approve donations from their phones.

At GoodRx, Chief Technology Officer Nitin Shingate expects people to send agents out to compare pharmacies and find the lowest price on a prescription before they reach the counter. Agents there will get limited permissions covering pricing information.

Agent builders get a tool of their own. A Poppy software development kit, released alongside Envoy, lets any agent work with the protocol, with Descope handling discovery and session management behind it. The kit is written in TypeScript and has no external dependencies.

#5558. Finastra's Innovating Finance Together Summit Explores What's Next for Financial Services Modernization

Event explores the priorities shaping financial services as institutions balance innovation, resilience, and growth

NEW YORK, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Finastra's third Innovating Finance Together Summit, held in New York, brought together financial industry leaders and innovators from across North America to explore the trends shaping lending, trade, and payments.

A central theme was that financial institutions are entering a new phase of modernization, where success is defined not by deploying new technology, but by extracting greater value from existing investments. Throughout the event, speakers highlighted that adoption has not necessarily kept pace with innovation, particularly as institutions navigate the convergence of AI, security, geopolitical volatility and evolving payments infrastructure.

Institutions should focus investment on a smaller, core portfolio, modernize existing platforms to improve interoperability, and use AI to deliver operational efficiencies while maintaining security, resilience and reliable money movement. Existing instant payments infrastructure remains underutilized, highlighting the need for modern API-based architecture and accessible data to support sustainable growth.

"What struck me most was how much common ground there is across the industry.  Banks want to innovate, but they also need to get more from the technology they already have while ensuring that their systems remain secure, reliable, and resilient. The conversation is shifting from what's possible to what actually delivers value for customers.  And that's exactly where it should be," said Chris Walters, CEO, Finastra."

Security and resilience emerged as critical priorities as financial institutions continue to modernize. As cyber threats become more sophisticated, financial institutions need technology environments that can adapt quickly, address vulnerabilities, and maintain resilience. Modern architecture can make it easier to deliver updates, strengthen security, and respond to emerging risks.

AI presents significant opportunities across lending, payments, and other banking operations, particularly where document handling, verification, and decision-making create bottlenecks across the workflow. Speakers emphasized the importance of starting with a clear business problem, rather than deploying AI for its own sake.  Success depends on understanding existing workflows, identifying where AI can make a difference, and keeping people involved in critical decisions, with security governance and accountability built in.

The underlying message was clear: extract value from the technology you have now. Competitive advantages will come from making smarter technology investments and getting more from existing systems while modernizing infrastructure, improving interoperability and adopting new capabilities that deliver measurable value.

#5557. "Where We Once Stood," a Vietnam War Documentary from Veterans United and Gary Sinise, Available to Stream on Prime Video Starting on Veterans Day

Veterans United Home Loans' first feature-length documentary follows a group of Vietnam Veterans returning to the country 50 years after the war's end

COLUMBIA, Mo., Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Veterans United Home Loans' first documentary, "Where We Once Stood," will be available to stream on Prime Video in the U.S. starting on Veterans Day. Executive produced and narrated by Golden Globe winner and longtime Veteran advocate Gary Sinise, the film follows a group of Vietnam Veterans returning to the country for the first time since the war.

Filmed in 2025 to mark the 50th anniversary of the Vietnam War's end, "Where We Once Stood" follows the Veterans as they revisit the pivotal places that defined their military service. Veterans United brought together Veterans from different branches of the military, many of whom had rarely spoken about their experiences, to face the memories they carried home and find healing alongside one another.

The documentary features Veterans from the U.S. Army, Marine Corps, Navy and Air Force. Among them are  Lt. Col. Robert "Bob" Jeffrey, who spent more than seven years as a prisoner of war in North Vietnam, including at the Hanoi Hilton, and Maj. James "Jim" Taylor, a Medal of Honor recipient who saved more than a dozen wounded soldiers during a nine-hour firefight in November 1967. Also featured is Capt. Buddie Joe "BJ" Penn, a naval aviator who became the first Black battalion officer at the U.S. Naval Academy and later the acting secretary of the Navy.

"I came home from Vietnam carrying a lot of anger and for years there were things I just didn't talk about," Penn said. "Going back with other Vietnam Veterans gave me the chance to share things I'd never told anyone before. Those conversations helped heal some of the wounds I have carried for more than 50 years. I don't think that healing would have happened if we hadn't made that trip together."

"None of the Veterans on this trip had returned to Vietnam since the war's end, and we wanted them to do it on their own terms," said Pam Swan, vice president of military relations at Veterans United Home Loans. "The men in this film represent just a handful of the millions who served, and their experiences are part of our nation's history. We owe it to that generation to make sure those stories are recorded, remembered and told in their own words."

The film screened in Washington, D.C., Nashville and aboard the USS Midway in San Diego.

More than 50 years after the end of the Vietnam War, the documentary offers viewers an opportunity to hear directly from those who served and better understand their experiences.

"These men returned to places where they fought and lost friends more than 50 years ago," said Gary Sinise. "Many Vietnam Veterans didn't receive the welcome home they deserved, and this film is another opportunity to recognize them and make sure their experiences aren't forgotten."

To watch the trailer and learn more about "Where We Once Stood" and the Veterans featured, visit WhereWeOnceStoodFilm.com.

#5556. Pump.fun Perps on Hyperliquid: How the 0.10% Builder Fee Works

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On a $10,000 Bitcoin perpetual order placed through Pump.fun, Pump.fun can charge up to $10.

Hyperliquid, the exchange that actually matches and settles the trade, charges a standard taker $4.50. Only one of those fees has a written rule sending it toward a token burn, and it's Hyperliquid's.

Most launch coverage focused on whether to buy HYPE or SOL. The more useful question for PUMP holders is where each dollar of perps fees goes. When you compare Pump.fun's fee schedule, its buyback methodology and Hyperliquid's fee documentation, then, you'll see they don't connect the way many people assume.

Pump.fun didn't build a derivatives exchange. Its perps run on Hyperliquid's order books through builder codes, a feature that lets outside apps send user orders to Hyperliquid and add their own fee on top. Hyperliquid's engine handles matching, margin and liquidations.

The product first appeared in Pump.fun's API around October 9, when Wu Blockchain spotted a /coins/perps endpoint showing prices, funding rates, open interest and maximum leverage, all pulled from Hyperliquid's mainnet. The same endpoint also listed SOL, Nvidia, Tesla, gold and crude oil contracts. Trading launched around October 16 and 17, with up to 40x leverage on BTC and 25x on ETH reported at launch.

Pump.fun updated its terms and conditions on October 17. The perps feature is blocked for users in the United States and Ontario, along with sanctioned parties.

Pump.fun's official fee schedule splits the cost of a perp trade into separate parts.

Here's the math on a $10,000 market order at entry-tier rates, assuming Pump.fun charges its full maximum:

For a maker order, the gap is wider: $1.50 to Hyperliquid and up to $10 to Pump.fun. At full rate, the app routing the trade earns more per order than the exchange that runs it. Note that 0.10% is the published maximum, not a confirmed rate for every trade.

This side of the trade has the clearest documentation. Hyperliquid says its fees are "entirely directed to the community," meaning its HLP vault, the assistance fund and market deployers.

The assistance fund converts trading fees into HYPE automatically as part of the chain's execution.

According to Hyperliquid's documentation,

So every Pump.fun perp trade feeds part of Hyperliquid's own token-burn mechanism through standard protocol rules. That share never touches Pump.fun's treasury.

There's one more possible layer. Some of the markets in Pump.fun's API, such as stocks and commodities, are the kind of contracts that third-party HIP-3 deployers usually run on Hyperliquid. Those deployers can set their own fee share. If Pump.fun lists them, another party joins the split.

Under Hyperliquid's builder code rules, the builder fee goes to the builder's address on Hyperliquid. Builders claim it through the standard referral-reward process. The fee is charged in the collateral asset, so for these markets it builds up in USDC on Hyperliquid, not in SOL on Solana.

That matters once you check Pump.fun's PUMP buyback methodology. The program puts 50% of revenue toward buying and burning PUMP. It defines revenue as income from:

Perps builder fees and bridge fees aren't on that list. The page also says buybacks aren't a commitment to future purchases, except as "deterministically programmed prior to April 29, 2026." Perps launched in October, so they weren't covered by that commitment.

To be fair to Pump.fun, the absence of a rule isn't proof that the money stays out of buybacks. Pump.fun could add perps to its revenue definition at any time. But as of today, no published Pump.fun document links a perps fee to a PUMP burn. Any connection would also need USDC moved off Hyperliquid and converted, because the buyback table records purchases in SOL.

This also changes how to read the buyback numbers I've covered before. The PUMP page shows $490.65 million in cumulative buybacks on its dashboard and $465 million in Newsletter #14. It also says the fee dashboard has misreported revenue and buyback amounts since Custom Pairs launched and that this "will be fixed soon." If perps revenue grows, Pump.fun's total income and the share that actually reaches PUMP burns could move further apart.

Hyperliquid makes the builder side of this traceable. It publishes daily fill files for each builder at:

[https://stats-data.hyperliquid.xyz/Mainnet/builder_fills/](https://stats-data.hyperliquid.xyz/Mainnet/builder_fills/){builder_address}/{YYYYMMDD}.csv.lz4

The builder address must be entirely lowercase. A builder's total collected fees also appear in Hyperliquid's referral info query.

Without Pump.fun's builder address in its fee schedule, terms or announcements, nobody outside the company can add up the actual perps revenue, which is the number that would show whether this product is a side feature or a real revenue line. Once that address is public, the next step is to check whether a matching amount ever shows up in the PUMP buyback table.

Until then, the honest answer is this: Hyperliquid's share has a documented path to a HYPE burn, while Pump.fun's share has a documented path into Pump.fun's own wallet.

SAN DIEGO, Nov. 4, 2026 /PRNewswire/ -- Mitchell, a leader in the development of innovative auto physical damage technology solutions, today announced plans to expand its collaboration with Tractable through a proposed, exclusive agreement focused on optimizing the vehicle intake process. #5554. Blueair 2-in-1 Pro review: Can one machine really do it all?

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The Blueair 2-in-1 Pro combines air purification and humidification in one appliance. Here's a look at its performance, features, price, and upkeep

If your home gets stuffy when the windows are closed and uncomfortably dry when the heat kicks on, you might find yourself shopping for an air purifier and a humidifier at the same time. The Blueair 2-in-1 Pro Purify + Humidify promises to take care of both problems with a single appliance.

Priced at $499.99, the tower combines HEPASilent air purification with evaporative humidification. It also has built-in sensors, automatic settings, and app controls that let you monitor air quality and humidity without constantly fiddling with the machine.

Having two appliances in one sounds convenient, especially if you're short on space. But at this price, convenience alone isn't enough. You'll still need to clean the humidifier, replace the filters, and find a permanent spot for a fairly large machine. The real question is whether the Blueair delivers enough performance to make those trade-offs worthwhile.

At $499.99, the Blueair 2-in-1 Pro is considerably more expensive than a standalone humidifier or many individual air purifiers. The price covers two functions in one 24.6-inch tower: HEPASilent air purification and InvisibleMist evaporative humidification. It’s designed for rooms up to 391 square feet, making it a better fit for a large bedroom or living room than a small bedside setup.

The purification system combines mechanical filtration with an electrostatic stage and is rated to remove up to 99.97% of airborne particles. The humidifier uses a washable wick to add moisture without producing visible mist. Because it relies on evaporation rather than ultrasonic mist, it also avoids the mineral residue, or white dust, that can come with hard tap water.

The 1.3-gallon tank is designed to provide up to 60 hours of humidification in auto mode, though actual runtime depends on room conditions and humidity settings. A top-fill design makes refilling easier, while a UV pump helps keep the water system fresh. The wick is designed to last up to a year.

The biggest advantage is having both systems work together. Built-in sensors monitor air quality and humidity, while auto mode adjusts operation to maintain the settings you choose. The companion app adds humidity targets, scheduling, filter-life tracking, and control over the unit's mood lighting.

The combination can be particularly useful during winter, when indoor heating often leaves rooms dry while closed windows allow dust and other particles to build up. Customer feedback is generally positive, with owners frequently mentioning quiet operation, straightforward setup, and noticeable improvements in room comfort. Some also appreciate being able to set a target humidity level and let the machine manage it.

The evaporative design is another practical plus. You can use regular tap water without worrying about the mineral dust associated with some ultrasonic humidifiers. The washable wick and automatic drying cycle also help make routine care more manageable.

The price is only part of the commitment. The machine has two separate components to maintain: the particle filter and the humidifier wick. The main filter is listed at $54.99, while a replacement wick costs $39.99. Both are designed to last up to a year, but replacement costs are still worth factoring into the purchase. The washable wick helps keep that expense down, though it doesn't eliminate the need for regular cleaning and care.

There’s also an important distinction between particle filtration and odor removal. The unit is designed to capture airborne particles such as dust and allergens, but its filtration isn't a strong solution for cooking smells, pet odors, or chemical vapors. If those are your main concerns, a purifier with more substantial activated-carbon filtration may be a better choice.

Size is another consideration. At 18.5 pounds and more than 2 feet tall, this is a substantial appliance, not something you'll want to move from room to room regularly. Some owners also report that the water-level display and app could be more reliable. And because both functions share one machine, a problem with the unit could leave you without either purification or humidification.

The Blueair 2-in-1 Pro makes the most sense for people who regularly deal with dry indoor air and want better particle filtration at the same time. It's especially appealing for larger bedrooms and living spaces where running two separate appliances would take up more room.

The evaporative humidification system is a meaningful advantage for households with hard water, and the app controls make it easier to maintain a consistent humidity level without constantly adjusting the machine. But the $499.99 price is a lot to spend if you only need one of its two functions.

If odor removal is a priority, or you want a compact humidifier for a smaller room, there are better options. For households that genuinely need both cleaner air and added moisture, though, the Blueair offers a convenient all-in-one setup—as long as you're comfortable paying more upfront and keeping up with its maintenance.

#5552. Top tips for flying like a pro

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Travel like a pro with practical air travel tips for smoother airport visits, smarter packing, and better seats

Air travel has a funny way of testing your patience. One delayed flight can throw off an entire itinerary, a packed carry-on can turn security into a stressful obstacle course, and somehow the gate always seems to change right after you've found the perfect place to sit.

The good news is that most travel headaches aren't completely unavoidable. Small habits—checking in early, packing smarter, choosing the right seat and knowing what to do when plans change—can make the entire experience noticeably smoother. The best travelers aren't necessarily the ones who fly the most. They're often the ones who've learned a handful of practical tricks that save time, reduce stress and help them stay flexible when airports get chaotic.

Reader's Digest has rounded up some of the simplest habits that can make flying easier, from handling cancellations more effectively to avoiding common airport mistakes before they happen. Many of these tips don't cost anything, and several take just a few minutes to put into practice before you leave home.

Whether you're heading out for a weekend getaway, a business trip or a long-awaited vacation, these practical strategies can help you move through the airport with a little more confidence—and hopefully spend less time dealing with travel frustrations and more time looking forward to your destination.

When a flight gets canceled, most passengers instinctively head straight for the gate desk. According to Reader's Digest, a better strategy is to join the line while calling the airline at the same time.

Gate agents are suddenly responsible for helping dozens—sometimes hundreds—of frustrated travelers all at once. Phone agents are often able to access the same reservation system and may reach your booking before the line moves very far.

This approach gives you two chances to solve the problem instead of relying on one.

If the phone agent finds another flight first, you can step out of line. If the call takes longer than expected, you're still holding your place at the counter.

It's one of those travel habits that becomes especially valuable during storms or other widespread disruptions, when every minute matters. Rebooking quickly can mean the difference between getting another flight the same day and waiting until tomorrow.

Reader's Digest points out that staying proactive during cancellations usually works better than waiting for the situation to sort itself out. The earlier you start exploring alternatives, the more options you're likely to have before other passengers claim them.

Checking in before you arrive at the airport does more than save a little time.

According to Reader's Digest, checking in early can also improve your chances of getting a better seat and may even help you earn bonus miles, depending on your airline.

Many airlines release or reshuffle available seats as check-in opens, so waiting until you arrive at the airport can leave fewer desirable options. If you're hoping for a window seat, an aisle seat or simply a little more legroom, checking in as soon as you're eligible gives you more flexibility. It also makes the airport experience simpler.

Instead of standing at a kiosk or waiting for an agent to print your boarding pass, you can head directly toward security if you're traveling with only a carry-on. Reader's Digest notes that this is one of the easiest travel habits to build because it takes only a few minutes and can pay off before your trip even begins.

Sometimes the smallest tasks have the biggest impact.

Few things slow down a security line faster than digging through your suitcase for a tiny bag of liquids.

Reader's Digest recommends keeping travel-size toiletries in an easily accessible pocket of your carry-on instead of burying them beneath clothes and shoes.The same can apply to electronics if you need to remove them during screening.

Having everything within reach makes the process smoother for you and for everyone waiting behind you. The standard liquid rules still matter too: containers should be 3.4 ounces or smaller and stored inside a quart-sized bag when required.

This becomes even more valuable when you're rushing through a busy airport or trying to make a tight connection. A little organization before you leave home can save several minutes, and a surprising amount of frustration.

A carry-on that fits one airline may not fit another. According to Reader's Digest, airlines use different size limits for overhead bags, and a suitcase that technically fit on your last trip could become a gate-check surprise on your next one. Even if you know your suitcase's advertised dimensions, it's worth measuring it after you've packed it.

A fully stuffed soft-sided bag can expand beyond its listed size. Checking the measurements ahead of time helps you avoid unexpected fees, last-minute repacking and the stress of wondering whether your bag will fit into the sizing frame at the gate.

It's a quick step that can prevent an expensive travel mistake.

First class may sound appealing, but it's not necessarily the smoothest place to sit. Reader's Digest explains that passengers who experience motion sickness often have a more comfortable ride near the middle of the aircraft, where movement tends to feel less dramatic.

Think of the airplane like a seesaw. The farther you are from the center, the more noticeable the motion can become. If turbulence usually leaves you feeling uncomfortable, choosing a seat closer to the wings may help make the flight feel steadier.

You may not eliminate turbulence entirely, but you can make it feel a little less overwhelming.

#5550. Data centers are learning to be flexible

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Data centers are driving up electricity demand, but flexible power use could ease grid congestion and speed up connections

Jim West/UCG/Universal Images Group via Getty Images

A version of this article originally appeared in Quartz’s AI & Tech newsletter. Sign up here to get the latest AI & tech news, analysis and insights straight to your inbox.

Picture a soccer club that bought a passenger van for its tournaments a few times a year. The van sits in a driveway the rest of the year. Buying it was the right call, because a van that wasn’t there on tournament weekend would have stranded the team.

The American power grid works the same way, and now we have numbers to show just how little of it gets used. This month, under a new state law, Virginia’s utilities reported theirs. Over the year ending in July, the distribution grid run by Dominion $D Energy, the utility behind the northern Virginia data center boom, was being used at 41% of its capacity on average.

Even in its busiest hours, the system averaged 80%, with some pockets running higher and others lower. In the state’s rural southwest, where demand has been falling, Appalachian Power reported 14% for the year and 54% at peak.

Grids are sized for the few hours a year when everyone runs the air conditioner at once, and building for those few hours is expensive. A data center that pulls full power around the clock raises that peak, and raising the peak means buying another van that mostly sits in the driveway, costing money while it gathers dust.

Researchers argued there might be a cheaper route than building, and it required something we prize in people: Flexibility. Duke $DUK researchers calculated that the existing grid could absorb nearly 100 gigawatts of new demand if the newcomers agreed to cut back its power use for roughly half a percent of the year.

The study caused a stir in energy circles, and Google $GOOGL hired its lead author. The idea came down to a trade. A customer accepts being throttled in the few hours when the local grid is stretched, and in return connects in months instead of years.

The clearest track record of this working belongs to California’s PG&E. EV charging companies, which draw heavily on the grid, saw the wait for power fall to four to eight months from one to three years before its Flex Connect pilot.

In the pilot’s first two years, the power participants asked for was there nine hours out of ten. In the hours it wasn’t, the limits cut into operations less than 1% of the time.

Batteries offered another way to ease the pressure at peak. In 2025, a data center company in Oregon secured a faster hookup from Portland General Electric $GE by agreeing to add a 31-megawatt battery, enough to run about 25,000 homes for two hours, that it could switch to if needed.

Others flexed the computing itself. Google started by putting off work that could wait whenever grids in Belgium and Taiwan ran tight. In 2024, it dialed back machine learning jobs three times when the grid around Omaha was under strain. This year it promised five utilities it would hold back as much as a gigawatt of data center demand when the grid was stretched.

Startups are selling software that slow, pause or relocate AI jobs when the grid is tight. There were plenty of ways to do it, and more kept coming.

Flexibility is already becoming required in some regions. A 2025 Texas law requires new large data centers to install equipment that lets the grid operator cut their power remotely in emergencies. Late last year, FERC, the federal agency that regulates the grid, directed the operator PJM to create interruptible transmission options for data centers built next to power plants. The Southwest Power Pool, which runs the grid across much of the Great Plains, made a similar move.

Of course, waiting is expensive, and data center queues in popular markets can run for years. Take an Nvidia $NVDA chip that costs $30,000 and is depreciated over three to five years, or $6,000 to $10,000 a year. Picture 100,000 of them in one cluster, waiting for power the way Microsoft $MSFT’s chief executive, Satya Nadella, said some of his company’s chips were last year. A year of waiting represents $600 million to $1 billion in potential computing value that goes unused.

The trade cost something on the other side too, although it was much less. For companies racing each other to build more powerful AI, even a few curtailed hours counted. If those 100,000 chips sat idle for the equivalent of 44 hours a year, the lost computing time would be worth $3 million to $5 million.

Flexibility will not fully replace the building the aging grid needs, because old equipment has to go regardless. But utilities planned to spend at least $1.4 trillion through 2030, with data centers and load growth among their top reasons, and a large transformer could take more than two years to arrive. Flexibility could shrink that bill, and that wait.

#5549. 10 of the biggest Social Security raises since automatic COLAs began in 1975

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Social Security COLA history includes 10 of the largest raises since 1975, from 14.3% for 1980 to 8.7% for 2023 and two 5.9% adjustments

Across five decades, the yearly raise for Social Security beneficiaries has ranged from 14.3% to nothing at all. That raise is the cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA. It sets how much benefit checks grow from one year to the next.

The automatic version of that raise traces back to the 1972 Social Security amendments. Those amendments linked future benefit increases to inflation. The first automatic COLA came with the 1975 adjustment, at 8.0%. Every COLA since then has been tied to the same price measure.

That measure is the Consumer Price Index for Urban Wage Earners and Clerical Workers, usually shortened to CPI-W. When the prices it tracks rise quickly, the COLA rises with them. When prices barely move, the raise shrinks. In some years there is no raise at all.

This list covers 10 of the largest automatic COLAs from 1975 through 2026, ordered from biggest to smallest. The 1977 and 2022 adjustments tied at 5.9%, and each gets its own entry. The 5.8% COLA for 2009 ranks 11th and falls just outside the selection.

The selection clusters heavily in one period. Every year from 1975 through 1982 appears, accounting for eight of the 10 entries. The 1980 COLA of 14.3% remains the largest of the automatic era, followed by 11.2% in 1981 and 9.9% in 1979. The other two entries are far more recent: 8.7% for 2023 and 5.9% for 2022.

Each of those recent raises was the largest in decades. The 2023 COLA was the largest since 1981, and the 2022 COLA was the largest since 1982. The adjustments that followed were smaller: 3.2% for 2024, 2.5% for 2025 and 2.8% for 2026. Beneficiaries received no COLA at all in 2010, 2011 or 2016.

The 2027 COLA has not been announced. This list stops at 2026. For readers tracing Social Security COLA history, the slides that follow place each of these 10 raises in that record.

The 1980 cost-of-living adjustment raised Social Security benefits by 14.3%. That is the largest automatic COLA from 1975 through 2026, and no adjustment in the decades since has matched it.

That puts 1980 at the center of a three-year stretch, 1979 through 1981, that produced the three largest automatic COLAs since 1975.

The gap between first and second place is wide. The 1980 figure topped the next-largest automatic COLA, for 1981, by 3.1 percentage points.

Only two automatic COLAs have reached double digits, and they came in back-to-back years. The 1980 adjustment is the higher of the pair.

No other pair of neighboring entries on this list sits that far apart. The rest of the selection steps down in much smaller increments, most of them a percentage point or less. The 1980 raise was more than twice the size of the 5.9% COLAs for 1977 and 2022, the smallest entries in this selection.

A COLA is a percentage, so its effect scales with the size of each check. Every beneficiary received the same 14.3% increase. A larger benefit therefore grew by a larger amount in dollars.

Every later COLA was applied to benefit levels that already included the 1980 raise, so the increase compounded over time.

The 1980 raise also far exceeded the adjustment that launched the automatic system. It came in 6.3 percentage points above the first automatic COLA, for 1975.

The modern era has not come near it. The 2023 COLA, the largest raise of recent decades, still fell 5.6 percentage points short of the 1980 mark.

More recent adjustments leave an even wider gap. The 1980 COLA was larger than the 2024, 2025 and 2026 adjustments added together.

It was also more than double the 2009 COLA, which ranks just outside this selection of the largest automatic raises.

The 1981 Social Security cost-of-living adjustment was 11.2%, the second-largest automatic COLA since the mechanism began in 1975. Only the 1980 adjustment was bigger.

The two years ran back to back. Together they account for the only double-digit raises from 1975 through 2026. Every other automatic adjustment in that span stayed below 10%.

The 1981 figure came in 3.1 percentage points below the 1980 COLA. It still exceeded every adjustment that followed it.

The steeper drop came a year later. The COLA for 1982 was 7.4%, a fall of 3.8 percentage points from 1981. That one-year decline was larger than the gap between the 1980 and 1981 raises.

The 1981 number later became the yardstick for a large modern raise. The 8.7% COLA for 2023 came closer to it than any adjustment since. It still fell 2.5 percentage points short. The two raises sit 42 years apart.

The 1982 raise arrived just one year after the 1981 COLA. Even so, it missed the 1981 figure by a wider margin than the 2023 adjustment did.

The 1981 adjustment closed out the double-digit years of the automatic era. No COLA since has reached 10%.

The 1979 cost-of-living adjustment raised Social Security benefits by 9.9%. It ranks third among automatic COLAs from 1975 through 2026, behind only the 1980 and 1981 adjustments.

The 1979 COLA fell 0.1 percentage point short of double digits. It is the only one of the top three that stayed below 10%. The two adjustments that followed both cleared that mark.

Together, 1979, 1980 and 1981 hold the top three places in the automatic era. They are the only years since 1975 with a COLA above 9%. They also ran back to back, with 1979 as the first of the three.

When the 1979 COLA arrived, it was the largest automatic adjustment yet. It was bigger than every raise before it, including the 1975 adjustment that launched the automatic system. It held that position for only a year. The 1980 COLA then surpassed it, and the 1981 COLA followed close behind.

In size, the 1979 raise sits nearer to 1981 than 1981 sits to the 1980 peak. The largest single jump in the run came between 1979 and 1980.

The 1979 figure also marked a break from the years just before it. The 1976 COLA was 6.4%. The 1977 COLA was 5.9%. The 1978 COLA was 6.5%. For three straight years, the adjustment stayed within a band of 0.6 percentage point.

The 1979 adjustment then landed 3.4 percentage points above the 1978 figure. That made it roughly one and a half times the size of the raise a year earlier.

The 1979 COLA was also 2.5 percentage points larger than the 7.4% COLA for 1982, the year after the three-year run ended.

No COLA after 1981 has reached the 1979 level. The closest later adjustment, for 2023, sits 1.2 percentage points below it. It was four percentage points larger than the 2022 COLA. The 2026 COLA was less than a third of the 1979 increase.

The 2023 cost-of-living adjustment lifted Social Security benefits by 8.7%. That made it the largest automatic increase since 1981, when the COLA reached 11.2%.

Those two adjustments sit 42 years apart. No COLA from 1982 through 2022 matched or exceeded 8.7%.

Among all automatic COLAs since 1975, the 2023 increase ranks fourth. Only the adjustments for 1980, 1981 and 1979 were larger. Those three came in consecutive years. That leaves 2023 as the only one of the four largest COLAs from outside that stretch.

The 2023 raise also topped the first automatic COLA. It finished 0.7 percentage points ahead of the 8.0% adjustment for 1975.

It still fell well short of the peak years. The 2023 figure trailed 1981's 11.2% by 2.5 percentage points. It sat 5.6 points below the 14.3% for 1980, the largest of the automatic era.

The 2023 adjustment is also the only COLA after 1982 to exceed 6%. Every other automatic COLA above that level came between 1975 and 1982. That put benefit growth back in a range not seen since the early years of the automatic system.

The 2023 increase followed a 5.9% COLA for 2022. The step from 5.9% to 8.7% added 2.8 percentage points in a single year. Each COLA applies to the benefit amount already in place. That means the 2023 raise built on checks that had already grown by 5.9% the year before.

Back-to-back large COLAs also appeared in the late 1970s and early 1980s. The 2022 and 2023 pair is the only consecutive set in this selection from after 1982.

The Bureau of Labor Statistics produces the CPI-W, the price measure behind the 2023 figure.

The next adjustment was far smaller. The 2024 COLA came in 5.5 percentage points below the 2023 figure. Through 2026, no later adjustment has come close to 8.7%. It remains the most recent entry in this list.

The 1975 cost-of-living adjustment raised Social Security benefits by 8.0%. It was the first automatic COLA, and it ranks fifth among the largest automatic adjustments from 1975 through 2026.

That debut grew out of the 1972 Social Security amendments. Before then, benefit increases came only when Congress passed a law. The amendments set up annual raises that would take effect without a new vote each year. The 1975 adjustment was the first one delivered under that system.

Only four automatic COLAs from 1975 through 2026 topped that first raise. Three of them came in a back-to-back run for 1979, 1980 and 1981. The fourth was the 2023 COLA, which beat the 1975 figure by 0.7 percentage point.

The distance to the very top is much larger. The 1980 COLA came in 6.3 percentage points above the 1975 raise. That made it nearly 1.8 times the size of the first automatic adjustment.

Most adjustments in the mechanism's first eight years came in below the 1975 raise. The 1976, 1977 and 1978 COLAs each landed below 7%. None came within one percentage point of the 1975 figure.

The 1982 COLA came closest among those lower years. It reached 7.4%, finishing 0.6 percentage point short of the 1975 mark. That gap is the smallest between the first automatic COLA and any adjustment ranked below it on this list.

Measured against the modern era, the 1975 raise still sits near the top. Only the 2023 COLA has exceeded it since 1981. The 1975 adjustment topped the 2022 COLA by 2.1 percentage points. It also beat the 2009 adjustment, which falls just outside this selection, by 2.2 percentage points.

Recent raises fall well below that starting point. None of the COLAs for 2024, 2025 or 2026 reached half of the 1975 figure. Half of 8.0% is 4.0%.

The 1982 COLA raised Social Security benefits by 7.4%. It ranks sixth among the largest automatic adjustments since they began in 1975.

That rate stood as a high mark for decades. No later COLA matched or passed it until 2023.

The 1982 increase closed a four-year stretch in which every automatic COLA came in at 7.4% or higher. That stretch began with the 1979 adjustment. It peaked with the 1980 adjustment, the largest of the automatic era.

Within that stretch, 1982 was the smallest raise. It was 3.8 percentage points below the 1981 COLA. It was also a little more than half the size of the 1980 adjustment.

The step down did not mean benefits stopped growing. A 7.4% COLA still raised benefits. The change was in pace: beneficiaries received a smaller raise than in each of the three years before.

Among the early automatic COLAs in this selection, 1982 sits in the middle. It came in 0.6 percentage points below the first automatic COLA, for 1975. It topped the 1978 adjustment by 0.9 percentage points.

The years after 1982 look very different. No COLA from 1983 through 2021 made this selection. Even the 2009 raise, the largest in that long gap, stayed below the 1982 rate.

Before 2023, the 2022 adjustment came closest to the 1982 rate. It still fell 1.5 percentage points short.

The 2023 COLA was the first to pass the 1982 rate. It beat that rate by 1.3 percentage points.

Recent raises sit far below the 1982 level. Each COLA from 2024 through 2026 was less than half the 1982 rate.

The 1978 Social Security cost-of-living adjustment was 6.5%. It ranks seventh among the 10 automatic COLAs in this selection, just ahead of 1976's 6.4% and behind 1982's 7.4%.

The gap below it is narrow. Only 0.1 percentage points separate the 1978 and 1976 raises. The gap above is wider, at 0.9 percentage points to the 1982 COLA. The 1978 figure was also 1.5 percentage points below the first automatic COLA, 8.0% for 1975.

The figure came from a formula, not a vote in Congress. Like every automatic COLA since 1975, it tracked the CPI-W, a consumer price index for urban wage earners and clerical workers. The Bureau of Labor Statistics publishes that index.

The 6.5% applied as a percentage, not a flat amount. Each beneficiary's monthly benefit rose by the same share. A retiree with a larger check therefore received a larger dollar increase than one with a smaller check. The relative gain was identical for both.

The raise also applied on top of benefits that earlier automatic COLAs had already lifted. In practice, the 1978 increase built on the 1975, 1976 and 1977 adjustments rather than replacing them.

The 1978 COLA also broke a pattern. The 1976 and 1977 adjustments had each come in smaller than the year before. At 6.5%, the 1978 raise was 0.6 percentage points higher than 1977's 5.9%. It was the first automatic COLA to exceed the one before it.

Larger increases followed immediately. The 1979 COLA reached 9.9%, 3.4 percentage points above 1978. The 1980 COLA of 14.3% was more than double the 1978 figure.

The 1978 raise outranks the 2022 COLA, which matched 1977 at 5.9%. It sits 0.7 percentage points above the 5.8% COLA for 2009, which narrowly missed this selection. Of the two modern raises on this list, only the 8.7% COLA for 2023 was larger, by 2.2 percentage points. The 2026 COLA, at 2.8%, was less than half of 1978's figure.

The 1976 Social Security COLA raised benefits by 6.4%. It was the second automatic cost-of-living adjustment, arriving one year after the 8.0% increase that launched the system.

It was also the first time the automatic raise came in smaller than the one before it. The 1976 increase landed 1.6 percentage points below the 1975 COLA. That drop showed the automatic formula could deliver a smaller raise as well as a larger one.

The decline continued for one more year. The 1977 adjustment fell another half a percentage point, to 5.9%. That left the 1976 raise in the middle of a three-year slide.

The direction reversed after that. The 1978 COLA of 6.5% edged past the 1976 figure by a tenth of a percentage point. Then 1979 brought a 9.9% raise, 3.5 percentage points above the 1976 level.

The first four automatic COLAs stayed within a narrow band. From 1975 through 1978, every adjustment fell between 5.9% and 8.0%. The 1976 raise sat in the lower half of that range.

The larger raises came later. The 1980 COLA of 14.3% was 7.9 percentage points higher than the 1976 increase. That made the 1980 raise more than twice the 1976 figure.

Among the 10 adjustments in this selection, the 1976 COLA ranks eighth. It trails seven larger raises and finishes ahead of only the 1977 and 2022 adjustments. The lower end of the list is tightly packed. The gap between the seventh-place 1978 COLA and the two 5.9% raises at the bottom is smaller than the drop from 1975 to 1976 alone.

From 1983 through 2026, only one automatic COLA topped 6.4%. That was the 8.7% adjustment for 2023. The 5.9% COLA for 2022 fell short of the 1976 level by half a percentage point.

Recent adjustments have run lower. The 1976 figure is exactly twice the 3.2% COLA for 2024. It is 3.9 percentage points above the 2.5% raise for 2025 and 3.6 points above the 2.8% raise for 2026.

The 1977 cost-of-living adjustment raised Social Security benefits by 5.9%. That figure ties 1977 with 2022 among the largest automatic COLAs since the mechanism began in 1975.

The 1977 raise was the third automatic COLA. It followed 8.0% for 1975 and 6.4% for 1976. The adjustment for 1978 then rose to 6.5%.

That makes 1977 the smallest increase of the first four automatic years. It came in 2.1 percentage points below the 1975 raise. It trailed 1976 by 0.5 percentage point and 1978 by 0.6 percentage point.

Those figures show a short dip rather than a lasting turn. The COLA eased for two years, bottomed out at 5.9% and then started climbing again. Within two more years, it had reached 9.9% for 1979.

The 1977 adjustment was also the lowest of the eight straight years from 1975 through 1982. Every other COLA in that stretch was at least 6.4%.

The two 5.9% years sit 45 years apart, and they arrived from opposite directions. In 1977, 5.9% was a low point inside a run of large raises. The double-digit COLAs for 1980 and 1981 were still ahead.

In 2022, the same percentage marked a high point instead. It came after 39 straight years, from 1983 through 2021, in which no COLA reached 5.9%. The raise that set the floor of the early automatic era stood above every COLA paid in those 39 years.

The 2009 COLA came closest to joining the tie. At 5.8%, it fell 0.1 percentage point short of the level shared by 1977 and 2022. COLAs are stated to one decimal place. That means 2009 missed the tie by the smallest margin the published figures can show.

Both 5.9% years trail the 14.3% COLA for 1980 by 8.4 percentage points. A 5.9% raise is less than half the size of that peak.

The 2022 Social Security cost-of-living adjustment was 5.9%, the largest automatic raise since the 7.4% COLA for 1982. It came 40 years after that 1982 raise.

The 2022 figure sits 1.5 percentage points below the 1982 raise. From 1983 through 2021, Social Security had 39 annual adjustment years. Every adjustment in that span came in below 5.9%.

The closest was the 2009 COLA of 5.8%. It fell 0.1 percentage point short of the 2022 figure. Three years in the same span produced no increase at all: 2010, 2011 and 2016.

Each COLA tracks inflation as measured by the CPI-W. A 5.9% adjustment therefore reflected faster growth in that index than any adjustment year from 1983 through 2021 had shown.

The 2022 raise matched the 1977 COLA exactly. That tie links one of the earliest automatic adjustments with one of the most recent. The two raises are 45 years apart. They share the lowest spot in this selection of 10.

The 2022 adjustment held the post-1982 high mark for only one year. The next COLA, for 2023, was 8.7%. That made 2022 and 2023 back-to-back raises above 5%. The 2022 figure was 2.8 percentage points smaller than the 2023 increase.

The three adjustments after 2023 were all smaller than the 2022 raise. The 2024 COLA came in 2.7 percentage points lower. The 2025 COLA was 3.4 points lower. The 2026 COLA was 3.1 points lower.

The 2022 raise is also smaller than the peaks of the early automatic era. The 1980 COLA, the largest since automatic increases began in 1975, was 8.4 percentage points larger. The 1981 COLA was 5.3 points larger, and the 1979 COLA was 4.0 points larger. The first automatic COLA, for 1975, also topped the 2022 figure by 2.1 points. The 1982 COLA was itself the smallest of the three adjustments from 1980 through 1982.
