#5548. How a $2,000 Social Security benefit changes from age 62 to 70

Free daily briefing on global business news.

How much Social Security increases each year you wait depends on your full retirement age, early-claiming cuts and 8% delayed credits, shown here age by age from 62 to 70

The same work record can produce two very different Social Security checks. A worker whose full retirement age is 67 and who claims at 62 receives 70% of the full benefit. If that worker waits until 70, the check rises to 124%. That makes the later check about 77% larger each month, and the cut for claiming early is permanent.

The answer to how much Social Security increases each year you wait depends on which side of full retirement age a person is on. Before that age, every month of waiting shrinks a reduction the Social Security Administration applies for early claiming. After it, every month adds a delayed retirement credit worth 2/3 of 1%. That works out to 8% a year for anyone born in 1943 or later. The credits stop accruing at 70.

Full retirement age is not the same for everyone. It is 66 for people born from 1943 to 1954 and 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later. For birth years 1955 through 1959, it rises two months per year. Claiming at 62 leaves 75% of the full benefit when full retirement age is 66, compared with 70% when it is 67. Waiting until 70 pays 132% in the first case and 124% in the second.

The math does not end with the worker's own check. Delayed credits raise the benefit a surviving spouse can receive, but they do not raise a spousal benefit paid while both partners are alive. Working while claiming before full retirement age can trigger an earnings test that temporarily withholds payments. Cost-of-living adjustments, federal income taxes and the separate Medicare timeline at 65 also shape what a household receives.

The 10 slides below lay out each rule in turn. They cover retirement ages by birth year, the formulas behind the cuts and credits, an age-by-age payment table and simple break-even calculations. They also cover the rules for spouses, survivors, working claimants, taxes and Medicare. No single claiming age fits every household. Health, work plans, marital status and other income all change how the trade-off between a smaller check sooner and a larger check later plays out.

Full retirement age is 66 for anyone born from 1943 through 1954 and 67 for anyone born in 1960 or later. For the birth years 1955 through 1959, it rises by two months for each year, under Social Security Administration rules.

That middle group follows a fixed schedule. Someone born in 1955 reaches full retirement age at 66 and two months. A 1956 birth year moves it to 66 and four months. For 1957, it is 66 and six months. For 1958, it is 66 and eight months. People born in 1959 reach it at 66 and 10 months.

The age matters because the Social Security Administration measures every claiming decision against it. The monthly amount paid at full retirement age is the full, unreduced benefit. Claiming before that age triggers a reduction. Waiting past it raises the check through delayed retirement credits.

The two ends of the claiming range do not move. The earliest age to start retirement benefits is 62 for every birth year. Delayed credits stop building at 70 for every birth year. Only the midpoint shifts.

That shifting midpoint changes the length of both windows. With a full retirement age of 67, the early window runs 60 months and the delay window runs 36 months. With a full retirement age of 66, each window runs 48 months. A longer early window means a deeper possible cut at 62. A shorter delay window means fewer months of credits before 70.

The exact birth-year figure matters because the early reduction and the delayed credits are both calculated month by month. A person born in 1958 who assumes a full retirement age of 66 would misplace the starting point by eight months. Any estimate of a claim at 62 or at 70 would be off as a result.

Full retirement age is a benefit-calculation term, not a required stopping point for work. Every figure tied to claiming early or late is calculated from this one age. That includes the size of the cut at 62 and the size of the raise at 70.

Claiming Social Security retirement benefits before full retirement age permanently shrinks every monthly check. The Social Security Administration calculates the cut month by month, and starting at 62 removes 30% of the full benefit for anyone whose full retirement age is 67.

The formula has two tiers. Each of the 36 months closest to full retirement age lowers the benefit by 5/9 of 1%. That equals about 0.56% a month, or about 6.67% for each full year.

Every month beyond those 36 is reduced at a smaller rate of 5/12 of 1%. That comes to 5% for each additional year. Only claimants who start more than three years before full retirement age reach the second tier.

The two tiers add up at 62. Someone with a full retirement age of 67 who claims at 62 is 60 months early. The first 36 months subtract 20%. The remaining 24 months subtract another 10%, for the full 30% cut.

A person whose full retirement age is 66 is 48 months early at 62. The first tier again takes 20%. The extra 12 months take 5%, for a total reduction of 25%.

People born from 1955 to 1959 fall between those two cases. Their full retirement age sits between 66 and 67. Someone born in 1957 has a full retirement age of 66 and six months. Claiming at 62 puts that person 54 months early. The first 36 months cost 20%, and the next 18 cost 7.5%. The total cut is 27.5%, leaving 72.5% of the full benefit.

Claiming closer to full retirement age shrinks the reduction. Starting 12 months early costs about 6.67% of the full benefit, all of it charged at the first-tier rate. Starting 24 months early costs about 13.33%. Starting 36 months early costs exactly 20%.

The second tier is cheaper per month than the first. Each of the 36 months nearest full retirement age costs about 0.56%. Each earlier month costs about 0.42%. Both rates apply to the same base, the full benefit.

The Social Security Administration treats the reduction as permanent. The smaller payment does not rise back to the full amount when the claimant later reaches full retirement age. An early claimant receives checks for more months, but each check stays smaller for life.

Social Security pays delayed retirement credits worth 8% of the full benefit for every year a worker waits to claim beyond full retirement age. That rate applies to anyone born in 1943 or later.

The Social Security Administration calculates the credit monthly, not annually. Each month of delay past full retirement age adds two-thirds of 1% to the benefit. A full year of those monthly increments produces the 8% annual figure.

The credits begin only once a worker reaches full retirement age. Waiting from 62 up to full retirement age shrinks or removes the early-claiming reduction, but it does not earn delayed credits. The 8% rate applies strictly to the stretch between full retirement age and 70.

Each year adds a fixed 8 percentage points of the full benefit. The increase does not compound on itself. Three years of delay add 24%, not a larger amount built on top of the previous year's raise.

Birth year determines how many years of credits are available. A worker born in 1960 or later has a full retirement age of 67. That leaves three years to accumulate credits before 70, for a maximum of 124% of the full benefit.

A worker born between 1943 and 1954 has a full retirement age of 66. That leaves four years of potential credits and a maximum of 132%. People born from 1955 through 1959 fall in between. Their full retirement age rises by two months per birth year. Each step removes two months of potential credits. Someone born in 1957, for example, reaches full retirement age at 66 and six months and can earn up to 28% in credits by 70.

The credits attach to the worker's own retirement benefit. They change the size of the check paid on that person's earnings record. The 8% rate stays the same whatever the size of the underlying benefit. A larger full benefit therefore gains more dollars from each year of delay.

A worker with a $2,000 full benefit and a full retirement age of 67 would collect $1,400 a month by claiming at 62 and $2,480 by claiming at 70. Each year of waiting in between raises the monthly check, but the size of the raise changes along the way.

The $2,000 figure is a round number chosen for illustration. It is not an average or typical benefit. The percentages behind it come from Social Security Administration rules, so the same pattern holds at any benefit size. A worker with a $1,000 full benefit would see every dollar figure here cut in half.

The earliest years climb in even steps. Waiting from 62 until 63 lifts the check to $1,500, or 75% of the full benefit. Waiting until 64 brings it to $1,600, or 80%. Each of those two years adds $100 a month.

The pace picks up between 64 and full retirement age. At 65, the check is about $1,733. At 66, it is about $1,867. At 67, the worker receives the full $2,000. Each of those three years adds roughly $133 a month. The larger step reflects how the early-claiming reduction works. It takes a bigger cut per month in the three years closest to full retirement age than in the years further out.

After 67, the steps grow again. Delayed retirement credits push the payment to $2,160 at 68, $2,320 at 69 and $2,480 at 70. Each year past full retirement age adds $160 a month, the largest annual step anywhere in the range.

Grouping the years shows where most of the gain sits. The five years from 62 to 67 add $600 to the monthly check, an average of $120 for each year waited. The three years from 67 to 70 add another $480, or $160 for each year. Per year of waiting, the later stretch adds more money than the earlier one.

Over a full year of checks, the age-70 claimant in this example collects $12,960 more than the age-62 claimant, before taxes.

The comparison shifts slightly for workers whose full retirement age is 66. On the same $2,000 full benefit, they would receive $1,500 a month at 62 and $2,640 at 70. That age-62 check matches what a worker with a full retirement age of 67 gets by waiting until 63. For these earlier birth years, the age-70 check is about 76% larger than the age-62 check. The monthly gap widens to $1,140.

These figures are fixed illustrations of monthly checks. They leave out annual inflation adjustments and income taxes, and they do not show lifetime totals. A larger check that starts later also arrives fewer times.

Social Security delayed retirement credits stop building at age 70, the point where a worker's own monthly retirement benefit reaches its maximum. Under Social Security Administration rules, waiting past 70 to file adds nothing more to the check.

Credits start accruing in the month a worker reaches full retirement age and keep adding up until the month they turn 70. Those are the only months that count. A worker who files at 71 or 72 gets the same base benefit as someone with an identical earnings record who filed at 70. The extra years of waiting produce no larger payment.

That makes 70 a firm boundary for anyone using delay to raise their payment.

Credits are counted month by month, not in whole-year blocks. A worker does not need to wait a full year to see an increase. Someone with a full retirement age of 67 who files at 67 and six months earns six months of credits, a 4% increase. Filing at 68 and three months earns 15 months of credits, or 10%.

Monthly accrual also means the filing date does not have to line up with a birthday. A worker can file in whichever month fits their job, health or household plans. The increase reflects exactly the number of months waited.

The cap is fixed at 70, but full retirement age has moved. As a result, the largest possible gain from delay depends on birth year. A worker with a full retirement age of 66 can earn up to four years, or 48 months, of credits. That is a total increase of 32% over the full benefit.

A full retirement age of 67 leaves three years, or 36 months, of credits before the cap. The maximum increase in that case is 24%. The later retirement age cuts the potential gain from waiting by eight percentage points.

Workers born from 1955 to 1959 fall in between. Someone born in 1957, for example, has a full retirement age of 66 and six months. That leaves 42 months of credits before 70, worth a 28% increase.

A simple break-even calculation puts the crossover near age 82.5 for someone who waits from a full retirement age of 67 until 70. For someone who waits from 62 to 67, it lands near age 78.7. Those ages mark when the larger, later checks catch up in total benefits collected.

Break-even is a race between two payment streams. The person who claims earlier starts collecting sooner and builds a head start. The person who waits gets bigger checks but must make up for the months of payments never received. The break-even point is where the two running totals match.

Both figures here assume a full retirement age of 67, which applies to anyone born in 1960 or later. The math runs on percentages of the full benefit. That means the results hold for a benefit of any size.

Start with the wait from 67 to 70. Holding off means giving up 36 monthly checks at 100% of the full benefit. In return, each later check pays 124% instead of 100%, a gain of 24 percentage points a month. Dividing the 3,600 percent-months forgone by that 24-point gain gives 150 months, or 12.5 years. Counting from age 70, the crossover arrives near 82.5.

The wait from 62 to 67 follows the same logic. Claiming at 62 would have paid 60 checks at 70% of the full benefit, a total of 4,200 percent-months. Waiting until 67 lifts each check by 30 points, from 70% to 100%. That gap closes after 140 months, about 11.7 years. Counting from age 67, the crossover lands near 78.7.

Before each break-even age, the earlier claimant has collected more in total. After it, the person who waited pulls ahead, and the lead grows with every additional monthly payment.

These are simple calculations, and they leave out several factors. They ignore cost-of-living adjustments, federal income taxes and investment returns. If early checks were saved and invested, the returns would push the crossover later. The math also looks at one worker's own benefit in isolation. It does not count anything a spouse or survivor might receive.

Break-even does not predict how long any particular person will live, and it does not identify the right claiming age. A person's health, plans to keep earning a paycheck, whether a spouse relies on the work record and savings outside Social Security all bear on that choice. What the calculation does show is how long a delayed claim takes to pay off in total benefits — a reference point for weighing those personal factors.

Waiting to claim does not make a spousal benefit any larger. Delayed retirement credits raise only the worker's own check, and the spousal benefit tops out at 50% of the worker's full benefit — the amount payable at the worker's full retirement age.

The Social Security Administration sets the spousal maximum from that full benefit. It does not use the larger check a worker locks in by waiting past full retirement age. Credits earned between full retirement age and 70 stay with the worker.

Take a worker with a $2,000 full benefit and a full retirement age of 67. The most a spouse can collect on that record is $1,000 a month. That ceiling holds whether the worker files at 67 or at 70.

Household totals show the effect. With the worker claiming at 67 and the spouse at the maximum, the couple collects $3,000 a month. With the worker waiting until 70, the total is $3,480. The extra $480 is a 24% raise on the worker's check. On the couple's combined income, it is a 16% raise.

Timing can also work against the spouse. A current spouse cannot collect a spousal benefit until the worker has filed for retirement benefits. A worker who waits until 70 can therefore also push back the start of the spouse's payments.

The spouse's own claiming age decides how close the payment comes to the cap. The full 50% is available only when the spouse claims at or after the spouse's own full retirement age. A spouse who files earlier receives a permanently reduced amount.

Waiting beyond that point adds nothing. Spousal benefits do not earn delayed retirement credits. A spouse who holds off past full retirement age gains nothing on the spousal portion.

A spouse who also has a work record is paid that own benefit first. If the spousal amount is higher, the Social Security Administration adds the difference on top. The total equals the higher of the two amounts, not their sum.

That leaves couples with two separate clocks. The worker's claiming age sets the size of the worker's check. The spouse's claiming age, measured against the spouse's own full retirement age, sets the size of the spousal check.

A surviving spouse can receive up to the amount the deceased worker was getting, or was entitled to, at the time of death. That ceiling includes any delayed retirement credits the worker earned. A worker's claiming age therefore shapes two checks: the worker's own and the one a widow or widower may collect later.

Social Security Administration rules count delayed credits toward the survivor benefit. The credits do not disappear when the worker dies. They become part of the amount the survivor's payment is measured against. This is the main reason waiting to claim can work as a form of protection for a spouse.

The rule applies whether or not the worker had started collecting. A worker who died after passing full retirement age without filing had been building credits each month of the wait. Those credits are part of the benefit the worker was entitled to at death.

The decision runs in both directions. A worker who claims before full retirement age accepts a permanent reduction. That smaller check also lowers the ceiling a survivor can reach. A worker who waits past full retirement age raises the ceiling with every month of delay, until the credits stop at 70.

The survivor's own timing matters too. A widow or widower who starts survivor benefits before reaching full retirement age receives less than the full amount the worker's record supports.

The effect is largest in a household where one spouse earned considerably more than the other. The higher earner's claiming age then sets the upper limit on the benefit available to whichever spouse outlives the other.

The trade-off is not one-sided. Waiting means a couple gives up years of payments before the larger check begins. If the higher earner dies before 70, the survivor's ceiling reflects only the credits earned up to the date of death. The couple's health, savings, work plans and the age gap between the spouses all shape how that trade-off plays out.

Claiming Social Security before full retirement age while still holding a job brings the earnings test into play. If pay from work goes above an annual limit, the Social Security Administration withholds some or all of the benefit for that year.

The limit is not fixed. It changes every year. Any dollar figure tied to it belongs to a single calendar year. Anyone planning around it needs the threshold the agency publishes for that year, not a number remembered from an earlier one.

Only earnings from work count toward the limit. Wages from a job and net earnings from self-employment are included. Pensions, investment income, interest and annuity payments are not.

The test has a clear end point. It covers only the months before a person reaches full retirement age. Once that age arrives, earnings from a job no longer cause any withholding, however high the salary.

Withholding is not a penalty. Money held back under the earnings test is not forfeited. When the worker reaches full retirement age, the agency recalculates the monthly benefit to give credit for the months in which checks were withheld. The result is a higher monthly payment from that point forward.

That recalculation matters for anyone weighing an early claim. Each month a benefit starts ahead of full retirement age adds to a reduction that lasts for life. Crediting back the withheld months trims that reduction, because those months no longer count as months of early benefits.

The timing still shapes household cash flow. A worker who claims at 62 and keeps earning above the limit may collect fewer checks in the first years than the benefit amount implies. The credit for those months comes later, built into a larger check after full retirement age, not as a lump-sum repayment.

The earnings test never reaches a worker who waits. Someone who holds off until full retirement age, or later to collect delayed retirement credits, can keep working without any withholding. For people who expect a paycheck well into their 60s, that removes one variable from the claiming decision.

Waiting to claim Social Security does not cost you any cost-of-living adjustments, which apply to your benefit whether or not you have started collecting. Federal taxes on benefits depend on income, and Medicare eligibility starts at 65 regardless of claiming age.

A cost-of-living adjustment, or COLA, is an annual percentage increase the Social Security Administration applies to benefits to reflect inflation. Delaying to 70 does not mean giving up years of those raises. The adjustments are built into a worker's benefit amount from age 62 onward, even before any check has been paid.

That means delayed retirement credits stack on top of a benefit that has already absorbed every COLA announced during the waiting period. Each adjustment is a percentage. It therefore adds more dollars to a larger monthly payment than to a smaller one.

Taxes run on a separate track. Whether benefits are taxed at the federal level depends on provisional income. The IRS calculates that figure by adding adjusted gross income, tax-exempt interest and half of a person's Social Security benefits. Depending on where that total falls, none of the benefit, part of it or up to 85% of it can count as taxable income. No more than 85% is ever taxed federally.

Claiming age can change how that calculation plays out in a given year. A larger delayed check raises the half-of-benefits portion of provisional income. Someone who claims early while still drawing a salary may also see more of the benefit become taxable. The income thresholds that decide those shares are set in dollar terms. The IRS lists them in Publication 915, its guide to taxing Social Security benefits.

Medicare follows its own clock. Eligibility generally starts at 65, regardless of whether a person has claimed retirement benefits. For anyone with a full retirement age of 66 or 67, Medicare coverage can begin before the full Social Security benefit is available.

The two programs still connect at enrollment. People who already collect Social Security when they turn 65 are generally enrolled in Medicare Parts A and B automatically. People who are delaying their benefits are not. They need to sign up through the Social Security Administration. Missing the initial enrollment window can trigger a Part B late-enrollment penalty that lasts for as long as the person has that coverage.

#5546. Zebec ZBCN Buyback: 40.5M Tokens Held, Not Burned, as Supply Stays Unchanged

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zebec says it bought back 40.5 million ZBCN in the third quarter and is keeping them "out of circulation."

On-chain, those tokens didn't reach Zebec's buyback treasury wallet during the quarter. They arrived on October 21, three weeks after Q3 ended, the same day Zebec announced the buyback, sent from what Solscan labels a Crypto.com hot wallet.

The amount matches Zebec's claim almost to the token. But the wallet's history also shows something "out of circulation" doesn't usually suggest: it has moved 59 million ZBCN out before. Let's go through the wallet to check what Zebec's buyback claim actually covers.

Zebec Network announced on October 21, in an X post, that it repurchased 40,536,539 ZBCN in Q3 for about $100,000. That implies an average price of roughly $0.00247. The money came from Zebec Cards and payroll fees across Zebec Enterprise and the SuperApp.

Zebec's explainer, Inside the ZBCN Buyback Program, says buybacks are "funded by operating revenue" from payroll, payments, cards and related services, not from treasury reserves. That's a real point in Zebec's favor.

The scale is small. ZBCN has a 100 billion maximum supply, so 40.5 million tokens is about 0.04% of it.

Zebec says the repurchased tokens "will not re-enter circulation." They weren't burned. ZBCN's total supply is exactly the same as it was before the buyback.

That's a deliberate policy. The program began in 2023 under the old ZBC token and originally included burns. In early 2024, the Zebec DAO approved ZIP-4, which paused burns while keeping recurring buybacks. Zebec says the DAO expects to decide by the end of 2026 whether to propose bringing burns back. Governance happens through the Zebec DAO portal.

The practical difference matters. A burn permanently destroys tokens. "Out of circulation" depends on Zebec continuing to hold them and on data providers leaving them out of circulating supply. The blockchain doesn't enforce either one.

Zebec's blog says repurchased tokens are held "in the designated on-chain Buyback Treasury Wallet and with Uphold Institutional," but doesn't give the address. The account linked with the announcement is EkXEg6de172aoLvr7w86YzQ2rf5oEFD3iUt8uQsLQuQW. ZBCN's Solana mint address is ZBCNpuD7YMXzTHB2fhGkGi78MNsHGLRXUhRewNRm9RU.

As of October 22, Solscan shows the wallet holding 108,256,701.48 ZBCN, worth about $246,157 at $0.002273.

The Q3 check passes. On October 21 at about 14:11 UTC, the wallet received two ZBCN transfers from an address Solscan labels "Crypto.com Hot Wallet":

Together, that's 40,535,224.09 ZBCN, just 1,315 ZBCN (about $3) short of Zebec's figure. That's a 99.997% match. The small difference is likely due to fees or rounding.

One detail stands out: the account is off-curve. Solscan shows "isOnCurve: FALSE," which means the address is derived by a program and has no private key of its own. Accounts like this are usually controlled by a program such as a multisig, so moving tokens requires that program's approval. That's a better setup than a single person's wallet, but it isn't a lock.

The timing shows how the program works. The wallet's transfer history suggests a repeating pattern, with each batch arriving after its quarter has ended:

Those three batches add up to the wallet's current balance within 0.01 ZBCN. So the "buyback treasury" holds the last three quarters of deliveries and nothing else.

This means that during each quarter, the purchased tokens weren't in the on-chain treasury. The pattern points to buying on an exchange, with tokens sitting in an exchange account until they're withdrawn to the treasury around announcement time. The chain doesn't show when the Q3 purchases actually happened, so for July 1 to September 30, the "$100,000 Q3 buyback" can't be checked on-chain. Only the October 21 delivery can.

That's common practice and not a sign of wrongdoing. But it means the on-chain record confirms delivery, not the purchases themselves.

If the balance only covers the last three batches, what happened to earlier buybacks? The transfer history answers that, too. The wallet has sent ZBCN out twice, both times to the same address, shown on Solscan as 9Sq2nZ...4TEine:

That's about 58.97 million ZBCN moved out of a wallet described as holding tokens that "will not re-enter circulation."To be fair, Zebec says tokens are "periodically consolidated with Uphold Institutional for custody," and these outflows may be exactly that. There's no confirmation that 9Sq2nZ...4TEine belongs to Uphold. Once tokens leave this wallet, readers can't follow them using Zebec's disclosures. These transfers also show what a burn would prevent: tokens in this wallet can, and do, move.

The Q3 claim holds up better than I expected. The wallet received almost exactly 40.5 million ZBCN, and the balance reconciles to the token. What the chain can't show is when the tokens were bought, or where earlier buybacks are now.

Three disclosures would close those gaps:

For now, Zebec did buy and deliver its Q3 tokens, and the supply is the same as it was before.

#5545. Wayfair posted its strongest sales growth since the pandemic, beating expectations

Free daily briefing on global business news.

U.S. revenue rose 11.4% to $3.0 billion, while international sales fell 2.3%, and net income was $62 million versus a loss a year earlier

Wayfair reported its strongest quarter of sales growth since the pandemic on Wednesday, as net sales in the third quarter climbed 9.7% over the prior year, reaching $3.42 billion.

Adjusted earnings per share came in at 93 cents, up from 70 cents a year earlier. Analysts had expected 79 cents a share and $3.38 billion in revenue, according to CNBC.

U.S. net revenue rose 11.4% to $3.05 billion, an increase of $312 million. International net revenue fell 2.3% to $380 million.

Wayfair posted net income of $62 million, or 45 cents a share, compared with a net loss of $99 million, or 76 cents a share, a year earlier, the company said in a filing with the SEC. Adjusted EBITDA was $236 million, for a margin of 6.9%.

Active customers stood at 22.2 million by Sept. 30, which is 4.7% more than the year-earlier tally. Orders delivered rose 12.2% to 11.0 million. Average order value fell to $311 from $317.

Free cash flow was $136 million, compared with $93 million a year earlier. Cash, cash equivalents and short-term investments totaled $1.1 billion at the end of the quarter.

CEO Niraj Shah said in a statement that Wayfair had predicted it would gain U.S. market share more quickly than it has in a long while. "With U.S. revenue growing double digits against a roughly flat category here in Q3, we've done exactly that," Shah said. He said the adjusted EBITDA margin was the company's best third-quarter result since 2020.

Chief Financial Officer Kate Gulliver told CNBC that Wayfair has attracted more shoppers thanks to loyal repeat customers, its newly opened stores, a high-end furnishings line and a focus on affordability. She said Wayfair's discounting this year has matched last year's levels, and that it plans to take a comparable tack through the holidays and the final three months of the year.

"We're able to meet the customer all the way from the opening price point up to luxury," Gulliver told Bloomberg.

#5544. A new pal for Pluto? Rubin Observatory finds its first dwarf planet candidate

by Alan Boyle on Oct 27, 2026 at 7:54 pmOctober 27, 2026 at 8:23 pm

Astronomers sorting through data from the Vera C. Rubin Observatory in Chile have found an icy world that has a good chance of joining Pluto in the solar system’s retinue of dwarf planets.

University of Washington astronomer Mario Jurić joined the astronomer who made the discovery, Matthew Holman of the Harvard & Smithsonian Center for Astrophysics, to announce the findings today at a meeting of the American Astronomical Society’s Division for Planetary Sciences in Spokane, Wash.

Jurić, the Rubin team’s solar system lead scientist, said the observatory’s capabilities made it possible to detect and characterize the new dwarf planet candidate, known as 2026 ED138.

“Rubin is giving us an unprecedented capacity to explore the sky through a combination of speed, depth, and precision,” Jurić said in a news release. “And the discovery is just the beginning: Once we identify a new object, we can search back months, and sometimes even decades, finding it in images where nobody knew to look. This ability to both discover and ‘precover’ objects is transforming how quickly and accurately we can determine their orbits and understand the distant solar system.”

2026 ED138 traces a tilted orbital path that takes it well beyond Pluto, the solar system’s best-known dwarf planet. It’s currently at a distance of 46 astronomical units, where 1 AU equals the average distance between Earth and the sun. Pluto, by comparison, is currently about 40 AU from the sun.

Astronomers suspect ED138 formed billions of years ago closer to the sun before being flung into a wider orbit by gravitational interactions with Neptune.

Based on an analysis of its distance, brightness and assumed composition, ED138 is thought to be somewhere between 600 and 1,500 kilometers (373 to 932 miles) in diameter. At that size, an icy object should possess enough gravity to pull itself into a round shape — satisfying the primary physical criterion for a dwarf planet.

ED138 may be Rubin’s first dwarf planet candidate, but it almost certainly won’t be the last. Thanks to the observatory’s Simonyi Survey Telescope — named after the family of Seattle software billionaire Charles Simonyi — the Rubin team detected more than 11,000 new asteroids even before June’s official start of a 10-year survey of the southern sky.

Rubin’s researchers analyze the data from those scans to find objects of interest — ranging from asteroids to gamma-ray bursts — and track them over time. On Oct. 13, Holman was running data through a search code that he developed with Kevin Napier, a colleague at the Center for Astrophysics. ED138 stood out due to its exceptional size and brightness.

“My first reaction was one of excited disbelief,” Holman said. “Objects like this are very rare, so I immediately started checking whether I or the code had done something wrong.”

To confirm the discovery, Holman, Jurić and their colleagues found 30 archived observations of ED138 dating back to March 4. The Asteroid Institute’s ADAM Precovery service found still more images of the object, going back to 2016, in the archives of a different astronomical survey.

The precovery data confirmed that ED138 was a special case.

“Finding an object this big, roughly 1,000 kilometers across, is something that happens maybe once in a generation,” Jurić said. “It’s the largest trans-Neptunian object found in about 20 years, and Rubin turned it up while we were still commissioning the telescope.”

In 2006, the International Astronomical Union defined dwarf planets as planetary objects that are big enough to crush themselves into a roundish shape — technically speaking, into a state of hydrostatic equilibrium — but not big enough to clear their orbital neighborhood.

So far, the IAU has classified five solar system objects as dwarf planets — including Ceres in the main asteroid belt, plus Pluto, Eris, Haumea and Makemake in the region beyond Neptune. 2026 ED138 joins a host of other celestial objects that are thought to be dwarf planets but haven’t yet been added to the IAU’s official list.

“The official list hasn’t moved since 2008,” Jurić told GeekWire in an email. “I’m not sure if there’s an active process that reviews candidates, and what are the timelines.”

Jurić and his colleagues hope additional observations will boost ED138’s chances of attaining true dwarf planethood.

“The next step in building the case would be to prove it’s round (in hydrostatic equilibrium),” he wrote. “The means to do that would be directly through occultations (and there’s a good chance of that, given it’s in a dense stellar field), and then thermal measurements plus modeling and light curves (or the absence of variability).”

#5543. AMC’s A-List members now make up 20% of U.S. attendance. Its $4 billion debt is the harder test

Fletcher Williams saw six movies at AMC theaters last month. At full price, that would have run about $150. He paid $29.99.

Williams, 25, is one of more than 1.1 million members of AMC Stubs A-List, the subscription tier that lets moviegoers reserve up to four films a week, including IMAX and Dolby Cinema, for a monthly fee of roughly $24 to $30 depending on the state. As audiences return to theaters in 2026, AMC Entertainment is counting on the program to turn occasional ticket buyers into regulars.

The open question is whether that loyalty can do what a run of hit movies has not yet done: make AMC consistently profitable while it carries roughly $4 billion in debt.

The rebound is real. AMC reported $1.60 billion in revenue for the second quarter of 2026, up 14.2% from a year earlier and the highest quarterly total in its 106-year history. Worldwide attendance rose 13.5% to 71.3 million.

Admissions brought in $863.1 million, up 13.2%. Food and beverage sales rose 15.3% to $576.1 million. The industry helped: the $2.99 billion domestic box office was the strongest second quarter in seven years, with six films opening above $75 million.

The hole was deep. AMC’s revenue fell 77% in 2020, from $5.47 billion to $1.24 billion, as the pandemic shut theaters. As recently as early 2025, chairman and CEO Adam Aron said the industry’s January-to-March domestic box office was its weakest since 1996, setting aside quarters hit by COVID.

Records have not yet meant profits. AMC posted an $11.4 million net loss in the second quarter as interest and other charges absorbed much of the gain. For 2025, it lost $632 million on $4.85 billion in revenue, according to Fortune’s company data.

For frequent moviegoers, the arithmetic is simple. A standard adult ticket at AMC typically runs $13 to $15 before premium formats like IMAX or 3D [source needed], so a movie a week can top $65 a month in tickets alone.

Williams first signed up in college, when he lived 15 minutes from an AMC. For the number of films he sees, he said, “The membership basically pays for itself.”

“$25 to $30 is roughly the equivalent of a single ticket for a new movie where I live. Paying that once a month for the ability to see up to 4 movies a week is incredibly worth it,” said Williams, who now lives in Los Angeles.

Members could see as many as 17 films a month, but the typical member sees two or three, according to AMC. Even at that pace, most come out roughly even or ahead.

AMC launched A-List in 2018, when Fortune tracked it as AMC’s answer to MoviePass. Membership has more than doubled over the past five years, and A-List members now account for about 20% of AMC’s U.S. attendance, Aron told analysts in July.

“We’ve seen significant membership growth in recent years, as movies have returned in much greater numbers to theatres, and at the end of the second quarter of 2026, A-List had grown to more than 1.1 million members,” AMC spokesperson Ryan Noonan wrote in an email. “A-Listers remain among our most engaged moviegoers, regularly seeing a broad range of films at AMC. We think the continued growth of A-List speaks volumes about how much our members enjoy the program and the value they see in it.”

For some members, the subscription has changed how they spend on entertainment, not just how often they go out.

“I think it’s changed how I approach entertainment more than anything. Instead of treating a movie as an occasional expense, I can make it a regular activity, and I’m more inclined to spend my entertainment budget on experiences I genuinely enjoy. I still have streaming services at home, but going to the theater offers something different that I can’t fully replicate on my couch,” said Noah Osborne, 28, of Phoenix.

“I’d say I probably spend a bit less on streaming services since I’m able to watch the movie in the theater. A-Listers also have great deals on concessions, so I’m able to save some money there too,” said Sophie Guaman, 28, of [New York City / New York state].

That concession spending matters to AMC, which earns heavily on food and drinks. Food and beverage revenue per patron hit records in both its U.S. and international businesses in the second quarter.

“The enthusiasm our members continue to show for the program has exceeded our expectations, especially in the way they talk about A-List, both online and with their family and friends,” Noonan wrote.

In October, AMC completed a $3.97 billion refinancing that pushed almost all of its debt maturities to 2031 and 2033 and, the company said, lowered its cost of capital. The deal buys time. It does not shrink the roughly $4 billion AMC owes.

That is the real test for A-List. A program that brings in a fifth of U.S. attendance can keep seats filled between blockbusters. Whether it can generate enough steady cash to help pay down debt is a different question.

The next read comes with AMC’s third-quarter report, covering July through September: whether attendance held after a record spring, and whether a bigger, more loyal audience starts to show up on the bottom line.

#5542. Amazon earnings preview: AWS is booked up, and Wall Street wants to know what comes next

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 8:11 amOctober 28, 2026 at 8:11 am

Amazon reports third-quarter earnings Thursday afternoon with more demand for its cloud services than it can serve, driven by AI labs such as Anthropic and OpenAI along with growth in its traditional cloud business.

One big question for Wall Street going into the report is what Amazon might signal about next year’s spending as it tries to keep up with that demand.

CEO Andy Jassy said on an Andreessen Horowitz podcast last week that AWS capacity is largely booked for this year and next, along with “a good chunk of ’28.”

Amazon has said it expects to spend about $220 billion on capital expenditures this year, largely on AI and cloud infrastructure, up from its earlier plan of $200 billion. Even at that level, Jassy said, Amazon is “leaving a meaningful amount of demand on the table.”

Past spending pushed Amazon’s free cash flow to negative $7.6 billion for the 12 months ending in June, as the cost to add data centers, chips and other equipment exceeded the cash its operations brought in. Jassy gave no indication of slowing down, saying the company “could invest a lot more and it wouldn’t be a bad use of capital.”

Core numbers: Analysts expect revenue of about $202 billion, up 12% from a year ago, according to Yahoo Finance. That’s at the top of Amazon’s own forecast of $197 billion to $202 billion.

Analysts expect earnings of $1.96 per share, about the same as a year ago.

Amazon’s sales growth will likely look slower this time, about 12%, down from 20% last quarter. A big reason is timing. Prime Day, the company’s biggest sales event of the year, fell in the second quarter this year, rather than the third quarter as it did last year, so this quarter is up against a tougher comparison.

Amazon estimated in July that the shift would take nearly 4 percentage points off its growth rate this quarter. It hits online store sales hardest: analysts expect them to grow only about 3%, according to Zacks.

AWS: Amazon Web Services, the company’s cloud business, generates the majority of its operating profit. AWS revenue grew 37% to $42.2 billion in the second quarter, its fastest pace since 2021 and the fifth straight quarter of faster growth.

Analysts expect AWS revenue of about $45.4 billion this time, up 37.5%, according to Zacks. Wedbush is more optimistic, projecting growth of about 41%.

AWS had $496 billion in signed contracts it hadn’t yet delivered as of June, more than double the year before. That means its growth depends largely on how quickly Amazon can bring new data centers online.

“Capacity, not demand, is the constraint,” Yorkville Ives analyst Dan Ives wrote of the industry in a note Sunday.

Jassy said on the a16z podcast that running AI models is still “an order of magnitude too expensive” for businesses to use them widely, and that Amazon’s custom chips, including its Trainium AI processors, are a big piece of bringing that cost down. Amazon said in July that its chip business was on pace for more than $25 billion in annual revenue.

Anthropic stake: Amazon’s reported earnings could look very different. That’s because its profit fluctuates significantly depending on the value of its stake in Anthropic.

Last quarter, $53.4 billion in pre-tax gains, mostly on Anthropic, pushed Amazon’s earnings to $5.75 per share, against expectations of $1.82.

Anthropic filed paperwork Monday for a planned IPO on the Nasdaq. Amazon’s stake in the AI company was valued at about $190 billion as of June 30, according to Amazon’s latest quarterly filing. That includes about $92 billion in gains on convertible notes, a form of loan that turns into stock, which haven’t yet been counted in Amazon’s profit. Those notes would convert to Anthropic stock when it goes public.

Anthropic is also one of Amazon’s biggest cloud customers. Its IPO filing shows commitments to spend at least $110 billion on Amazon’s computing capacity into the 2030s, behind the $114.5 billion it committed to Google, as GeekWire reported Tuesday. Anthropic also said in the filing that it has asked its cloud providers for more computing power than they were willing to supply.

Shopping agents: Amazon blocked Meta’s new Muse AI agent from its store last month, escalating a fight over who controls the customer relationship when software does the buying. Amazon said Muse broke its rule requiring agents to identify themselves.

Agents that shop on a customer’s behalf could bypass Amazon’s advertising business, which depends on people browsing its pages. Ad revenue grew 26% to $19.8 billion last quarter, and analysts expect about $20.8 billion this time, up 18%, according to Zacks.

“Investor questions remain on agentic commerce risk, particularly to advertising, but we see limited risk,” Wedbush analyst Ygal Arounian wrote in an Oct. 16 note, citing Amazon’s logistics advantage and its role connecting shoppers with sellers.

Amazon is trying to give shoppers fewer reasons to look elsewhere. It now lists 250 million products sold on other retailers’ sites, about 2.5 times as many as in March, The Information reported Wednesday. On the seller side, Amazon opened its tools to outside AI agents in September, starting with Anthropic’s Claude.

Cloud rivals: Microsoft and Alphabet report quarterly results Wednesday afternoon, a day before Amazon. Microsoft’s report is its first under a new structure that breaks out Azure cloud revenue every quarter.

Check back with GeekWire on Thursday afternoon for coverage.

#5541. French bank Crédit Mutuel Arkéa said hackers stole money in cyberattack

Free daily briefing on global business news.

The French lender said customer assets were not affected, while reports put the amount taken at $133 million, a figure it has not confirmed

Crédit Mutuel Arkéa said it was the target of a cyberattack on Wednesday that enabled fraudulent transactions at the French bank.

The bank said the incident has been contained and operations are resuming during the morning, after the group and its subsidiaries completed verifications and added security measures. It said customers' assets were not affected and that the attack delayed the execution of certain transfers.

Hackers took money from the bank once they had broken into its IT networks, according to Bloomberg. A bank spokesperson declined to say how much was stolen.

Reports put the amount at €118 million ($133 million), according to AFP. The bank has not confirmed that figure, which independent investigator ZachXBT first made public earlier this week. The bank said the amounts affected are still being assessed and would not undermine its financial strength and soundness.

ZachXBT said the stolen funds were moved via several accounts set up at cryptocurrency exchanges, according to AFP. The bank has not disclosed the method of the attack or identified the party responsible.

After detecting the attack, the bank said, it contacted the relevant authorities and supervisory bodies. As a precaution, it briefly halted some transactions to protect its operations and stop additional fraudulent transfers.

The bank warned that phishing attempts are possible following the attack. It urged customers to share no personal or banking information, including login IDs, passwords, bank card numbers and SMS validation codes. Customers who are in doubt about a message should contact their bank adviser directly, it said.

Crédit Mutuel Arkéa, based in Brest, includes the federations Crédit Mutuel de Bretagne and Crédit Mutuel du Sud-Ouest. It has more than 5.8 million members and customers and total assets of €211.5 billion.

The bank said its teams remain mobilized to assess the consequences of the attack and strengthen security, and that it will provide updates as new information becomes available.

#5540. Uber's revenue growth slowed as driver shortages weighed on ride-hailing

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Mobility revenue fell 2% in the quarter, while Uber forecast fourth-quarter gross bookings growth of 18% to 22%

Uber $UBER reported third-quarter revenue growth of 10%, to $14.8 billion, as revenue in its Mobility ride-hailing segment fell 2%.

Uber did not have enough drivers to satisfy demand in markets including India, Brazil and Canada, and costlier fuel plus the Middle East conflict added to the strain, according to Reuters.

The 10% increase was the slowest revenue growth since the first quarter of 2021, according to Reuters. That compares with growth of 14% in the first quarter and 12% in the second.

Uber said business model changes reduced total revenue growth by 8 percentage points. Those changes were in the U.K., according to The Wall Street Journal.

"Elevated fuel prices and tighter driver availability weighed on supply growth in several international markets," Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said in prepared remarks, according to Reuters. Tighter immigration flows hurt Canada, where supply falls short of demand, he said.

Uber is putting money into recruiting, keeping and winning back drivers, and said its Mobility business picked up in October, according to Reuters. The Middle East conflict took 75 basis points off Mobility bookings growth in the quarter, and Uber builds in a 100-basis-point reduction for the final three months of the year.

Gross bookings rose 20% to $59.8 billion. Mobility bookings grew 18%, Delivery 22% and Freight 35%. Delivery revenue rose 23% and Freight revenue 34%. Trips grew 16% to 4.1 billion.

"Uber delivered its fifth consecutive quarter of 20%+ Gross Bookings growth, driven by record audience and consumer engagement," Khosrowshahi said in a statement.

Net income attributable to Uber was $512 million, down from $6.6 billion a year earlier. The year-ago figure included a $4.9 billion tax benefit. The latest quarter carried a pre-tax net loss of $476 million tied to repricing the company's equity investments. Non-GAAP earnings per share rose 35% to $0.88.

For the fourth quarter, Uber expects gross bookings between $63.25 billion and $65.25 billion, which would be growth of 18% to 22% from a year earlier after adjusting for currency swings. It expects non-GAAP earnings per share of $0.95 to $0.99, up 34% to 39%.

Blue Origin is taking over an industrial building in Des Moines, Wash., where the Jeff Bezos-founded space company plans a mix of lab, development and light production work, the company confirmed to GeekWire.

The 265,922-square-foot facility, known as Prologis Park SeaTac 3, was previously a Bartell Drugs distribution center just south of Seattle-Tacoma International Airport. Blue Origin said that at full capacity over the long term, the site is expected to support hundreds of employees.

Blue Origin’s new location is around the corner from where Shield AI is building X-Forge 3, a 420,000-square-foot facility that will make the company’s X-BAT autonomous fighter jet. Shield AI said last month it expects to have 4,000 workers in the region by the early 2030s, and that it’s looking for another 1 million square feet.

“It’s all about labor and access to power,” Mallory told KING 5, referring to the advanced manufacturing projects coming to the area.

Blue Origin is headquartered in nearby Kent, Wash., about 5 miles from the Des Moines site.

The company is working to get its New Glenn rocket flying again after one exploded during a ground engine test in May, which damaged its Florida launch pad. New Glenn is slated to carry Blue’s Blue Moon Mark 2 lander on NASA’s Artemis 3 mission, a test in Earth orbit planned for mid-2027 ahead of a crewed moon landing targeted for 2028.

#5538. CEOs need a new playbook after a midterm rebuke of Trump

Good morning. It’s official. While the final tally will take time to work out, the Democrats came charging back into Congress yesterday, winning back control of both the House and the Senate in the midterm elections. This was a vote on the state of the economy, but it was also a vote on the state of democracy.

Left or right, the strong turnout for the midterm elections is a testament to Americans’ faith in democracy. While donors poured a record $12 billion into midterm campaigns, $446 million of which came from Elon Musk alone, the most powerful currency in the country remains one vote per citizen. Democrat James Talarico won the Senate seat in Texas, where Musk spent about $200 million trying to defeat him. If anything, such excessive spending from the world’s richest man sparked a backlash and counter-campaign insisting Texas was not for sale.

On the economic front, it’s clear that policymakers need to now prioritize addressing the cost of living, from grocery and gas costs to housing and health care, not to mention that debt. The debate around AI and data centers is likely to become more intense. And on the governing front, voters have made it clear that they want a strong check on this president after two years of watching the legislative branch give him a free pass on everything from dismantling federal agencies and redirecting federal funds to waging war and imposing tariffs. What they don’t want: two years of bitter investigations and gridlock instead of getting things done.

Whatever happens next in Washington—or doesn’t happen, given the divided government—business leaders can take this moment to remind people that the strength of this country lies not just in free and fair markets but in free and fair elections. That will be especially important if political leaders try to stir up doubt about the legitimacy of the results, though President Trump said last night that he would accept the outcome.

Whether he’s true to his word is anybody’s guess. But gone are the days when wooing Trump was sufficient to get things done. Now, funding ballrooms, bearing gifts, and pouring praise on this president may be a liability. The president told voters to act as if his name was on the ballot, so they did. In many races where Trump personally campaigned and supported candidates, voters rejected his picks. They rejected the Ohio gubernatorial candidate who ran a repulsive ad exploiting the childhood trauma of his opponent. They rejected the billionaires trying to buy their hearts and votes. They rejected the gerrymandering that was supposed to produce reliable results.

#5535. Dario Amodei wants ‘a country of geniuses in a data center.’ Realizing that vision requires risky financial mechanics, Anthropic’s IPO filing shows

Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei has written about creating AI powerful enough that it will be like “having a country of geniuses in a data center.” But the company’s recently-unveiled IPO prospectus sheds new light on the kind of precarious financing Anthropic will require to turn that vision into reality.

This week the company updated its prospectus to include its third quarter financial results, which showed a squeeze on the company’s margins as computing costs have risen. The company also revealed additional data center spending commitments. The company has now pledged to spend a whopping $895.4 billion stretching out to 2045.Some of the companies selling Anthropic the chips and cloud services it needs are also helping it finance those very same purchases. Broadcom has agreed to absorb losses under a $63 billion equipment-financing arrangement if Anthropic defaults, with its maximum potential liability reaching about $43 billion once the equipment is deployed.

Such backing helps Anthropic obtain computing capacity without paying the full equipment cost upfront. Google and AMD also tie some funding to Anthropic leasing or deploying their hardware. Suppliers providing guarantees could face payouts to lenders and developers they backstop just as weaker AI demand reduces their own sales and market valuations.

In the $63 billion transaction announced on Oct. 26, Bank of America, Citi, Morgan Stanley and Blackstone will finance a newly formed company that buys Broadcom chips and networking equipment and leases them to Anthropic. Deliveries are expected to begin in 2027. Anthropic will pay rent for those chips over time, providing the income financiers rely on to recover their investment.

If Anthropic defaults on its lease, however, Broadcom has agreed to cover the difference between 72.5% of the amount still owed under the lease and what the equipment sells for. For example, if $100 remains owed and the equipment sells for $60, Broadcom would pay $12.50.

Gil Luria, the head of technology research at D.A. Davidson tells Fortune that Broadcom basically has to cut a deal like this in order to make sure it doesn’t lose sales to rival Nvidia, which has also offered to backstop some of its biggest chip buyers. “In order to stay competitive with Nvidia’s support of its customers, other large semis companies like Broadcom and AMD have had to step in to support their customers as well,” Luria said. Luria upgraded Broadcom to buy on Oct. 27.

Financiers’ ability to recover money after a default also depends on whether other customers can use the chips. Comparing Nvidia GPUs with Google’s specialized AI chips, known as TPUs, which are built by Broadcom, Andrew Giudici of credit-rating agency KBRA told Fortune, “Custom TPUs generally have greater re-leasing risk than Nvidia GPUs because they are designed for a more specialized ecosystem and have a narrower pool of potential users”.

Residual-value support, such as Broadcom’s agreement,  can help financiers recover money when equipment cannot be sold or re-leased for as much as expected, Giudici said. “However, it effectively transfers a portion of that risk to the support provider.” That makes the supplier’s creditworthiness, the enforceability of its commitment and the extent of its coverage important to assessing the financing, he said.

Cash-rich suppliers with substantial businesses outside AI have capacity to absorb losses, Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh, a professor of real estate and finance at Columbia Business School, said. But weaker AI demand could hit those partners’ hardware sales, cloud revenue and investment values at the same time as calls on their guarantees. “Separate contracts can transmit the same underlying demand shock across multiple balance sheets,” he said. “Individual loans can become safer while the broader system becomes more concentrated but also harder to assess.”

Anthropic’s IPO filing says its ability to expand computing capacity may depend on a small number of cloud providers, partners and financiers remaining willing and able to support them. Two of the most important, Amazon and Google, are also spending more cash on their own AI buildouts than their operations bring in. Amazon reported negative free cash flow of $42.4 billion over the preceding 12 months, primarily because of increased AI-related equipment investment. And Google’s parent Alphabet free cash flow was negative $9.1 billion in the third quarter. Both still generate substantial cash and can borrow readily, but their spending means that continued support for Anthropic increasingly competes with their own buildouts for capital.

CEO Dario Amodei has described how an AI company could grow extraordinarily quickly and still buy more computing capacity than it could afford. In a February interview with podcaster Dwarkesh Patel, he illustrated the financial danger with a hypothetical company buying computing capacity on the assumption that revenue would grow tenfold annually. Even fivefold growth could leave it unable to afford what it had ordered. The market could become enormous and still develop too slowly for the purchases made in anticipation of it. “If you’re off by a couple years, that can be ruinous,” he said.

Under a March 2026 agreement, Anthropic can issue up to $42 billion in convertible notes to Broadcom to cover eligible quarterly rent, preserving cash it would otherwise need to pay out. Interest increases the debt, and the holder can choose to convert it into Anthropic shares at a discount.

Notes issued under the facility normally carry 9% interest, with the interest added to the debt, and with the notes deemable for stock at 90% of the market price. But notes issued when specified revenue conditions are unmet carry a 13% interest rate and convert at 85% of market price, giving noteholders more shares for each dollar and further diluting existing shareholders. Sustained failure to meet the agreement’s conditions can end access to further funding. Anthropic says the revenue-growth thresholds are significantly below its recent actual growth rates. The company reported 45% quarterly revenue growth in its third quarter financial results, and a year-over-year growth rate in excess of 1,000%.

Google and AMD also tie funding to hardware commitments: certain Google funds become available as Anthropic takes on TPU lease obligations, while AMD’s investment becomes available as its GPUs reach delivery and deployment milestones.

“Hardware-linked equity investments expose Amazon and AMD without making them blanket guarantors,” Van Nieuwerburgh told Fortune. If Anthropic cannot pay, Broadcom and Google bear losses within their backstops’ contractual limits, while lenders retain the uncovered risk, he said.

Anthropic says it has spent years enabling Claude to run across Amazon, Google, Nvidia and AMD chips, allowing it to allocate work according to price and performance. But funding attached to one supplier’s equipment does not automatically follow it to another. That could make it difficult for Anthropic to continue to be as flexible as it has been in which kind of chip it chooses for which workload.

Anthropic reported $146.6 billion in liquidity at September 30, including cash, short-term investments and available bank credit. That gives it substantial resources to meet payments and fund expansion, although the bank credit would add borrowing if drawn.

Trzcinka sees that liquidity as a positive for bondholders, but said whether Anthropic achieves an investment-grade rating for its debt “will depend on how the rating agencies assess its substantial future commitments, short operating history, and deeply interconnected relationships.”

“The company has now disclosed its commitments, which are larger than we initially estimated at $895 billion, compared to our prior estimate of roughly $600 billion,” he said. His view is that those commitments and relationships would limit its ability to obtain financing at investment-grade spreads – the relatively low premiums over benchmark interest rates typically paid by investment-grade borrowers.

“The key question is whether revenue can compound fast enough to absorb the future commitments and outpace compute cost,” he said. He is watching whether Anthropic takes on additional commitments and how its liquidity holds up. “Draws on the revolver [credit facility] would also be a potential warning sign,” he said.

Through Anthropic Direct, a program under which Anthropic plans to build out its own cloud computing infrastructure, the company separates its commitments to data-center space from the larger investment in the chips that will run inside those data centers, giving it more time to assess demand before ordering equipment. It can reserve dedicated facilities operated by third parties on its behalf, then make the chip investment later. Data centers take longer to prepare than the equipment they house, the filing says. As the dedicated infrastructure comes online, Anthropic says it can replace the more expensive short-term compute with lower-cost, long-term capacity.

In the representative AI data-center project modeled in Van Nieuwerburgh’s paper, computing equipment and related systems account for roughly two-thirds of the initial cost, with the facility and power infrastructure making up the rest.

The data-center commitments Anthropic makes before buying chips can still leave it paying for space that demand may not fill. A facility with secured power “could certainly become a stranded asset if data center demand ultimately disappoints,” Van Nieuwerburgh said, meaning it could be left without enough business to justify its cost and no obvious buyer to which the data center can be sold.

Anthropic says reducing its reliance on partners to pay for future facilities and equipment depends in part on obtaining financing from independent sources on its own credit. An IPO would add cash from shareholders that it could use for those purchases without waiting for a particular supplier’s hardware to reach a delivery or deployment milestone. Combined with Direct’s later equipment decisions, independently raised cash could let Anthropic compare hardware and funding options with less need for the company selling the machines to help pay for them.

IPO proceeds could give Anthropic more freedom to choose its hardware and financing. But as Van Nieuwerburgh put it, “Supplier financing supports construction; ultimately, paying for it requires revenue from end customers.

Wen Shao is a reporting fellow at Fortune covering AI, with a focus on the companies, economics, and infrastructure shaping the industry.

#5534. PicoBrew’s patents are back on the market, six years after the Seattle homebrew startup’s collapse

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Oct 28, 2026 at 10:36 amOctober 28, 2026 at 3:08 pm

The patents behind PicoBrew, the Seattle startup that once promised to do for home beer what Keurig did for coffee, are up for sale again — six years after the company collapsed into receivership and after two changes of ownership.

Hilco Global, an Illinois-based diversified financial services company, announced this week that its Intellectual Property Services group has been retained by PicoBrew’s current owner to market the startup’s technology to potential buyers.

The sale includes 17 patents and patent applications, two of them pending, along with engineering and design files and product concepts. Buyers can bid on all or part of the portfolio, and non-binding indications of interest are due Nov. 18. Hilco is pitching the assets to companies in coffee, tea, kombucha, spirits, beverage appliances and housewares.

The seller is Pico Craft Group, which Hilco described as led by a former PicoBrew investor. After PicoBrew’s 2020 collapse, its bridge lender took over the assets. That lender, PB Funding Group, was managed by former Microsoft software developer Greg Whitten, The Seattle Times reported at the time. Pico Craft Group bought the assets from the lender in 2024 for an undisclosed amount, according to Hilco, which did not say who runs the group.

“PicoBrew was a true innovator in the consumer and commercial craft beverage space, and its portfolio has applications well beyond beer,” Eric Hurwitz, a senior director at Hilco, said in a news release.

The portfolio covers technology from PicoBrew’s full product line, according to the release, including the Pico Pro and Pico C home brewing appliances, the PicoStill accessory for spirits, the Pico U Multibrew platform for beer, coffee, tea and kombucha, and Z-Series brewing machines and KegSmarts kegerators for commercial use.

Bill Mitchell, a former Microsoft vice president and longtime homebrewer, founded PicoBrew in 2010 with his brother Jim Mitchell, a food scientist, and Avi Geiger, an engineer who also worked at Microsoft. Their countertop machines automated the brewing process using PicoPaks, ingredient packs based on recipes from craft breweries.

The startup became a Kickstarter regular. Its 2017 campaign for the Pico Model C raised $1.93 million from 4,301 backers, a record at the time in the site’s food category, and the $549 machine landed at retailers including Best Buy, Williams-Sonoma and Amazon. A 2018 campaign for the Pico U pushed PicoBrew into coffee, tea and kombucha.

But the company struggled to land more funding. In February 2020, after failing to close a new round, PicoBrew entered receivership. It had raised more than $15 million and cut its staff to fewer than 40, down from a peak of more than 80.

PicoBrew ceased operations in 2020, and no one has supported existing devices since, according to Hilco. Any decision about future support would be up to a buyer. The King County Superior Court approved the 2020 sale, which freed PicoBrew’s bridge lender from the company’s liabilities and from responsibility to past customers, The Seattle Times previously reported.

Some owners kept their machines brewing without the company’s servers by using a workaround developed by a Facebook group of PicoBrew users, The Spoon reported in 2020. The founders were let go after the receivership, according to the site.

When PicoBrew went up for sale in 2020, Mitchell told GeekWire that hardware takes time and multiple funding rounds backed by firm investor commitment.

He shared advice he’d gotten from Dan Leviton of Maveron: “Startups only fail for one of two reasons — they run out of heart, or they run out of money.”

#5533. Kraft Heinz is raising its annual sales forecast after beating earnings expectations

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Kraft Heinz expects 2026 organic net sales to fall 0.5% to 1.25%, narrowing a prior forecast of a 0.5% to 2% decline

Kraft Heinz $KHC raised the low end of its 2026 organic net sales forecast on Wednesday as it reported third-quarter results with lower sales and profit.

The company now projects a full-year organic net sales decline of 0.5% to 1.25%, an improvement on the earlier outlook of a 0.5% to 2% drop. The outlook includes an approximate 100 basis point impact from incremental SNAP headwinds, the company said.

Kraft Heinz raised its adjusted earnings per share forecast to a range of $2.07 to $2.13, from $2.03 to $2.09. It lowered its expected effective tax rate on adjusted earnings to about 23.5% from about 24.5%. Its forecast for constant currency adjusted operating income, a decline of 16% to 18%, was unchanged.

Net sales fell 2.0% to $6.1 billion in the third quarter, and organic net sales fell 1.1%. Net income attributable to common shareholders was $544 million, or 46 cents a diluted share, compared with $615 million, or 52 cents, a year earlier. Adjusted EPS was 53 cents, down from 61 cents. Operating income fell 14.6% to $0.9 billion.

Analysts expected adjusted earnings of 42 cents a share, according to The Wall Street Journal. Eight analysts surveyed by Zacks Investment Research expected 43 cents, according to The Associated Press. Analysts expected revenue of $6.09 billion, according to The Wall Street Journal.

Kraft Heinz stock rose 3.1% in premarket trading.

By region, North America net sales fell 3.4% and Europe and Pacific Developed Markets net sales fell 5.6%. Emerging Markets net sales rose 13.8%.

Volume and mix fell 1.1 percentage points. The company cited declines in North America across meats, sauces and refreshment beverages, along with an approximate 80 basis point headwind from inventory pull forward into the second quarter. Price was flat.

Higher procurement and logistics costs, higher variable compensation expense and increased advertising expenses weighed on operating income, the company said.

"Our 2026 operating plan to turn around the U.S. business and accelerate growth internationally is on track," CEO Steve Cahillane said in a statement. "Relative to last year, our market share, sales, and volume trends are improving in every region."

Cahillane said the company is raising the low end of its organic net sales outlook to reflect the momentum it has built.

Kraft Heinz is holding a live question-and-answer session at 9 a.m. ET.

#5532. Stock markets celebrate a ‘stunning rebuke’: Trump says he will accept midterm losses—but don’t expect defeat to change him

It was a “stunning rebuke” to President Trump. That’s not Fortune’s opinion, by the way. The words “stunning rebuke”—and variations on that theme—were the choice of dozens of front pages reporting on the midterm election results today.

“Democrats Take Congress in Stunning Rebuke of Trump,” the WSJ said. “Party Flips Senate and House as Voters Deliver Stunning Rebuke to Trump,” the NYT declared. “Americans deliver stunning rebuke to Donald Trump as blue wave sweeps country,” the FT wrote. “Texas Turns Blue in Stunning Rebuke of Donald Trump, Elon Musk and GOP,” Bloomberg said.

France’s Le Monde originally headlined its story as a “stunning rebuke for Trump” but, perhaps sensing that the term was already overused, later changed it to “spectacular rejection” (you can see the original in the URL).

The results were so sweeping—the Senate stood at 54-44 in favor of the Democrats this morning, with the House at 228-129—that even Trump appears to accept that reality has changed around him. He told Fox News last night, “I think the Democrats did a good job, I really do, I think they did a good job. They fought hard.”

Crucially, Trump also said he would accept the results. He told the NYT he was “absolutely willing to accept those results” and would work with Democrats. “We’ll, you know, look forward to working with them … We’ll probably work something out.”

But don’t mistake this for a sign that Trump will be chastened and change course on the issues that cost him the election, such as the war, tariffs, and the price of gas. Chris Ruddy, the president’s friend and CEO of Newsmax, told the BBC this morning that although the results were “horrendous” for Trump, “he’s not a man that reflects. He’s got sort of two drives, fast and faster, in his gearbox. I think he’s going to continue to pursue his policies by executive order and there will be a lot of battles.”

"The president likes to respond usually with brute force," Ruddy said.

Suppliers of plywood are doing a roaring trade in Paris right now. All over the French capital, shop owners and restaurateurs have boarded up their windows against les manifestations—protests over a lack of education funding which have frequently devolved into rioting. Shops that aren't boarded up sometimes have cracked windows, where the looters have failed to gain entry.

Fixed to the boards are paper signs, saying “Nous sommes ouverts!” (We are open!) Business hasn’t stopped just because of politics.

In fact, as Fortune discovered on a visit to Paris recently, the capital is not—as social media would have you believe—a disaster zone of barricades and flying bottles. Quite the opposite. If you hadn’t read the news, you wouldn’t even know there were protests going on. Yes, there were 770 arrests nationwide on Saturday and Molotov cocktails were thrown at the police. But I took an Uber twice through la Place de la République—that’s the square with a big statue that demonstrators often climb onto—and didn’t see anyone there.

The city was not, as some Wall Street analysts have suggested, on the brink of civil breakdown.

The best example of this phenomenon—that the reality of the French protests is in fact much more boring than the viral videos suggest—was captured by this Instagram account, which intercuts scenes of chaos from the TV news with humdrum images of Parisiennes picking through street markets and drinking coffee in the autumn sunshine.

Yes, there is a beefed-up police presence. Les flics could be seen on many street corners, wearing armored vests. There were, perhaps, a few more sirens than normal. But nothing that would make a New Yorker blink.

After the interior minister admitted in October that the police had “lost control” of the protests, the French government is simply not sitting still for any more trouble.

With the street protests contained, that pushes the economic issue—the protesters want more spending and fewer cuts, which the bond market is unlikely to tolerate—into next April’s elections. Neither of the two most popular candidates, Marine Le Pen on the right and Jean-Luc Mélenchon on the left, has produced spending plans that the market takes seriously.

France is thus playing a game of chicken with the European Central Bank. If it fails to get its fiscal house in order, a debt crisis will emerge. At that point, the ECB has two choices: a) Buy French bonds in a bailout, devaluing the euro, and importing inflation throughout Europe. b) Do what the ECB did to Greece in 2015, when it forced Athens to accept austerity measures in return for a bailout. That program reduced Greek GDP by 25% over the following years. Unemployment hit 28%.

In both cases, the cure is worse than France’s current sickness. The protesters and their politicians might want to heal themselves before Frankfurt steps in.
