#5531. Mortgage applications slipped again even as rates fell for a third straight week

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Purchase applications fell 2% and ran 19% below a year earlier as the 30-year rate eased to 7.30%, MBA data showed

The Mortgage Bankers Association said total mortgage application volume fell 1.2% last week on a seasonally adjusted basis as the average 30-year fixed rate declined for a third straight week, according to CNBC.

Applications to buy a home slid 2% compared with the week before, leaving them 19% under where they stood 12 months ago, according to CNBC. The MBA's purchase index has fallen in all but one of the past nine weeks and is hovering near its weakest reading since January 2025, according to Bloomberg. Refinance applications rose 0.1% for the week and stood 60% below their year-earlier level, according to CNBC.

The contract rate for 30-year fixed mortgages eased to 7.30% from 7.37% for the week ending Oct. 30, covering conforming loans up to $832,750, according to CNBC. Points slipped to 0.75 from 0.76 for borrowers putting 20% down, a figure that counts the origination fee. The rate remains nearly a point above where it stood a year ago, so borrowers have scant motivation to refinance.

"Mortgage rates drifted down to their lowest level since September 2026 last week in the wake of the Federal Reserve's decision to hold on additional rate hikes at its October meeting," said Mike Fratantoni, MBA senior vice president and chief economist, according to CNBC.

The average rate for 5/1 adjustable-rate loans eased to 6.29%, down from 6.41%, according to CNBC. Fratantoni said more borrowers are turning to adjustable-rate loans because they carry smaller starting payments, and ARMs now account for the largest share of applications since September 2025.

A separate survey by Mortgage News Daily showed rates moving higher at the start of this week after a report on job openings came in above expectations, according to CNBC.

Applications had dropped 5.3% in an earlier October reading, when the 30-year rate slipped to 7.41% from 7.50%. That 7.50% level, reached in the week ended Oct. 9, was the highest since November 2023.

The housing market has weakened since rates returned to 7% in mid-September, according to Bloomberg. According to Bloomberg, an index tracking contract signings for previously owned homes hit a record low in September.

#5530. F5 stock suffers worst day in more than a decade as AI spending shakes investors

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 10:56 amOctober 28, 2026 at 11:05 am

Shares of F5 fell about 20% on Wednesday, a day after the Seattle-based company beat Wall Street’s estimates and said it would boost spending to capitalize on expected growth in the AI security market.

The application security and delivery company’s stock was trading around $368 late Wednesday morning, down from $459 at Tuesday’s close, wiping out about $5 billion in market value. That put F5 on pace for its biggest one-day drop in more than 13 years, according to Barron’s. Before the drop, F5’s shares had climbed nearly 80% this year.

F5’s revenue for its fiscal fourth quarter rose 13% to $917 million, and product revenue jumped 23%. Adjusted earnings of $4.42 a share beat estimates of about $4.30.

Slower growth ahead: Investors seem to be focused on the outlook. F5 expects revenue to grow 8% to 9% in fiscal 2027, down from 11% this year, and adjusted earnings per share to grow 3% to 5%. It’s also projecting lower margins as memory and storage components get more expensive, and as it doubles its team of AI security sellers.

F5’s hardware business is also cooling off. Systems revenue jumped 29% in the quarter as customers replaced aging equipment, but F5 Chief Financial Officer Cooper Werner said on the earnings call that those replacements will taper off in the second half of fiscal 2027.

The AI bet: F5 is spending more to go after AI security. CEO François Locoh-Donou said on the call that the company will double its team of specialist AI security sellers in fiscal 2027 and more than double its marketing in that area. It’s also adding compensation incentives for all of its field sellers to discuss AI security with customers.

F5’s adjusted operating margin fell to 33.7% in the quarter, from 37% a year earlier.

Locoh-Donou said F5’s AI-related bookings topped $100 million in fiscal 2026, up about 300%. Most of that came from AI data delivery, which moves data to and from AI systems, rather than security. More than 300 customers are using an AI-powered web application firewall that F5 launched in March.

The company estimates the AI market it sells into will grow from about $1 billion this year to $11 billion by 2030.

Wall Street reaction: Piper Sandler downgraded the stock to neutral, according to The Motley Fool. Analysts at William Blair, which rates F5 “market perform,” wrote in a research note that “the AI opportunity has yet to contribute meaningfully to the top line.”

We’ve contacted F5 for comment on the stock decline.

F5 has been building out its AI security business, including its acquisition of SurePath AI. Locoh-Donou talked about the company’s path from the early web to AI security on a GeekWire Podcast episode marking F5’s 30th anniversary. He said companies adopting AI are losing track of what those systems can access, and that juggling separate tools to manage it is a burden, which is why F5 is building a single AI security platform.

This week, F5’s board authorized an additional $1.5 billion in stock buybacks, on top of $322 million remaining in its existing program.

#5528. Reed Jobs’s Yosemite raises $350 million second fund to make cancer non-lethal

For Jobs—an investor and, yes, Steve Jobs’s son—the aim’s far more precise: To make cancer non-lethal. The rhetorical distinction is important.

“I don’t think you’ll cure cancer because we’re human,” said Jobs. “Any human cell could become cancerous, right? And we’re not going to stop having human cells. So, the idea that none of them could ever become cancer is preposterous. That risk’s never going away.”

And medicine, however advanced it may be, seldom makes diseases vanish. But there’s a path to a world where cancer is much less intractable. Consider, Jobs says, the trajectory of AIDS as a guide to what might be possible for cancer treatment.

“There’s no vaccine for [AIDS], unfortunately,” he said. “I’d love for there to be, but in the absence of that, it’s a far less scary disease now in the United States because it’s non-lethal. With a cocktail of drugs, you can actually prevent mortality. In many ways, I think that’s a massive victory and, in some ways, the most essential victory. Because it’s victory over death, and that’s what I want for cancer patients.”

For Jobs, this has been his life’s work—he started working in cancer labs as a teenager when his father got sick (Steve Jobs would pass away in 2011). Today, he’s a VC, the founder of venture firm Yosemite, which he started after spinning out of Laurene Powell Jobs’s Emerson Collective in 2023. Yosemite (and Jobs) are devoted to cancer-focused investing, both in startups and via scientific grants.

Yosemite has now closed its second fund at $350 million, a serious jump from January’s first close at $200 million, Jobs exclusively told Fortune and the Term Sheet Podcast. Jobs’s LPs include Amgen, AbbVie, MIT, Memorial Sloan Kettering, and VC legend John Doerr. Yosemite’s model is unique: Jobs, in some ways, is operating in a traditional venture model, investing in startups early and taking sizable stakes en route to an exit (he’s clear the goal is venture-scale returns). But Yosemite also offers philanthropic grants to scientists.

“With philanthropy, we can fail really cheaply,” said Jobs. “That’s the real wisdom behind this… One of the difficult and suboptimal things about my industry is how slow it is. And look, that’s really important from a regulatory standpoint. But it also means you can waste a lot of money on things that aren’t going to work, which is obviously really bad. What we’ve learned is that we can test new ideas really quickly and cheaply in universities with grants. And before we waste a lot of time, money, and resources, we can kind of flip over that first card.”

Yosemite’s first fund, closed in 2024 at $263 million, included AI drug discovery startup Chai Discovery, cervical cancer screening company Teal Health, epi-therapeutic medicine maker Tune Therapeutics, and care navigation startup Sage Care. This variety reflects how Jobs believes the healthcare system and science will ultimately have to evolve.

“I don’t think a company alone is going to make cancer non-lethal,” said Jobs. “I think it’s going to be a consortium of things. It’s going to be a really long push, probably cancer by cancer, more likely than not.”

When Jobs started Yosemite in 2023, biotech was in a slump, one that’s turned around substantially in recent years. The biggest changes are scientific advancements over the last three years, he said.

“You couldn’t have told me four years ago that we’d be sitting here today and we would have the advancements in GLP-1s, in immunotherapy, in vaccines now, and against pancreatic cancer that we’ve achieved,” said Jobs. “Those things have happened and have been titanic for the industry.”

I asked Jobs what advice his father would have for him.

“I think he’d say stay on the path, because something we have in common is we’re really good long-term builders,” said Jobs. “Yosemite is not going to, as you know, reach its zenith of success in the next year or two. This is a long-term play that’s going to take my whole life.”

#5527. Seattle farmworker payroll startup Ganaz acquired as CEO Hannah Freeman steps away

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Lisa Stiffler on Oct 28, 2026 at 1:38 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 1:47 pm

Seattle startup Ganaz, which provides payroll and HR tech for agricultural workers and employers, has been acquired by Beacon Holdings.

Ganaz co-founder and CEO Hannah Freeman announced the deal Wednesday on LinkedIn, saying the public benefit corporation “is in great hands” at Beacon, which “is building momentum for our next exciting season.”

Freeman indicated she is stepping away from the company to “catch my breath, spend more time with my daughter, and dream about what’s next,” she wrote. “I’ll miss our team & customers, but will be cheering you on from the sidelines.”

Ganaz launched in 2017 and has raised more than $10 million, with its last disclosed funding round in June 2021. That financing valued the company at $26 million, according to PitchBook. Terms of the acquisition were not disclosed.

Beacon, based in Toronto, buys software businesses serving traditional industries and provides shared technology and operational resources. The company said in September that its portfolio included 45 software businesses.

Ganaz’s platform provides employee onboarding, training, communication and analytics tools. It also offers a Mastercard payroll card that gives unbanked workers access to digital banking. Employers save time and money by skipping paper checks, while workers keep more of their pay by avoiding check-cashing and high remittance fees.

Ganaz received GeekWire’s 2023 Geeks Give Back Award. “We founded Ganaz to make life better for farm workers, and we do that by building technology that agricultural employers love and can’t live without,” Freeman told GeekWire in 2023. “We build our tools to help both workers and employers prosper, and that kicks off a virtuous cycle that helps agricultural communities prosper as well.”

At that time, the startup was serving more than 250,000 agricultural workers in the U.S. and Mexico and 100 employers in the sector.

The company has about 17 employees, according to LinkedIn. Freeman did not say in her post whether Ganaz will continue as a subsidiary or whether its employees will receive job offers from Beacon. GeekWire has reached out to Freeman for comment and will update the story with any reply.

#5526. CVS Health is splitting into two companies, separating its pharmacies from insurance

Free daily briefing on global business news.

CVS Health expects the separation of Aetna and Caremark from about 9,000 pharmacies to be completed in the first half of 2028

CVS Health $CVS announced plans to split into two independent public companies on Wednesday, separating its retail pharmacies from Aetna and CVS Caremark. The decision came after the board conducted a strategic assessment of the business.

One company will hold Aetna, CVS Caremark, CVS Specialty, Oak Street Health and Signify Health. It will keep the CVS Health name in the interim. The second company, called CVS Pharmacy, will hold about 9,000 pharmacies, the mail pharmacy, MinuteClinic (including virtual care) and the Health100 technology services business.

CVS Health Chairman and CEO David Joyner will hold the same roles at the healthcare solutions company once the split is complete. Prem Shah, group president of CVS Health, will become CEO of CVS Pharmacy. The company said it will announce other leaders and board members at a future date.

“From a position of strength, and a focus on the long term, we plan to create two focused companies to improve consumer engagement, affordability, and care coordination,” Joyner said in a statement, according to CNBC.

Joyner told Bloomberg that cutting the retail unit loose from the rest of the company would give it room to grow more rapidly than it could under the existing umbrella.

CVS Health expects the separation to be completed in the first half of 2028. It is intended to be tax-free to the company and its shareholders for U.S. federal income tax purposes. CVS Health shareholders will own stock in both companies.

Completion is subject to final approval by the board, effectiveness of a Form 10 registration statement filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, and confirmation of the tax-free treatment. CVS Health said it expects both companies to hold solid investment-grade ratings and to pay a dividend.

CVS Pharmacy plans to expand services from its nearly 30,000 pharmacists and to pursue partnerships with payers, pharmacy benefit managers and manufacturers, the company said. Until the split is complete, CVS Health will operate as it does today. Customers, patients and clients will continue to receive their medicine, care and benefits without interruption, the company said.

In a separate release on Wednesday, CVS Health reported third-quarter results and lifted its full-year 2026 earnings forecast, which now stands at a minimum of $8.20 per share versus the earlier $7.90 to $8.10 range.

The plan would partly unwind the 2018 deal, valued at $78 billion, in which CVS bought Aetna and formed the combined company, according to CNBC.

Lawmakers in Arkansas and Tennessee have enacted measures over the past two years intended to stop a single company from both administering drug coverage and owning storefront and mail-service pharmacies, according to The New York Times.

#5525. Current price of oil as of November 4, 2026

At 7 a.m. Eastern Time today, the price of oil sits at $105.84 per barrel, using Brent as the benchmark (we’ll explain what that means shortly). That’s a decrease of $4.61 since yesterday morning and $41 more than at this time last year.

Nobody can predict the future path of oil prices with certainty. A range of factors influence how oil trades, yet supply and demand remain the main drivers. When fears of economic slowdown, conflict, or similar shocks rise, oil prices can move sharply.

The price you see at the gas pump reflects more than just crude oil. Also built in are the costs of refining, distribution through wholesalers, various taxes, and the margin your neighborhood station charges.

Crude oil is still the largest single driver of the final pump price, typically representing over half of each gallon’s cost. Spikes in oil prices tend to push gas prices higher in short order. But when oil prices decline, gas prices often ease down gradually, a behavior known as “rockets and feathers.”

In the event of an emergency, the U.S. maintains a stockpile of crude oil known as the Strategic Petroleum Reserve. Its main goal is to safeguard energy security when disasters strike—think sanctions, severe storm damage, or war. It can also do a lot to ease the pain of sudden price jumps when supply gets disrupted.

It’s not a permanent fix, as it’s more meant to provide immediate support for consumers and ensure critical parts of the economy like key industries, emergency services, public transportation, and so on can keep operating.

Both oil and natural gas play key roles as major sources of energy. A big change in oil prices can affect natural gas by proxy. If oil prices increase, some industries may swap natural gas for some segments of their operations where possible, increasing the demand for natural gas.

Oil prices are often measured by two key benchmarks:

Between the two, Brent is a better representation of global oil performance because it prices much of the world’s traded crude. It’s also often the best way to review historical oil trends. In fact, the U.S. Energy Information Administration now leans on Brent as its primary reference in its Annual Energy Outlook.

When you look at the Brent benchmark across multiple decades, you’ll see that oil has been anything but consistent. It has experienced spikes driven by wars and supply cuts, as well as crashes linked to global recessions and an oversupply (called a “glut”). For example:

In short, oil’s historical performance has been far from steady. It’s massively affected by wars, recessions, OPEC whims, evolving energy initiatives and policies, and much more.

Looking to stay up-to-date regarding the latest energy developments? Check out our recent coverage:

The current price of oil per barrel depends largely on supply and demand, including news about potential future supply and demand (geopolitics, decisions made by OPEC+, etc.). In the U.S., prices also move based on how friendly an administration is to drilling, as it can affect future supply. For example, 2025 saw the Trump administration move to reopen more than 1.5 million acres in the Coastal Plain of the Arctic National Wildlife Refuge for oil and gas leasing, reversing the Biden administration’s policy of limiting oil drilling in the Arctic.

The price of oil updates constantly when the “futures” markets are open. A futures market is effectively an auction where people agree to buy or sell oil in the future. As long as people and companies are trading contracts, the oil price is changing.

In short, shale is rock that contains oil and natural gas. Think of shale as energy yet to be tapped. The more shale the U.S. accesses, the more energy we’ll have—and the more easily oil prices can keep from spiking as much thanks to a greater supply.

When oil is expensive, it tends to make everyday items cost more. This can be related to energy (your heating, gas utilities, etc.), but it’s also due to the logistics involved with making those items accessible to you. Shipping, for example, can affect the price of things at the grocery store, as it’s more expensive to get those products from warehouses and farms onto the shelf.

#5524. 9 companies cutting jobs in 2026, from Amazon and UPS to Meta and Block

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Amazon, UPS, Oracle, Meta, and Heineken are among 9 companies cutting staff or planning cuts in 2026 as AI and weak demand reshape payrolls.

Opening a work inbox in 2026 can feel like a gamble, with the next restructuring memo as likely to come from a delivery service or a brewer as from a software firm. U.S. layoffs topped 1.1 million in 2025, and firms cited artificial intelligence adoption, economic uncertainty, and the push to trim costs. The new calendar brought no relief. Headcount reductions in the first weeks of 2026 spread across a wide range of industries and reached tens of thousands of workers. Anyone who draws a paycheck, manages a team, or owns shares in a public corporation has a stake in where the next round lands and what pushes executives to shrink their workforces.

The labor market and the broader economy told two different stories as 2025 closed. Hiring slowed in December, capping a year of weak payroll gains that left many people looking for work frustrated. Output kept climbing. Strong consumer spending powered a 4.3% annual growth rate in the July-September quarter, the best showing in two years. The Federal Reserve Bank of Atlanta forecast a slowdown to 2.7% for the final three months of the year, and economists held on to their optimism through the hiring lull. The gap between expanding output and sluggish recruitment matters to job seekers weighing a career move. A healthy economy did little to shield wage earners from a slow job market, which suggests headline growth figures offer an incomplete read on individual prospects.

FOX 13 Tampa Bay has kept a running list of companies shedding staff since Jan. 27, 2026, updating it through July 6 with reporting drawn from LiveNOW from FOX, FOX Business, Business Insider, and The Associated Press. The roundup applies no scoring system of its own. Some entries rest on statements from the companies themselves, while others come from outlets citing unnamed sources. The compilation points to WARN Tracker, a website that monitors the WARN notices employers file before dismissing employees. WARN Tracker's tally shows more than 100 companies planning job cuts in 2026, though part of that total traces back to earlier announcements. This article draws nine companies from the list, a group that spans technology, delivery, finance, brewing, apparel, and manufacturing. The selection follows no order of size and makes no claim to completeness.

Amazon $AMZN announced on Jan. 28 that it is eliminating roughly 16,000 jobs, its second mass layoff in about three months. Beth Galetti, a senior vice president at the company, sent the memo that broke the news to employees.

The January announcement followed an October 2025 reduction that removed about 14,000 white-collar positions. The January figure exceeds the October total by about 2,000 jobs. Combined, the two waves reach roughly 30,000 roles.

Workers who survived the October cut had little time to settle before the next memo arrived. Two large rounds in quick succession, the second bigger than the first, point to a restructuring still in motion.

Amazon framed the downsizing as part of an ongoing drive to strip out management tiers, give staff more ownership, and clear away red tape. Thinner management fits the white-collar profile of the October cut. A campaign pitched as continuous leaves room for more job losses at Amazon.

UPS announced it would eliminate up to 30,000 operational jobs, a reduction aimed at the hands-on side of the delivery company's business. The words "up to" mark a ceiling. The final count could settle below that mark, and the announcement leaves the company room to stop short of it.

Operational roles set this plan apart from much of the 2026 list. Amazon $AMZN's earlier round fell on white-collar staff, and Meta $META's Reality Labs plan targets a division built around metaverse products. UPS is thinning the part of a package carrier that moves boxes from one place to another.

Scale gives the UPS ceiling added weight. At its upper limit, the plan would run nearly twice the size of Amazon's January round, the headline cut from the year's most prominent tech employer.

The announcement, as reported, offers no total headcount for UPS. Readers can't tell what share of the workforce the plan would touch, a gap that makes the cut harder to measure against companies such as Heineken, which framed its reduction as a portion of total staff.

The UPS plan carries the 2026 contraction past corporate desks and into the work that keeps goods in motion.

Oracle $ORCL may slash 20,000 to 30,000 positions, FOX Business reported, citing the tech magazine CIO. The range works out to 12% to 18% of the company's global workforce of roughly 162,000 employees. The two sets of numbers agree, with 12% of 162,000 coming to about 19,400 and 18% to about 29,200. The report gives no date, and nothing in it shows that any Oracle worker has lost a job.

Even the bottom of that range would place Oracle among the heaviest reductions in this group. Twenty thousand jobs would exceed Amazon $AMZN's January round of about 16,000, and the top figure equals the 30,000 operational jobs UPS has said it could eliminate. Measured as a share of staff, the plan would run deeper than the roughly 10% Reuters sources attached to Meta $META's broader cut. It would also land at four to six times Morgan Stanley $MS's 3%, roughly twice Heineken's share of nearly 7%, and below Block $SQ's 40%.

A 10,000-position spread between the two ends suggests the plan, as reported, has not settled into a firm number. At the low end, Oracle would keep about 142,000 workers. At the high end, about 132,000 would remain. The smaller of those totals would outnumber Heineken's entire pre-cut workforce of roughly 87,000.

Oracle has put no figures of its own on record. Amazon, UPS, Heineken, Nike $NKE, and Block each announced their reductions, and Meta disclosed its Reality Labs cut itself. Oracle's numbers reached the public secondhand, passing from CIO to FOX Business.

Meta's broader plan also surfaced through Reuters sources, yet that reporting came with a scheduled date of May 20. Oracle's report lacks even that, leaving its workers no sense of when notices might arrive. Until Oracle confirms the figures, the reported range describes a possibility, and readers should give it less weight than cuts a company has stated in its own name.

Meta $META plans to eliminate more than 1,000 jobs in its Reality Labs division as the company steers investment away from metaverse products. The move links the size of a team to the money behind its work. Meta is pulling dollars from the metaverse, and the staff who build those products stand to lose their positions. Meta announced this reduction itself, which places it on firmer ground than the wider plan that surfaced through anonymous sources.

A larger reduction appears in reporting from Reuters. Sources told the news agency that Meta planned an initial round of layoffs on May 20, one that would remove about 10% of its global workforce, or nearly 8,000 employees. The same reporting described the company as preparing to shed thousands of jobs, with deeper job losses expected later in the year. No update in the coverage confirms that the May 20 round took place, so the figure stands as a reported plan.

The reported round would dwarf the Reality Labs announcement. Nearly 8,000 positions would amount to about eight times the more than 1,000 jobs at stake in the metaverse unit. Pairing 10% with 8,000 implies a payroll near 80,000 worldwide. Against a base of that size, the Reality Labs trim reaches a little over 1% of the total. Neither account specifies whether the Reality Labs jobs fall inside the reported 10% or come on top of it. A downsizing of the scope Reuters described would stretch past any single division and extend across the whole company. Any deeper round later in the year would push the share beyond 10%.

A Meta executive has declined to rule out further departures. Janelle Gale, the company's chief people officer, told employees in an internal meeting that Meta could not guarantee an end to layoffs, according to People Matters. Staff outside Reality Labs have little reason to treat the metaverse pullback as the final word on Meta's headcount.

Heineken plans to eliminate up to 6,000 jobs worldwide, a reduction the Dutch brewer announced on Feb. 11 that equals nearly 7% of its roughly 87,000 employees. The 6,000 figure works as a ceiling. The final tally could land below it. Heineken expects its productivity program to reduce headcount by 5,000 to 6,000 positions over the next two years, according to Reuters.

Heineken expects its earnings growth to slow in 2026 and pins the forecast on weak demand across the beer industry. Reuters reports that the brewer's guidance calls for profit to rise 2% to 6% this year, down from the 4% to 8% it targeted for 2025. Tight household budgets and recent bad weather have cut into beer sales across the sector. Rival Carlsberg has announced job cuts as well, and it forecast the identical 2% to 6% range a week before Heineken, according to Reuters. Heineken brews Tiger and Amstel alongside the lager that carries its name. A slump that spans the industry leaves little shelter in a stable of several brands.

Heineken's stated reason for the cuts sets the brewer apart from much of this list. Block $SQ ties its staff reduction to a push into artificial intelligence, and Meta $META is steering money away from metaverse products. The brewer's explanation turns on its customers and their appetite for beer. Longer-term pressures add to the strain, with alcohol makers confronting more health warnings, competing alternatives, and disruptors such as weight-loss drugs.

The worldwide reach of the plan marks another contrast. Stanley Black & Decker $SWK's cut focuses on one Connecticut factory, while Heineken's job losses span its global workforce. The burden won't spread evenly, though. Finance chief Harold van den Broek said some of the cuts will center on Europe and on non-priority markets with weaker growth prospects.

At the full 6,000, the plan would leave Heineken with about 81,000 employees. Reuters reports that organic operating profit grew 4.4% in 2025, topping the 4% analysts had expected. The brewer faces unhappy investors who argue it has fallen behind on efficiency, and the cuts aim to free up savings as the company pledges faster growth with fewer resources. Heineken is paring its payroll early in a year it expects to bring slower profit expansion, a move timed to trim costs before the slowdown reaches its results.

Morgan Stanley $MS cut 3% of its staff, about 2,500 employees, and distributed the reductions through all of its business divisions. No single unit carried the burden on its own. Every part of the bank gave up some headcount.

The two figures together put Morgan Stanley's payroll at roughly 83,000 people before the layoffs. About 97% of them kept their jobs. Losing 2,500 positions at once still leaves a sizable group of people searching for new work, yet it amounts to a thin slice of an organization that large.

The firmwide reach sets this move apart from job losses aimed at one plant, one product line, or one division elsewhere on this list. Morgan Stanley spread the pain evenly enough that no corner of the firm escaped it. The pattern points to a bank paring each of its existing divisions and keeping its overall structure in place.

Nike $NKE announced earlier this year that it is cutting 775 jobs. The company attached an exact headcount to the reduction, with no range or rounding around the figure.

Several other cuts in this group surfaced as approximations or upper limits. Nike's precise tally stands apart from them.

Stanley Black & Decker $SWK said it will cut about 300 positions in New Britain, Connecticut, by closing a factory that builds single-sided tape measures. The toolmaker described the shutdown as one piece of a restructuring in progress.

The company traced the closure to what it called a sustained drop in demand for single-sided tape measures. Its explanation narrows the cause to one product category. Stanley Black & Decker cited no broad downturn and no companywide pivot. The stated problem is a shrinking market for a specific tool.

A single product's fading sales set this cut apart from several others in the roundup. Tech firms on the list frame their reductions around bets on artificial intelligence or shifts in investment priorities. The toolmaker offers a plainer account. Customers want fewer of one item it makes. The plant that builds that item will close.

Stanley Black & Decker's description of the decline as sustained signals that the company does not expect orders to rebound. A permanent closure fits that reading.

The ongoing overhaul places the New Britain closure inside a wider effort the company has not finished. The New Britain case shows the year's job cuts reaching past software and services onto factory floors, where weak sales of one product can shut down a whole facility.

Block $SQ cut its staff by 40% to expand its artificial intelligence business, a move that put two of every five employees out of work. Pinterest $PINS, the San Francisco company that also shifted resources toward AI-focused roles, announced it would reduce its headcount by just under 15%. Block's cut runs more than twice as deep, the largest proportional reduction among the companies in the roundup that disclosed a workforce share.

Block owns the payment services Square and Cash App. Both brands answer to a parent operating with three-fifths of its former workforce. Jack Dorsey presented the layoffs as a choice about structure. He wrote that AI tools and smaller, flatter teams are changing how leaders build and run a company. He added that the cuts did not stem from any trouble at Block.

Dorsey's account separates Block from employers on the list that tied their cuts to weak demand or a dimmer profit outlook. He describes a deliberate redesign, a wager that a leaner organization equipped with AI can do the work a larger one handled. Pinterest's move points in a similar direction. It is giving priority to AI-powered products as it trims staff. Together, the two cases show AI serving as a stated reason for cuts at companies that cite no slump in demand.

Tech experts told CBC News that pandemic-era overhiring and inflated AI promises have fed job losses across the industry. Their explanation complicates Dorsey's. He credits the tools themselves, while the experts point to the hiring binge and the hype that preceded them. If the experts have it right, some of the cuts at Block may correct past hiring as much as they prepare the company for AI. Either reading lands in the same place. Block is betting that a smaller staff, armed with new tools, can operate Square and Cash App.

#5523. Microsoft Azure revenue surges 48% to $33.2B, beating expectations as cloud and AI demand grows

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 1:47 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 4:30 pm

Microsoft’s Azure cloud business brought in $33.2 billion in revenue in the September quarter, up 48% from a year earlier, blowing past the company’s own forecast and beating Wall Street’s expectations.

The growth suggests that Microsoft is selling cloud and AI computing about as fast as it can install it. Azure revenue rose $10.8 billion from a year earlier, driven by demand for services across the platform, Microsoft said in its quarterly filing. That came even as some new data center capacity arrived late.

For investors worried about Microsoft’s record capital spending, it’s a sign that the company’s massive AI and cloud infrastructure buildout is turning into sales. Microsoft’s shares rose nearly 4% in after-hours trading following the earnings report.

Overall, Microsoft reported revenue of $92.3 billion for the first quarter of its 2027 fiscal year, up 19% and above the $90.75 billion analysts expected, according to Yahoo Finance. Earnings were $4.89 per share excluding the impact of its OpenAI investment, compared with expectations of $4.72.

It’s the first time Microsoft has reported Azure’s quarterly revenue figure, not just its growth. The disclosure is part of a new financial structure that took effect this quarter, splitting the company into two segments: Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer.

Capital spending came in below Microsoft’s forecast. The company spent $45.2 billion, including finance leases, short of the more than $50 billion it expected. Some data center capacity that third parties were supposed to deliver in the quarter was delayed, the company said.

Google Cloud, which includes Google’s Workspace productivity apps, brought in $30.7 billion in revenue in the quarter, up 103% from a year earlier, Alphabet reported Wednesday afternoon.

Amazon reports earnings Thursday afternoon, including AWS results.

Update, 3:05 p.m.:Microsoft expects Azure growth to accelerate again this quarter, to 49% to 50% excluding currency changes, CFO Amy Hood said on the earnings call. “Customer demand continues to exceed available supply,” she said.

Hood said Azure’s growth came from Foundry, Microsoft’s service for building AI apps and agents, and from engineering work that let Microsoft sell unused capacity on its existing servers. That helped make up for delays in new data center capacity that outside providers were supposed to deliver.

Those delays pushed some spending later into the fiscal year. Microsoft now expects to spend about $170 billion on capital expenditures in calendar 2026, down from about $175 billion. It expects to spend more than $50 billion this quarter, and Hood said spending will accelerate in the first half of calendar 2027.

Hood also said Microsoft may tap additional sources of financing to help pay for the buildout, “when we believe it is attractive to do so.” The company still expects to bring in more cash than it spends this fiscal year.

Microsoft’s expense forecast for the December quarter includes an estimate for the buyout offer it announced Monday, Hood said, though she didn’t give the amount.

The company expects total revenue of $96 billion to $97.1 billion for the December quarter, above the $95.7 billion analysts expected, according to Yahoo Finance.

#5522. Wall Street seeks shelter in Treasuries as midterms threaten to throw Washington into a fiscal gridlock

With only a couple of seats left to be called in the midterm elections, a “blue wave” is preparing to wash through Congress. Voters made it clear they were unhappy with Republicans in the first two years of President Trump’s administration, with 54 Democrats elected to the Senate and 44 Republicans, as of this writing, per CNBC.Consumers will want to see action on issues close to home from their newly elected officials, namely affordability and inflation. Military conflict with Iran has pushed up oil prices and, as a result, gas prices. That action came after Trump’s tariff scheme, which targeted exports from foreign countries, but economists say it resulted in increased costs being passed back to consumers.

While Main Street has a checklist of action it wants to see, Wall Street is hedging on how the new power dynamics on Capitol Hill will play out.

In the early hours of this morning, yields on longer-dated bonds trended downward as demand inversely rose. 30-Year Treasuries pushed below 5.3%, while the 10-year pushed down toward 4.9%.

Demand for the securities shows bonds remain the destination of choice in a market flight to safety—a question which seemed to hang over the market this summer as yields rose over 5%.

A more divided government increases the likelihood of government standoffs, particularly over spending. “Fiscal gridlock seems the likely default,” UBS’s Paul Donovan told clients this morning. “President Trump has seemingly retreated from an earlier pledge to veto everything the Democrats suggest, Treasuries have initially strengthened on the results.”

Beyond a shield against volatility, investors have additional motivations to look to bonds in the current political climate. President Trump and his team may now find it harder to push through policy packages that might require more spending and, as a result, more government borrowing. Likewise, Democrat spending packages could face roadblocks from a still sizeable Republican presence in Congress and Trump’s veto power.

Markets are also bracing for near-term volatility in equities, as UBS’s chief investment officer, Mark Haefele, noted to clients, “particularly in tech and other areas sensitive to greater regulatory scrutiny.” With AI driving stock gains this year, investors may seek to balance any hiccups with the dependable asset of Treasuries.

While spending gridlock may frustrate policymakers, it might calm the nerves of debt hawks. Concern over the fiscal trajectory of the U.S. is mounting, owing to federal deficits of between 6% and 7% of GDP, and interest payments on the national debt now demand more than $1 trillion a year.

A gridlock could slow the path of any spending bills, allaying some concerns about the U.S. budget picture. As Deutsche Bank’s Jim Reid noted this morning: “There’s been a rally for U.S. Treasuries … given that divided government has generally made it harder for fiscal stimulus to be passed. So that’s eased concerns on the fiscal trajectory a bit.”

Policymakers’ appetite for a conversation on fiscal responsibility may be gauged sooner rather than later. The current federal government funding package runs out on December 11 and will require bipartisan support to prevent a government shutdown.

While the officials elected in the midterms won’t be in office until the New Year, a shift in the tide may give Democrats more motivation to hold the line or make bolder demands in return for support.

The odds of a government shutdown jumped to 45% overnight on the prediction market platform Kalshi, up from around 30%.

Eleanor Pringle is an award-winning senior reporter at Fortune covering news, the economy, and personal finance. Eleanor previously worked as a business correspondent and news editor in regional news in the U.K. She completed her journalism training with the Press Association after earning a degree from the University of East Anglia.

#5520. Bigger than Bing or Xbox: Microsoft’s OpenAI haul reaches $10B in quarterly revenue

by Todd Bishop on Oct 28, 2026 at 4:28 pmOctober 28, 2026 at 4:33 pm

OpenAI generated $10 billion in revenue for Microsoft in the quarter ended Sept. 30, about 11% of the Redmond company’s total revenue, according to its quarterly filing Wednesday.

The amount is up sharply. In the fiscal year that ended in June, Microsoft recorded $24.1 billion in revenue from its business with OpenAI, or about $6 billion a quarter on average.

That $10 billion surpasses some of Microsoft’s longest-running businesses. Xbox brought in $5.4 billion in the quarter. Search and advertising, which includes its Bing search engine, generated $6.6 billion. Windows licenses sold through PC makers, along with Surface and other Microsoft devices, brought in $3.6 billion.

The total covers revenue-sharing payments from OpenAI, as well as other business between the companies, such as OpenAI’s use of Azure to train and run its AI models. Microsoft didn’t say how much came from each, or how much of Azure’s growth came from OpenAI.

Azure revenue rose 48% to $33.2 billion in the quarter, beating Wall Street’s expectations and the company’s own forecast of 44% to 45% growth.

Microsoft has begun disclosing its revenue from OpenAI because its stake of about 24% makes OpenAI a “related party” under accounting rules, requiring it to report the business they do with each other.

Microsoft first reported the number in its annual report in July, as a full-year total. This is the first time it has given a quarterly figure.

The original AI alliance: Microsoft first invested in OpenAI in 2019, eventually committing $13 billion, and became its exclusive cloud provider. ChatGPT ran on Azure when it launched in late 2022.

The companies have loosened their ties since then. OpenAI restructured as a public benefit corporation in October 2025, and Microsoft gave up its right of first refusal to supply OpenAI’s computing capacity. OpenAI committed to buy an additional $250 billion in Azure services. An April 2026 agreement gave OpenAI broader freedom to use other cloud providers.

OpenAI has also agreed to keep sharing revenue with Microsoft through 2030.

In addition, Microsoft sells access to OpenAI’s models to business customers through its Azure OpenAI Service, and the models became the foundation for its Copilot products, putting Microsoft at the front of the generative AI boom. That revenue comes from Microsoft’s own customers, so it isn’t part of the $10 billion.

Microsoft, for its part, now builds its own AI models and offers models from Anthropic and others.

Many customers, not a few: Asked by Bernstein Research analyst Mark Moerdler whether AI growth on Azure was coming from big businesses or AI-native companies, Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella didn’t mention OpenAI.

He said he doesn’t want Azure’s AI business to depend on a few big customers, and that broad adoption by businesses is just getting started.

Nadella described it as “a decade-long thing,” and contrasted it with relying on “four customers who buy a lot of capacity from you” to show a few quarters of growth. That, he said, is “not a business as far as I’m concerned.”

He added that Microsoft has large customers who want to buy capacity, “and as long as the pricing is right, we may sell them some. If not, we will be patient.”

Later in the call, Goldman Sachs analyst Gabriela Borges brought up the fact that OpenAI made up 11% of revenue. Nadella didn’t address the number but praised OpenAI’s latest models and said customers are increasingly mixing models from different companies, or training their own.

He cited Microsoft’s tools for routing each task to whichever AI model handles it best. If you use AI coding agents, Nadella said, you want Anthropic and OpenAI “to compete for your workload, not like once a quarter, but for every task.”

New risk language: Microsoft also expanded a warning in its quarterly filing about the risks of depending on outside AI providers. The company builds products such as Copilot on AI models from outside companies, including OpenAI and Anthropic. It now says it has “limited visibility into or control over” how those models are designed, trained, secured and tested.

Without naming OpenAI or Anthropic, the same section notes that some of these AI partners are also “significant customers of Azure,” and that the benefits Microsoft expects from those relationships “may not be realized or sustained.” It says those partners could change how much they buy, and that Microsoft itself may change how it allocates scarce data center capacity or prices it.

Microsoft is an investor in both companies. According to its latest filing, it owns about 24% of OpenAI, down from about 25% in June and about 27% after OpenAI’s restructuring a year ago, and has put $12.0 billion of a promised $13.0 billion into the company.

In addition, Microsoft agreed last year to invest up to $5 billion in Anthropic, and its results for the June quarter included a $3.2 billion gain on that investment. Microsoft hasn’t disclosed the size of its Anthropic stake, and Anthropic’s IPO filing earlier this week didn’t specify it either.

#5519. PancakeSwap's 69% CAKE Emission Cut Would Make CAKE Less Deflationary

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Cutting CAKE emissions by 69% sounds like the most token-friendly move PancakeSwap could make. But run last week's burn figures through "The Flip," and CAKE's net deflation doesn't speed up. It falls by about 30%.

That's the part missing from coverage of the vote, which is currently running about 98% against. Reports have focused on the drop from 22,500 to 7,000 CAKE per day. They haven't covered the burn the proposal removes to fund higher LP payouts. I rebuilt the supply math using PancakeSwap's own weekly burn breakdown. The result is more interesting than a straightforward "cut emissions, good for CAKE" story.

The Flip governance vote is a binary For/Against vote. It opened on October 21 at 08:07 UTC and closes on October 24 at 08:07 UTC. As of Thursday afternoon, the vote page showed:

One address, 0x3D...e1ad, cast 765,559 votes against, about 61% of all voting power used so far.

That share has fallen as more voters joined, and the result would be lopsided even without that wallet. Excluding it, "Against" still has more than 95%. With only 32 votes cast, though, this is mainly a verdict from a small group of large veCAKE holders, not a broad community poll.

The proposal, first posted on PancakeSwap's forum on October 14, has two parts.

Emissions: Daily CAKE emissions would drop from 22,500 to 7,000, with the remaining 7,000 going to a new ecosystem fund called the Pantry. The cut happens in two stages: first to 11,000 per day, then to 7,000 once CAKE reaches its Tokenomics 3.0 goal of about a 20% supply reduction.

PancakeSwap estimates LPs would have earned about $62 million more if this split had applied to 2025 volume.

Here's PancakeSwap's burn report for the week ending October 20, as published in its weekly update:

Current emissions are 22,500 per day, or 157,500 per week. That puts this week's net deflation at about 201,000 CAKE.

Now apply The Flip to the same week. The v3 and Infinity burns are mostly gone, while v2 and "Other" stay, leaving about 190,000 CAKE of weekly burn. At stage one, emissions fall to 77,000 a week, so net deflation drops to about 113,000 CAKE, a 44% decline. At stage two, emissions fall to 49,000 a week, and net deflation recovers only to about 141,000 CAKE. That's still 30% below where it is today.

The emission cut saves 108,500 CAKE a week at full rollout. But the removed v3 and Infinity burn totaled 168,600 CAKE that week. The burn being given up is larger than the emissions being saved.

The previous week tells the same story. Working backward from the week-over-week changes, the burn was about 530,000 CAKE: roughly 272,000 from v2 and 191,000 from v3. Net deflation was about 373,000. Under The Flip, it would have been about 249,000 at stage two, which is 33% lower.

There's one real offset. The non-stablecoin part of the new 12% treasury fee still funds buybacks, and PancakeSwap hasn't said how large that is. So my figures are a floor, not an exact forecast. It's also possible that higher LP payouts attract more liquidity and volume, and the team projects up to 30% more liquidity. That would increase v2 burns over time.

PancakeSwap's own estimate, based on 10 weeks of activity, is that v2 burns alone would keep CAKE net deflationary by about 190,000 CAKE a week after emissions. That's plausible, and CAKE would keep shrinking. But it's still a slower pace of deflation than what CAKE has been running at, sold under the headline of a 69% emission cut.

The final cut to 7,000 a day depends on reaching the 20% supply reduction target. CAKE supply is 329,915,408, down 11.5% from 372,837,045 in April 2025. The roughly 20% target sits near 298.3 million, which leaves about 31.6 million CAKE still to burn.

Coverage has suggested stage two could arrive about 12 months after stage one. Here's how long 31.6 million CAKE actually takes at stage-one net deflation:

Hitting the target in 12 months would require about 608,000 CAKE of net deflation every week. That's more than CAKE's gross burn in either recent week. On these numbers, stage one could stay in place for years. The "69% cut" headline is really a 51% cut for the foreseeable future.

LPs aren't the ones voting this proposal down. Voting power comes from veCAKE, which means locked CAKE, not liquidity positions. LPs are the group that stands to gain the most, with an 88% fee share.

veCAKE holders have different incentives. Today, they direct the 22,500 daily emissions through gauge voting, and an ecosystem has grown around that control. The Flip would reduce that budget to a 7,000-a-day fund managed by PancakeSwap's team. It would also cut the burn support that has been shrinking supply. For someone holding CAKE for its scarcity, The Flip gives up a definite burn today in exchange for a possible liquidity gain later.

That's why the vote is so one-sided. The people being asked to approve The Flip aren't the people it pays. If it fails on Saturday, I'd expect the next version to keep some v3 burn share. Otherwise, the emission cut doesn't do what the headline suggests.

#5518. ‘The opportunity outweighs the challenge’: Bahrain leads drive to restore tourism in the Gulf after eight months of conflict and collapsing visitor numbers

Gulf states are preparing to launch a joint global tourism campaign as the region seeks to rebuild traveler confidence following months of conflict with Iran.

Bahrain’s minister of tourism, H.E. Fatima bint Jaffar Al Sairafi, told Fortune that the campaign would encourage international visitors to travel across several Gulf countries on one vacation. Bahrain proposed the initiative at a Gulf tourism meeting in Manama, the kingdom’s capital, in September, where it secured approval.

“All the countries are on board and the plan will be implemented very soon.” Al Sairafi said at the Gulf Gateway investment forum in Bahrain. Tourism in the Gulf states generated nearly $131.9 billion in 2025. But since the war began, the World Travel & Tourism Council estimated in March that the region was losing around $600 million per day in tourism revenues.

Read more: ADNOC to expand AI use across its operations to strengthen resilience

“[We want to] promote our countries in terms of multi-destination itineraries rather than solo itineraries, that’s actually where our strength is,” Al Sairafi said. Gulf tourism leaders had been “very disheartened” by the Iranian attacks after years of expansion in the sector, she added arguing that closer regional cooperation offered a way to rebuild.

The initiative would bring together Bahrain, Saudi Arabia, the United Arab Emirates, Qatar, Oman, and Kuwait as they seek to restore confidence in a tourism market where visitor numbers have collapsed.

In 2025, the region welcomed 75.7 million international tourists, according to UN Tourism, representing a 4.9% increase on the previous year.

The Gulf Cooperation Council (GCC) publicly announced approval of a tourism recovery plan on Sep. 10, and Al Sairafi confirmed that the global campaign was close to launch.

Al Sairafi said that the conflict had accelerated cooperation between Gulf tourism authorities, turning the region’s shared exposure to disruption into an incentive to market destinations together. “I really believe that the recent developments that have happened over the past few months are one of the main drivers for us to actually combine our effort,” she said.

Her model is based on the multi-country European vacation. Visitors making a long journey from Europe or Asia, including China, will be encouraged to explore neighboring Gulf states using the region’s road and air connections.

“Rarely do we only visit one country,” she said of trips to Europe. “We want to create a destination where people enjoy all the cultures of all the GCC states and spend time and money equally.”

Making those trips easier to book will also require coordination. Al Sairafi said that aligned tourism calendars, better transport connections, and cooperation between airlines, hotels, and booking platforms would be needed.

The research agency, ORF Middle East, said that support for tourism businesses and efforts to restart events could become harder to sustain if the conflict drags on. With increased tensions and potential renewed disruption, the joint promotion offers no guarantee of a return to previous tourism numbers.

Al Sairafi pointed to Bahrain’s international conference calendar as evidence that confidence was returning. Business visitors were extending their stays and booking guided tours, she said, bringing spending beyond the events themselves.

According to the ministry, Bahrain’s visitor numbers increased more than 50% between the launch of its tourism strategy in 2022 and 2025, while tourism revenue rose more than 30%. Al Sairafi says recovery would mean renewed annual growth in arrivals, revenue and overnight stays.

“I believe that the opportunity that we see outweighs the challenge,” she said.
