#5492. Washington governor rips Microsoft over TV ad in leaked audio

by Todd Bishop on Oct 30, 2026 at 5:21 pmNovember 2, 2026 at 6:29 am

Washington Gov. Bob Ferguson called out Microsoft for bankrolling a political action committee responsible for a TV ad describing state government as broken, according to newly leaked audio from a Seattle Chamber leadership conference last week.

Remarks at the Seattle Metropolitan Chamber of Commerce’s Regional Leadership Conference, held at the Suncadia resort near Cle Elum, Wash., are supposed to be off the record. But The Washington Observer, an independent newsletter on state politics, published the audio Friday, saying it was obtained from an unnamed source.

In the audio, Ferguson zeroed in on a line near the start of the ad — that in Washington, “it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”

The governor repeated the words “it used to be” for emphasis, in a tone of disbelief.

“What’s up with that?” Ferguson asked the crowd of business and government leaders. “First, does anyone else in this room believe that? I sure as hell don’t.”

“I talk to people every day who have that idea, that dream. They’re chasing it and they’re getting it,” he said. He cited the record $3.5 billion that Seattle-area startups raised in the third quarter, more than triple the same period a year ago, according to PitchBook data.

The Microsoft relationship: Ferguson, who noted that he had worked as a lawyer for Microsoft, said he loves the company and respects what it does. But he seemed especially peeved that the ad ran during the Seattle Seahawks game, where it reached people across the state and those from elsewhere who might want to come here and start a company.

“If we’re partners, partners should treat partners like partners, right?” he said.

He asked the room to imagine him running a multimillion-dollar ad criticizing Microsoft. “You guys would think I lost my mind if I did that,” he said.

Ferguson called Microsoft a key partner and a member of his economic roundtable, and said he works well with the company. “But it works both ways,” he said.

Ferguson acknowledged that the state has problems. “Are there challenges? Sure,” he said. But he said he didn’t think the ad was “helpful for where we all want to go.”

He told the crowd he welcomes constructive feedback, but asked business leaders to think about how they communicate, and to talk up the state’s workforce, economy and startup funding along with its challenges.

“What we have here is so bloody special,” he said.

Ferguson, who took office in January 2025, also reminded the room that he isn’t going anywhere. “I plan on being governor for a long time,” he said, adding that he works with all of them, “Microsoft included.”

The Observer noted that $10 million, roughly what the group has left to spend, would be a good start on a campaign to run someone else for governor in 2028.

The newsletter said it stripped the audio from a video of Ferguson’s remarks, to protect its source. Among those in the audience was Michael Mattmiller, who represents Microsoft in Olympia. He and Ferguson “kinda-sorta hugged it out afterward,” the Observer reported.

Who’s behind the ad: The campaign comes from Washington Needs to Compete, a PAC funded in large part by Microsoft and its current and former executives. The group has raised about $13.8 million, according to state campaign finance records, including more than $5 million directly from Microsoft.

Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella and former CEO Steve Ballmer each gave $250,000, and Vice Chair and President Brad Smith gave more than $500,000. Other backers include T-Mobile, F5, Alaska Airlines and Weyerhaeuser.

Washington Needs to Compete has spent about $3 million so far, according to state records. Most of it has gone to state legislative races, the Observer reported, including more than $700,000 backing Rep. Amy Walen, D-Kirkland, in the 48th District, home to Microsoft’s Redmond headquarters.

The group spent $97,000 to air the ad during the Seahawks’ Oct. 15 Thursday night loss to the Denver Broncos on Prime Video and $130,000 during their Oct. 25 Sunday night win over the Kansas City Chiefs on NBC, according to the Observer.

Microsoft referred GeekWire’s inquiry to the group, which the company described as a growing coalition of more than 60 funders that want to keep the state competitive.

A press representative for the group sent a statement from Nick Streuli, an officer of Washington Needs to Compete. Streuli runs the government relations firm Sundial Advocacy and was previously policy and outreach director for former Gov. Jay Inslee.

“Washington Needs to Compete is committed to our state and wants to see it succeed,” Streuli said in the statement. “Rising costs are making it harder for businesses to invest and grow here. We are starting a conversation about our economic challenges and how to solve them.”

What the ad says: The spot opens with a nod to “inventors in garages,” “mom-and-pop shops down Main Street” and farmers “feeding the world,” before declaring, “In Washington, it used to be all you needed was an idea, a dream and the guts to chase it.”

Then it turns: “But today, Olympia is broken, spending more while you get less.” Jobs are leaving, the ad says, and “it’s harder than ever to afford a home and raise a family.”

It doesn’t name Ferguson or any legislation. It ends by saying Olympia needs to “quit wasting money, fix what’s broken and put Washington families first.”

Taxes and the business climate: Ferguson this year signed a 9.9% tax on household income above $1 million, known as the millionaires tax, which takes effect in 2028 and is projected to raise about $3 billion a year. Initiative 645, which would repeal it, is on the Nov. 3 ballot.

In September, Smith joined former Gov. Chris Gregoire and dozens of regional officials to launch a partnership aimed at reversing the Seattle area’s economic slide. “The warning signs are flashing on our economy,” Smith said at the time.

The region lost nearly 7,000 jobs in 2025, according to the group, and Washington has fallen from 32nd to 47th in CNBC’s ranking of states by cost of doing business since 2017.

In the same CNBC study, Washington ranks 11th overall, up from 14th last year, and fifth for its economy. WalletHub ranks Washington’s economy second in the nation, behind Massachusetts.

Washington’s gross domestic product grew faster than any other state’s in the first quarter of 2026, driven largely by its tech sector, according to federal data released in June.

Long-term plans: On its website, Washington Needs to Compete describes itself as businesses and residents building “a modern, permanent political organization” to support leaders and ideas that “strengthen our economy, improve affordability and expand opportunity,” through elections and public education.

The site lists its top five contributors as Microsoft, T-Mobile, the Washington Coalition for Responsible Taxes and Spending, F5 and Smith.

The group is saving most of its money for future campaigns, the Observer reported.

Updated Nov. 2 with comment from Washington Needs to Compete.

#5491. He Left Google to Fix a ‘Really Stupid’ Household Product. The ‘Delightful’ Solution Has Generated $20 Million in Revenue.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Matic co-founder Mehul Nariyawala says the goal is to sell 30,000 robots by the end of the year.

For Mehul Nariyawala, a household product’s costly mistake was the jumping-off point for a $20 million company. Nariyawala had a $1,000 robot vacuum, which he watched destroy a rug in his home while he was away. The machine had powerful suction but wasn’t intelligent enough to free itself from the rug. It got stuck, kept running for 45 minutes and tore away a patch of the rug.

“That was a realization that, Wow, this thing is really stupid,” Nariyawala tells Entrepreneur in a new interview. Worse, he found that many robot vacuums could not reliably return to their own charging docks. “To me, it’s an oxymoron to call these things robots because if it’s a robot and it can’t even find its own dock, what good is it?” he says.

That irritation planted the seed for Matic, the home-robotics company Nariyawala co-founded with CEO Navneet Dalal after the pair left Google Nest in 2017. Nariyawala is Matic’s president. Their goal was not simply to make another robot vacuum. It was to build a machine that could safely and quietly navigate the disorder of an actual home, avoiding pets, toys, cords, spills, furniture and the people moving through it.

Nariyawala says Matic has sold more than 13,000 robots since its November 2024 launch, generating an estimated $15 million to $20 million in revenue. Matic’s robot vacuum costs $1,495. Nariyawala said the company employs about 110 people and is aiming to sell 30,000 robots by year-end.

Before they started building Matic, the co-founders did something less glamorous: They wrote a 21-page “problem memo.”

Instead of jumping to a solution, Nariyawala says, they asked what customers disliked about current products, why robot vacuums failed them and what a genuinely useful home robot would need to do.

“We just kept going again and again and again at every level until we deeply understood the problem,” he says.

Nariyawala’s path to Matic began in India, where he grew up. He moved to the United States in high school and attended the University of Maryland for undergraduate studies. After graduating in 1999, he joined a startup based in Northern Virginia that burned through $30 million in 11 months.

“It turned out to be a spectacular failure,” he says. “That was my how-not-to-ruin-a-startup 101.”

After a stint in consulting at Accenture and an MBA from Chicago Booth, Nariyawala joined Like.com in 2005, an early Silicon Valley computer-vision startup. There, he met Dalal, a researcher and engineer whose doctoral work became influential in the field of classical computer vision.

Google acquired Like.com in 2010. Nariyawala and Dalal then formed Flutter, a gesture-recognition startup that let people control iTunes and Spotify using a webcam. Users could wave to change a song or make a shushing motion to mute audio. The app reached No. 1 in Apple’s Mac App Store in 73 countries in 2012, according to Nariyawala.

But the founders learned a crucial product lesson: A flashy interface does not necessarily create a business.

“No one wakes up in the morning and says, ‘Today I’m gonna buy gestures,’” Nariyawala says. “It’s a really cool app but not necessarily a product that can potentially generate revenue.”

Google acquired Flutter in late 2013. The founders later moved to Nest, where Nariyawala led products in the Nest camera portfolio, including the Nest Cam, Nest Hello doorbell and related devices. Dalal led perception and computer-vision work on the same set of products.

At Nest, Nariyawala learned that a product is more than its hardware or software. It encompasses every point a customer encounters the company, from learning about the product to purchasing, onboarding, receiving support and deciding whether to stay loyal to the brand or not.

“One of the biggest learnings there was that it’s really just about the entire experience of the product,” he says.

Customer support, he argues, is especially important for an expensive consumer device. “When they reach out to you, that’s the first time they’re meeting humans behind Matic,” he says. “How we respond to that is actually really, really critical.”

Matic’s founding idea grew from both professional experience and family life. While working on Nest cameras, Nariyawala noticed that many indoor cameras were pointed outside. He could personally relate. His wife had done the same thing, and after leaving Google, he says she did not want any indoor cameras monitoring their home.

The pair saw a broader opportunity in the gap between the robotics ambitions emerging in self-driving cars and the mediocre performance of household cleaning robots. If companies believed they could develop vehicles capable of safely navigating roads, Nariyawala wondered, why was no one making a household robot that could move through a living room without crashing into objects?

Nariyawala says that homes are among the most difficult environments for robots because they are cluttered, dynamic, and highly personal. Furniture shifts. Lighting changes. Children leave toys out. Pets cross a room. A cord may be on the floor one day and gone the next.

Matic’s answer was a vision-based system built around two RGB cameras and local computing. Rather than use the flat, circular shape common in robot vacuums, the company opted for a taller machine that gives its cameras a more useful perspective of the room.

“We wanted to build a vantage point that was much more like a human crawling child,” Nariyawala says.

That concept reflects Dalal’s broader philosophy: Do not bet against nature. Human beings learn to perceive their surroundings before they learn more complex skills, Nariyawala says. Young children learn where they can walk, what they should avoid, how to get from one room to another, and how not to fall down stairs. Matic’s early work focused on giving a robot some of those same foundational abilities.

“The indoor world is entirely built by humans for humans,” he says.

Nariyawala and Dalal did not immediately seek venture funding. Having founded companies before and seen what happens after an acquisition, they wanted to build Matic for the long haul. Their ambition extended beyond cleaning floors.

“We’re really building the Apple of home robotics,” Nariyawala says.

That long-term vision informed an unusual early decision. The cofounders self-funded Matic for roughly its first year and a half. They agreed not to raise outside capital until they had a working prototype and had addressed major technical risks.

“Raising funding is never easy, but when you have gone through an exit and you try to do a second startup, it is slightly easier,” Nariyawala says. “But because it’s slightly easier, you don’t actually spend more time thinking through and developing your idea, and that sometimes plays a catastrophic [role].”

The team focused on proving key capabilities: depth perception using two cameras, voice and gesture recognition, quieter cleaning and a wheel-base design. Its first prototype arrived in 2018. By spring 2019, it had developed an early demonstration in which a person could speak to the robot, point to a mess and tell it to clean a specific spot.

Only then did the founders begin raising money. “Venture capital funding, or institutional funding, is like rocket fuel,” Nariyawala says. “The best time to go get rocket fuel is when your rocket is ready and docked.”

In 2019, Matic attracted early investment from entrepreneurs including Jack Dorsey, Stripe cofounders Patrick and John Collison and Nest cofounder Matt Rogers.

Matic has raised $115 million in outside investment to date, with additional personal investment from the founders.

The journey took longer than planned. The founders originally thought they might ship around 2020 or 2021. Matic instead began shipping in November 2024.

In August, the U.S. Federal Communications Commission (FCC) banned foreign-made advanced robots, including robot vacuums. The ruling prohibited new foreign-made models from getting future import and sales approval.

Nariyawala says he reached out to the FCC after the ban was announced and showed them a path to how Matic will source as many components in the U.S. as possible moving forward.

“The FCC and government have been very much accommodating and understanding what we’re doing,” Nariyawala says. “Their entire point is that yes, you guys are heading in the right direction. So as long as it’s heading in the right direction, we’re supportive of it. We just have to show that we’re pushing in that direction.”

Matic now positions its vacuum as an intelligent, autonomous machine rather than a device that follows a fixed or random cleaning routine. Nariyawala contrasts that vision with early robot vacuums, which he compares to a blindfolded person bouncing from wall to wall.

“Hardware is hard,” Nariyawala says. “If hardware is 10 times harder than software, then building a robot is 100 times harder than software.”

Many current robot vacuums use a form of LiDAR sensing, he says, which can help a machine detect walls and certain obstacles but does not provide enough context to distinguish among a person, a cabinet, a pet, or a pile of clothes.

“It has no contextual awareness,” he says.

Matic’s system is meant to create a three-dimensional, evolving understanding of a home. Nariyawala describes this as an “absolute map,” rather than a map that only orients the robot relative to its charging dock. The distinction matters, he says, because a robot should be able to understand its environment even if the dock is moved.

Matic recently introduced “Cues,” an update enabling users to communicate with the robot through voice commands and gestures. Through the update, the robot can understand more than 70 spoken languages, and users can point to an area they want cleaned to have the robot take care of a mess.

The robot has an accompanying app that remains necessary for onboarding and detailed settings, such as setting no-go zones, but the company wants routine interaction to feel more natural.

“If this is truly an intelligent robot, then we should be able to communicate with it in the same exact way that we communicate with each other,” Nariyawala says.

The approach is designed for households that include children, older adults, people who do not want to use another app and family members who may not speak English — personalized experiences for different users.

Matic has focused less on traditional marketing than on getting customers to talk about the product. Nariyawala says roughly two-thirds of orders have come through word-of-mouth referrals, and the company did little marketing before this year.

“The only evergreen marketing channel is a great product,” he says. “When you build something really unexpected, delightful that customers love, they can’t help talking about it.”

For Nariyawala, Matic’s floor-cleaning robot is only the first stage. The company’s roadmap imagines a “trusted organizer” that can handle simpler tasks, followed by a more capable household robot that can take on complex planning and execution.

But he returns repeatedly to the same principle that shaped the company’s original 21-page memo: The technology is not the product. The customer’s problem is.

“Customers don’t want hardware or robots,” he says. “They want a solution to their problems.”

For Mehul Nariyawala, a household product’s costly mistake was the jumping-off point for a $20 million company. Nariyawala had a $1,000 robot vacuum, which he watched destroy a rug in his home while he was away. The machine had powerful suction but wasn’t intelligent enough to free itself from the rug. It got stuck, kept running for 45 minutes and tore away a patch of the rug.

“That was a realization that, Wow, this thing is really stupid,” Nariyawala tells Entrepreneur in a new interview. Worse, he found that many robot vacuums could not reliably return to their own charging docks. “To me, it’s an oxymoron to call these things robots because if it’s a robot and it can’t even find its own dock, what good is it?” he says.

That irritation planted the seed for Matic, the home-robotics company Nariyawala co-founded with CEO Navneet Dalal after the pair left Google Nest in 2017. Nariyawala is Matic’s president. Their goal was not simply to make another robot vacuum. It was to build a machine that could safely and quietly navigate the disorder of an actual home, avoiding pets, toys, cords, spills, furniture and the people moving through it.

#5490. Exclusive: Numeracle Raises $28M To Keep Legitimate Business Calls From Spam Label

Numeracle has raised $28 million from Edison Partners to help businesses whose calls are incorrectly labeled as spam or blocked by phone carriers, it tells Crunchbase News exclusively.

The McLean, Virginia-based company verifies businesses and links their identities to the phone numbers they use to contact customers. It shares that information with the systems carriers use to screen calls and works to remove incorrect labels.

The financing brings Numeracle’s total funding to $34.8 million since its 2018 inception. That total includes a $6.8 million Series A raised in December 2023, founder and CEO Rebekah Johnson told Crunchbase News in an interview. Edison was the sole investor in the new round. Numeracle declined to disclose its valuation.

The company says it has roughly 4,000 business customers and about 85 employees. It became profitable this year, sooner than Johnson had expected.

Numeracle plans to use its new capital to hire and expand internationally. The company also plans to adapt its business verification tools for use beyond phone calls. For example, Johnson said the company is eyeing messaging, chat apps, marketplaces and AI agents.

Its expansion comes as businesses simultaneously face two related problems. For one,  fraudsters are increasingly impersonating them. Meanwhile, call-screening systems can prevent their own calls from reaching customers.

For example, that could mean a patient ignoring a call from a hospital about an upcoming procedure. For a bank, it could mean a customer declining a legitimate call because the phone displays a fraud warning.

Numeracle charges an annual subscription to monitor and address incorrect spam labels. Customers can also pay a per-call fee to display their business name, logo and reason for calling on a recipient’s phone.

Johnson, an engineer who previously worked in regulatory compliance at telecom provider West, said she recognized the problem while participating in the Federal Communications Commission’s Robocall Strike Force in 2016.

She warned carriers that their efforts to identify unwanted calls would also affect legitimate businesses because the screening systems lacked information about who was calling.

About three months later, she said, a carrier’s federal regulatory counsel called her while she was in her parents’ kitchen.

“Everything you said was going to happen is happening. What do we do?” she recalled him asking.

Johnson said that conversation prompted her to start Numeracle.

She was a newly single mother who had lost her job and used her life savings to start the business. Living on a farm in Grand Bay, Alabama, without internet access, she worked from cafes.

“When you need to feed your children and provide a roof over their head, you’re going to count every penny,” Johnson said.

That experience shaped her spending decisions as Numeracle grew, she said. The company operated for several years before raising its Series A.

Johnson said about 90% of Numeracle’s sales inquiries come through unpaid inbound channels. With the new funding, she plans to spend more on marketing to specific industries, including healthcare.

The company’s customers also include businesses in financial services, home services and higher education, as well as government organizations and charities. Johnson declined to identify individual customers.

Numeracle first checks that a business is real and does what it claims. Once it passes those checks, the company links it to the phone numbers it uses and shares that information with the systems carriers use to flag or block calls.

Other companies can also pay Numeracle to run those checks on businesses they’re considering taking on as customers.

Johnson said Numeracle built its own verification tools because existing services weren’t thorough enough. Fraudsters have an incentive to get through: If Numeracle approves them, their calls are less likely to be flagged as spam.

AI has made it more difficult to tell which businesses are real, she said. Numeracle has encountered fake companies with state registrations, employer identification numbers and supposed employees who have active LinkedIn profiles.

“The scary part for me isn’t necessarily the AI voices,” Johnson said. “It’s actually AI-built businesses.”

She said Numeracle uses AI to help identify those fabrications, though she declined to describe the methods in detail.

Numeracle currently operates in the United States. Johnson said interest from Europe has prompted it to move forward with its international expansion plans, with some of the new funding going toward that effort.

The broader question for the company is whether businesses will pay to use its verification services across other forms of communication. For now, its business centers on a more immediate problem — helping customers recognize a legitimate phone call.

For Lenard Marcus, a general partner at Edison Partners, Johnson’s telecom and engineering experience was one major reason to invest. In an interview with Crunchbase News, he said her industry knowledge helped her build both the product and relationships with companies that could bring it to customers.

He was also drawn to how much Numeracle had accomplished with relatively little funding, describing Johnson as “someone who was frankly doing more with less.”

Customer interviews helped make the case. Marcus recalled one contact center operator who said Numeracle had increased the number of calls answered from 19,000 to 22,000 out of 40,000 calls a month. For businesses trying to reach prospective customers, that increase in conversations could lead to more sales.

Marcus also believes that Johnson’s years in telecom give Numeracle an advantage over newer competitors. In addition to understanding how the different parts of the industry work together, Johnson has used those relationships to get Numeracle in front of large companies, he said.

“She’s sales. She’s engineering, and she’s just a very, very good leader,” Marcus added.

Looking ahead, the investor also sees demand across healthcare, retail, home services and finance, with AI making impersonation more prevalent.

“This is a communications problem, not one for one industry,” he said.

#5489. Coinbase's October 26 Perpetual Conversion: The Crypto Index the CFTC Waiver Excludes

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Coinbase wants six futures contracts to stop expiring on October 26. The CFTC letter it leans on covers five of them by design, and its own footnote points away from the sixth.

The Division of Market Oversight issued Letter 26-29 on October 3, 2026. The CFTC announced it two days later, on October 5, in Release 9308-26. Coverage then focused on the headline that exchanges can now strip expiry dates from perpetual-style index futures. The Merkle flagged the relief's hard October 20 stop on October 19, and outlets like Finance Magnates and FinanceFeeds ran the same window. That coverage, however, predates what Coinbase filed next. This breakdown sets the October 19 filing beside the letter's text, because the two don't line up cleanly.

Meanwhile, the CFTC is working on retail crypto leverage through a different door. As NullTX's earlier breakdown shows, the actual-delivery ANPRM (2026-20888) takes comments until December 14. Perpetuals on registered exchanges skip that process. Instead, they move through staff letters and self-certification.

Coinbase asked for the relief on October 1, and the Division granted it two days later. The letter says staff won't recommend enforcement if a DCM drops expiry dates from existing perpetual-style contracts, as long as the DCM meets eight conditions. First, it must gather feedback from holders of open positions. Next, it must give at least five calendar days' notice and let them close out under the old terms. It must also disclose the risks and change no other material term. Finally, it must file under the CFTC's rules, notify the Division and certify compliance.

Coinbase's Submission #2026-67 then names six contracts: US500, Tech100, Defense10, AI10, China10 and Coin50. It says everything except the expiry stays the same, and that the exchange knows of no substantive opposition. The contract list reached the CFTC by email on October 16.

Letter 26-29 defines its scope by asset class. A footnote shuts out any perpetual-style contract referencing something other than a broad-based security index. Coin50, by contrast, follows the Coinbase 50 Index, and Rule 1148 in the filing itself calls it a futures contract based on a cryptocurrency. In other words, the letter's scope and Coin50's own rule text point in opposite directions.

Crypto contracts did have their own relief. Letter 26-19, issued June 12 to Bitnomial and Coinbase Derivatives, covered digital commodities only and carried the same eight conditions. Even so, it says its positions expire on June 30, 2026. It rests on the Commission's May 29 order and its perpetuals policy statement.

Letter 26-29 sets October 20, 2026 as the day its no-action positions expire. It doesn't say whether implementation itself must happen by then, or only the notice and filing. Coinbase filed on October 19, one day early, but picked October 26 to go live. That choice matters. Ten business days from October 19 lands on November 2, and Coinbase specifically asked to skip that wait. As a result, going live on October 26 depends on the relief still applying.

Without relief, the Division's own words make the path clear. Letter 26-19 says certifications that remove expiry dates will generally draw a stay under Regulation 40.6(c). A stay then gives the Commission another 90 days to review and opens a 30-day public comment period.

Neither side has explained the gap. Searches of news coverage and official channels turned up no statement from Coinbase or the CFTC on whether Coin50 sits inside Letter 26-29, on what authority covers it after October 20, or on why the filing's October 26 date falls after the letter's expiry. We also found no CFTC stay notice and no extension or amendment of Letter 26-29. Likewise, the Coinbase posts we found cover other perpetual launches, not this conversion.

That silence doesn't mean a problem exists. Coinbase may be relying on authority the documents don't mention, and the CFTC may read the letter's dates differently than we do. Still, the paper trail shows a crypto-based contract sitting under relief written for stock indexes, with a start date that falls after that relief expires.

Three developments would settle it: a CFTC stay notice, a new or amended staff letter, or a clarification from Coinbase Derivatives.

Whichever arrives first tells us whether the first U.S.-listed crypto index perpetual goes live on schedule or lands in a 90-day review.

#5487. The Gap Between Your Expertise and Your Content Marketing Is One of the Most Expensive Disconnects You Can Make

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Years of insight often stay trapped in private conversations when they could become the most valuable material for building a public brand.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Spend 30 minutes with an excellent veteran broker and something interesting usually happens. They’ll explain why a specific neighborhood that looks identical to the one next to it consistently outperforms it at resale. They’ll describe the exact moment in a negotiation when a seller’s resolve breaks and how they learned to recognize it 15 years ago. They’ll tell you which renovation projects reliably return value in their market and which ones buyers quietly discount even when they look expensive. They’ll mention the pattern they’ve watched repeat with first-time buyers for two decades that no amount of pre-purchase education seems to prevent.

Then you look at their Instagram and it says JUST SOLD in large letters over a photograph of a front door.

That gap, between what someone actually knows and what they make public, is one of the more expensive disconnects in professional marketing. And it’s not unique to real estate. Lawyers who’ve spent 20 years navigating a specific type of litigation have pattern recognition their clients would genuinely value if it ever made it out of client conversations. Executives who’ve managed through three recessions understand something about organizational behavior that no business school curriculum captures. Financial advisors who’ve watched clients make the same behavioral mistakes across multiple market cycles carry insight that the average investor would pay serious attention to if it were ever made accessible.

The problem is rarely that these people lack something worth saying. It’s that what they know has become so familiar to them that they’ve stopped recognizing it as knowledge.

There’s something that happens when you’ve seen the same pattern play out hundreds of times. It stops feeling like insight and starts feeling like obvious. The broker who’s watched buyers consistently underestimate carrying costs on older properties no longer experiences that as a revelation. It’s just a thing they know. It stopped surprising them around year six. So it doesn’t occur to them that a first-time buyer encountering this reality for the first time might find it genuinely useful to hear before they’re already in contract.

This is the core problem. Expertise normalizes. The more you know about something, the worse you tend to be at judging what’s interesting about what you know. Familiarity is the enemy of recognizing value.

Which means the job of turning expertise into public-facing content is rarely about inventing new ideas. It’s about extraction. Pulling out what’s already there, what’s been sitting in client conversations and private observations for years, and making it visible to people who haven’t spent a decade accumulating the same experience.

Most professional marketing starts with a version of the same question. What should we post this week? A social media manager gets brought in, templates get built, a content calendar gets assembled and the result is a reliable stream of announcements, generic industry commentary, and the kind of motivational content that gets produced when nobody can think of anything specific to say.

A social media manager cannot manufacture 10 years of pattern recognition. They can execute. They can produce. They can distribute. But the raw material has to come from somewhere, and if it isn’t being extracted from the actual expertise of the professional, it gets replaced with something generic that could have come from anyone.

The better starting question is not what we should post. It’s what we actually know that the market hasn’t heard clearly yet. Those are genuinely different questions, and they produce genuinely different answers.

The questions that tend to unlock useful material are specific, and most professionals haven’t been asked them in the context of their public content.

What do clients ask you repeatedly? Repeated questions are a signal. They mean the market is confused about something and hasn’t found a satisfying answer yet. Every repeated question is a piece of content waiting to exist. The broker who gets asked every spring whether it’s better to buy now or wait through summer has answered that question a hundred times privately. They’ve never written it down publicly once.

What does your industry believe that you think is wrong? Contrarian expertise is some of the most valuable material a professional can produce, and most of them are sitting on it quietly. The financial advisor who thinks conventional wisdom about a specific type of account is actively harmful to the clients who follow it. The broker who’s watched a popular renovation strategy underdeliver in their specific market for fifteen years while the rest of the industry keeps recommending it.

What can you predict because you’ve seen it 100 times? Pattern recognition accumulated through repetition is something generalists and newcomers genuinely cannot replicate. The experienced professional who knows which type of seller is going to change their mind about price after the first two weeks on market, or which buyer behavior signals that an offer isn’t going to survive inspection, is carrying proprietary knowledge. Most of them have never thought of it that way.

What seems obvious to you but consistently surprises clients? This is often the richest material. The things that feel too basic to mention are often the things the audience most needs to hear. The curse of expertise is assuming shared context that doesn’t exist.

What happened recently that reminded you of something you learned 10 years ago? This one turns experience into timely commentary without requiring a formal opinion column. It’s just: Here’s what I watched happen this week and here’s the pattern underneath it that I’ve seen before.

Those answers become articles. They become media commentary when a journalist needs a credible source. They become speaking topics. They become the newsletter that clients actually read because it contains something they couldn’t have gotten from a generic industry publication.

Here’s the distinction that matters. Expertise kept inside client conversations helps the specific people sitting across from you at that moment. It builds a reputation slowly, through word of mouth, one relationship at a time.

Expertise that gets externalized travels without you. An article that captures a genuine insight reaches people who have never met you and may never hire you but who now associate your name with a perspective they found useful. A piece of commentary that captures something real about market behavior becomes a credential that a press mention or a referral can point to. The insight that got shared in a client meeting last Tuesday becomes, when written down, something that works on your behalf indefinitely.

Great thought leadership is usually extraction, not creation. The material is already there. Most experts just haven’t been asked the right questions to get it out.

Spend 30 minutes with an excellent veteran broker and something interesting usually happens. They’ll explain why a specific neighborhood that looks identical to the one next to it consistently outperforms it at resale. They’ll describe the exact moment in a negotiation when a seller’s resolve breaks and how they learned to recognize it 15 years ago. They’ll tell you which renovation projects reliably return value in their market and which ones buyers quietly discount even when they look expensive. They’ll mention the pattern they’ve watched repeat with first-time buyers for two decades that no amount of pre-purchase education seems to prevent.

Then you look at their Instagram and it says JUST SOLD in large letters over a photograph of a front door.

That gap, between what someone actually knows and what they make public, is one of the more expensive disconnects in professional marketing. And it’s not unique to real estate. Lawyers who’ve spent 20 years navigating a specific type of litigation have pattern recognition their clients would genuinely value if it ever made it out of client conversations. Executives who’ve managed through three recessions understand something about organizational behavior that no business school curriculum captures. Financial advisors who’ve watched clients make the same behavioral mistakes across multiple market cycles carry insight that the average investor would pay serious attention to if it were ever made accessible.

#5485. Want to Reach More Prospects Faster? Stop Chasing Volume

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

Sales teams are killing their outbound channels by answering falling response rates with ever more volume. The solution, however, is easier than the industry realizes.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Back in the mid-2010s, I was one of those sales reps with a pretty bullish mentality towards outbound email outreach. Unfortunately, the tables turned, and my response rates to cold email outreach plummeted 90%. Over the last decade, the same amount of outreach has begun producing just a tenth of the results; not only for me, but for sales reps everywhere.

The problem wasn’t email. The problem was how we, as outbound sales reps, responded to the decrease in positive outcomes. As a collective, the sellers changed buyer behavior and now, we’re seeing this pattern repeat itself. This time, it’s happening on the phones, and if sales leaders don’t learn from what happened to email, reps will inevitably burn through another channel.

Following the COVID-19 pandemic, sales across industries began to encounter new obstacles. Email providers like Microsoft and Google became stricter about bulk sending and began blocking and blacklisting domains that engaged in it. As a result, the sales leaders I worked with and I saw email outreach response rates drop from 2 to 3% to 0.2 to 0.3% — a substantial decline, to say the least.

By 2024, the channel had become untenable for cold outbound. With the dwindling number of responses, the common fix was to send more emails to bridge the gap. However, trying to fix the problem with more of the same activity that caused it was like pouring gas on a fire.

For sales leaders, it’s important to recognize that when results drop, volume isn’t the solution just because it feels like the safe answer. Many of us turned to a volume push because it is measurable and easy to hand out. Unfortunately, it is rarely the right solution. Volume is the easiest lever to pull, but it treats the symptom and ignores the cause.

Today, sales teams are turning back to the phones for cold outreach. As someone who works with hundreds of sales leaders and their teams, I’ve noticed a concerning trend developing. Most of these teams — if not all — are bringing the outdated volume playbook with them.

What is likely not realized is that, in the same way email providers intervened, phone carriers are intervening as well. In the last few years, carriers have started cracking down on mass-dialing activity and, to stop it, have implemented ‘spam likely’ caller ID labels.

More dials lead to more spam flags, which lead to fewer answers, which lead to more dials. In other words, if volume centricity persists, the phone channel will soon be as untenable as email. Once a number is flagged, even the prospects who would have welcomed the conversation no longer pick up.

If there’s only one thing you take away from this article, let it be this: when a drop in results happens across your sales team, rather than assuming it’s a quota problem, treat it as a warning signal.

Chief Revenue Officers, Chief Sales Officers and Heads of Sales are up against board mandates that demand they do more with fewer resources. My advice, which I’ve seen deliver time and time again, is to measure outcomes per activity, not total activity. Precision beats volume every time. A rep who books three meetings from 40 calls is building something sustainable. A rep who books the same three meetings from 400 dials is burning through goodwill, phone numbers and their own morale.

To that point, it’s also crucial to fix the inputs before attempting to scale them. Contact data is wrong 15 to 25 percent of the time, so without addressing those inaccuracies, deploying that data to dial at volume multiplies waste. Every call to a wrong number is a wasted dial and one more signal that can get your numbers flagged. Cleaning your lists, verifying direct dials and prioritizing the right accounts will do more for your pipeline than another 100 dials a day.

It’s the responsibility of sales leaders and reps alike to protect the channels we depend on. Think of it like foraging. An experienced forager takes only what they need and leaves the roots in the ground, so the plant keeps producing season after season. Pull up the whole plant to fill your basket faster, and you’ve just had your last harvest from that spot. Blasting a channel with volume is the sales equivalent of pulling up the roots.

Although my mentality towards cold email outreach has evolved since the mid-2010s, what I’ve come to learn is that I wasn’t wrong about email — I was wrong about scale.

At the end of the day, every channel has a reputation, and burning it hurts everyone who uses it, including you. Before it’s too late for the phone channel, let us all keep in mind that the channel isn’t the problem; the appetite for volume is.

If we, as a collective, can resist the instinct to lean on quantity, we’ll not only get more quality outcomes, but we’ll also be leaving the roots intact and harvesting from our channels for a lifetime.

Back in the mid-2010s, I was one of those sales reps with a pretty bullish mentality towards outbound email outreach. Unfortunately, the tables turned, and my response rates to cold email outreach plummeted 90%. Over the last decade, the same amount of outreach has begun producing just a tenth of the results; not only for me, but for sales reps everywhere.

The problem wasn’t email. The problem was how we, as outbound sales reps, responded to the decrease in positive outcomes. As a collective, the sellers changed buyer behavior and now, we’re seeing this pattern repeat itself. This time, it’s happening on the phones, and if sales leaders don’t learn from what happened to email, reps will inevitably burn through another channel.

Email providers like Microsoft and Google became stricter about bulk sending and began blocking and blacklisting domains that engaged in it. #5484. The Crunchbase Tech Layoffs Tracker

Tech Layoffs Continue In A Week Led By EBay And Electronic Arts

Nearly a dozen tech companies reported a reduction in force in the past couple of weeks, affecting at least 1,790 workers.

The majority of this week’s tally comes from eBay, which reported its second round of 2026 layoffs. According to a report in Reuters, the San Jose, California-based e-commerce giant is trimming its workforce by 1,100, or 9%, in an effort to “simplify operations and shift resources to its fastest-growing areas.”

The gaming sector also ranked high in this week’s count with a pair of companies reporting layoffs. Leading that industry count in the disclosed number of workers affected is Redwood City, California-based Electronic Arts. Per a report in Variety, the software provider is restructuring its studios business, which includes the total shutdown of its BioWare games studio in Edmonton, Canada. Since this is a global cut, it’s unclear how many U.S. workers will be affected.

And, in a workforce reduction that hasn’t made it to the layoff stage, yet, earlier this week Microsoft said it is offering voluntary buyouts to about 60,000 of its global employees. Per a report in Reuters, a source said the Redmond, Washington-based tech giant is making the offer available to staff company-wide, with the exception of its marketing, commercial business and security divisions.

The following companies were added to the tracker this week:

Layoffs during the weeks ended Oct. 28, 2026: At least 1,790 U.S. tech sector employees were laid off or scheduled for layoffs, per a Crunchbase News tally.

In 2025: Around 127,000 workers were let go from U.S.-based tech companies according to our tally.

In 2024: At least 95,667 workers at U.S.-based tech companies lost their jobs in 2024, according to a Crunchbase News tally.

In 2023: More than 191,000 workers in U.S.-based tech companies (or tech companies with a large U.S. workforce) were laid off in mass job cuts.

In 2022: More than 93,000 jobs were slashed from public and private tech companies in the U.S.

This tracker includes layoffs conducted by U.S.-based companies or those with a strong U.S. presence and is updated at least bi-weekly. We’ve included both startups and publicly traded, tech-heavy companies. We’ve also included companies based elsewhere that have a sizable team in the United States, such as Klarna, even when it’s unclear how much of the U.S. workforce has been affected by layoffs.

Layoff and workforce figures are best estimates based on reporting. We source the layoffs from media reports, our own reporting, social media posts and layoffs.fyi, a crowdsourced database of tech layoffs.

We recently updated our layoffs tracker to reflect the most recent round of layoffs each company has conducted. This allows us to quickly and more accurately track layoff trends, which is why you might notice some changes in our most recent numbers.

If an employee headcount cannot be confirmed to our standards, we note it as “unclear.”

A layoff can be either a permanent termination of someone’s employment — usually for cost-saving reasons — or a temporary one because there’s not enough work to justify a full workforce. Tech company layoffs generally fall into the permanent category.

A mass layoff is when a significant number of a company’s employees are cut in a short period of time, often as a result of economic conditions.

Tech layoffs started to surge in 2022 and continued in 2023 and 2024. Companies have given various reasons for conducting layoffs.

Some companies — especially those in the e-commerce sector — nearly doubled their employee headcount to meet consumer demand during the COVID-19 pandemic’s stay-at-home mandates, and later found that they were overstaffed as daily life returned to normal.

Large tech employers such as Salesforce and Google parent Alphabet noted that their post-pandemic layoffs followed several years of rapid hiring fueled by fast growth — between 2019 and 2022, some companies nearly doubled their employee headcount. Some large tech companies also cited slowing sales and fears of a recession as reasons for downsizing.

Venture-backed startups, meanwhile, also cut jobs as a way to cut costs and preserve their cash reserves, as venture funding fell significantly after the peak in 2021. Some startups that ran out of cash and couldn’t raise new funding found themselves filing for bankruptcy or shutting down.

Intel Corp. laid off the largest number of people among U.S. tech employers in 2024, by our count. The semiconductor giant laid off more than 15,000 employees last year.

It was followed closely by electric-car maker Tesla, which cut more than 14,000 roles, and networking company Cisco, with more than 10,000 total roles cut.

In 2023, Amazon layoffs led the numbers with 16,000 roles cut. Layoffs at Alphabet, the parent company of Google, totaled about 12,000, and Microsoft’s layoffs totaled about 10,000 workers in 2023, as did Facebook parent Meta’s layoffs.

Many venture-backed tech startups have also done layoffs as venture capital investment has fallen sharply since the peak in 2021, and falling startup valuations factor into their decisions to conduct layoffs.

Yes, more layoffs are likely coming. While there are signs that the volume of layoffs is tapering, experts we talked to expect job cuts in the tech sector to continue for the foreseeable future as large tech companies and startups continue to battle economic headwinds.

Seed and early-stage startups in particular may continue to conduct layoffs in an attempt to extend their cash runways in a difficult venture funding environment.

Tech layoffs noticeably increased at the start of 2022, ramped up in 2023, waned somewhat in 2024 and have continued in 2025.

Signs that may indicate a company is more likely to conduct layoffs include:

Layoffs declined in 2024 compared to the previous year, but are expected to continue into 2025, although likely not at the level seen in 2023. Startups that need to preserve cash to extend their runways are more likely to conduct layoffs.

Tech layoffs will likely slow when venture capital funding increases and the startup economy stabilizes, as well as when market conditions improve and more startups gain liquidity via IPOs.

Startups that raised capital during the venture funding heyday at inflated valuations in 2021 are more likely to need to conduct layoffs if they’re not able to sustain their previous valuations or growth projections.

Tech layoffs started surging in the 2022 market correction, with an estimated 93,000 U.S. tech workers laid off that year. That figure more than doubled in 2023, with around 200,000 U.S. tech employees laid off, according to our Tech Layoffs Tracker. Layoffs abated again in 2024, with around 95,000 reported tech layoffs.

Keep in mind, many companies don’t report detailed layoffs figures, and some companies continue hiring after cuts for positions deemed more beneficial to the business.

No, according to experts in the sector, who say a sale is unlikely to solve a tech company’s cash-flow issues.

This is especially true as fewer startup M&A deals are happening in the current downturn.

Tech layoffs have hit across departments at many companies.

Many layoffs from the large tech giants were software engineers. Startups tend to be more likely to retain engineers in favor of doing layoffs in their talent and recruiting, marketing and other departments.

Google cut roles in its sales, recruiting, product and engineering teams. Amazon layoffs included jobs in its AWS cloud unit, at its social video platform Twitch, and in its advertising department. Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg said the company’s recruiting department would be the first to see job cuts.

#5483. Pope Leo XIV on AI

by Oren Etzioni on Nov 1, 2026 at 10:11 amNovember 1, 2026 at 10:57 am

On Friday, 17 days after his surgery for lung cancer, Pope Leo XIV stood before a room of AI luminaries at the Vatican and delivered a speech on AI. No pope has engaged with AI as seriously, or as deeply, as Leo XIV. The timing shows how much AI matters to him. His remarks were important, on target, and blessedly short: about 740 words, compared with roughly 42,000 in Magnifica Humanitas, the AI encyclical, which I wrote about in May.

“The future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.”

I agree with four of his five points. The fifth, a call for international institutions to govern AI, is where we part ways.

First, “the future of artificial intelligence is not pre-determined.” He wants us to ask of AI, “What purpose should it serve?”

Second, “machines are tools, not persons.” Granting AI legal personhood, he warns, risks “leaving those who suffer harm to confront a faceless entity.”

Third, “certain decisions must never be delegated.” Decisions over life, freedom and the use of force have to stay with people, and he urged the states meeting in Geneva in November to “take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Fourth, intelligent technologies “must never become ends in themselves or serve merely the interests of a privileged few.”

Fifth, “What we currently need are institutions capable of putting these principles into practice, particularly effective international institutions that can safeguard the global common good.”

I disagree with the fifth for two reasons.

The first is that the UN, the obvious candidate, has shown a remarkable inability to act. When Russia invaded Ukraine in 2022, the Security Council couldn’t even pass a resolution calling for its withdrawal, because Russia holds a veto. Days later, the General Assembly demanded the same withdrawal by a vote of 141-5, and Russia ignored it.

The second is that international institutions are poorly suited to governing a technology that changes every few months. The pope’s own example makes the case. States have discussed autonomous weapons under a UN weapons convention in Geneva since 2014, with a formal expert group since 2016. After 12 years, the review conference that meets Nov. 16-20 will decide whether to begin negotiating a treaty.

“Take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.”

Thousands of AI researchers, me among them, have called for a ban since 2015. There still isn’t one, and I don’t expect Geneva to deliver it. In those same 12 years, AI went from labeling photos to writing software. I suspect real international cooperation on AI won’t come until the major powers face something like the mutually assured destruction that drove nuclear arms control.

Several AI thinkers spoke at the meeting before the pope did.

Max Tegmark of MIT warned against handing decisions to machines, citing tech executives’ predictions that “AI will be in charge, not humans.”

I agree that people have to stay in charge. When AI causes harm, a person chose to deploy it, and that person should answer for it. That’s the pope’s point about the faceless entity. Tegmark and I disagree about a lot (we debated AI risk in September), but not about this.

Stuart Russell of UC Berkeley went further. “We must turn aside from this trajectory before it is too late and pursue other trajectories,” he said, adding that if developers succeed in building machines more capable than humans, “there’s a good chance that every human being will die.”

I don’t share that view, and the pope didn’t go there either. His concerns are autonomous weapons, accountability and who benefits from AI, and those dangers are already here.

Gary Marcus, an NYU cognitive scientist who also spoke, wrote that “Pope Leo XIV is by far the clearest thinker on AI among prominent world leaders.” I agree.

Marcus also wants red lines for open-ended AI agents that “can kind of do anything on the internet.” Red lines are easy to draw and hard to enforce, which brings us back to the fifth point.

Marcus uses GPS navigation to illustrate a better approach. A GPS navigation app is a form of intelligence, he said, but “GPS navigation systems do not hack into Australian government websites.” He was referring to the OpenAI agent that broke into an Australian government Medicare portal in June.

A GPS app’s access to the internet is narrow and restricted. Daniel Khashabi of Johns Hopkins and I call this bounded autonomy. Alignment tries to make an AI agent choose well. Bounded autonomy limits what the agent is allowed to do: how much it can spend, which tools it can use, and which irreversible actions need a person’s sign-off. The company that deploys the agent sets those bounds in software, so nobody has to wait for a treaty.

In May, I wrote that the Pope can talk, but only we can walk. The first point is the one each of us can act on. AI’s future depends on our choices, and we make some of them every day in what we use, buy and build.

Pope Leo leaves for Uruguay, Argentina and Peru on Nov. 6. I wish him safe travels and a full recovery.

#5482. Startup uses motion sensors and AI to tell families when an aging parent’s routine changes

Chronicling the Seattle and Pacific Northwest startup scene. SEE MORE

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 2, 2026 at 9:31 amNovember 2, 2026 at 9:31 am

Thessai, a Bellevue, Wash., startup led by a former Microsoft HoloLens executive, is rolling out a home monitoring system for older adults that flags trouble without cameras, microphones or wearables.

Motion sensors placed around the home feed Thessai’s AI software, which learns a person’s normal patterns over time, such as when they wake up, how often they use the bathroom and how much they move around. The system then sends an alert through a mobile app when something falls outside that baseline: a long stretch of inactivity, unusual movement at night, or a front door opening at 2 a.m.

Founder and CEO Michael Nassirian started the company after his mother-in-law fell at home and was injured. She had a phone and an emergency button within reach but didn’t use them, and she told no one until the next day, when she needed an ambulance.

The family looked for a way to keep tabs on her and found only wearables and cameras, which she refused. So Nassirian bought motion sensors at Home Depot, put them around her home, and wrote software to alert his wife if her mother stopped moving.

Keeping quiet about a fall or health scare is common among older adults, Nassirian said.

“Number one, they say, ‘I’m OK.’ Number two, ‘I don’t want to bother you,’” he said. “And number three, and most important, is embarrassment. They do not want to advertise it.”

Pendants and smartwatches with fall alerts have long been the default, but they only help if people use them. A review of nearly 120 fall-detection studies co-authored by a University of Alberta researcher found that older adults who fall often don’t use their devices to reach a caregiver. Thessai joins a crop of companies pitching camera-free ambient monitoring instead, including Cherish, which makes radar-based sensors, and Butlr, which uses thermal heat detection.

Nassirian spent nearly two decades at Microsoft, working on Office, Windows and later HoloLens, where he was a partner quality architect. Before that, he spent about 14 years at Texas Instruments in test engineering. He has a master’s in biomedical engineering from the University of Texas at Austin, and since leaving Microsoft he has founded and advised several startups, including ARVR Academy and Predictive AI Research.

After relatives started asking for monitoring systems of their own, Nassirian formally founded Thessai in 2024 and has self-funded it so far. The company sells two packages, Basic and Premium, to families with an older relative living alone. Its Enterprise package gives senior-living operators a dashboard for monitoring multiple residences.

The Basic package, which includes motion sensors and a hub that plugs into the home’s Wi-Fi, costs $195 plus a $38 monthly subscription. Premium adds features such as a panic button and two-way voice check-ins through the hub, and costs $249 plus $59 a month. The sensors run on batteries that Nassirian said last at least a year and a half.

Nassirian said independent-living communities have been the strongest market so far. Memory-care facilities already have staff watching residents closely, he said, while independent-living operators are pitching Thessai to renters as a “smart home” feature.

Nassirian said the older adult decides what gets monitored. Through the app, they can switch off sensors in certain rooms, the bathroom for example, and limit tracking to the kitchen and living room. Caregivers can also tune alerts to cut down on noise, so a parent who routinely sleeps late, for example, doesn’t set one off.

Thessai is going after a large and growing market. Older adults overwhelmingly want to stay in their homes (75%) and communities (73%), according to AARP’s 2024 Home and Community Preferences Survey, and households led by people 80 and older are set to double by 2040.

The startup soft-launched in May and has a few hundred customers, split between families and senior-care operators, Nassirian said. Its advisory board includes Chuck Lytle, who founded Bellevue-based senior housing companies Lytle Enterprises and Leisure Care.

Nassirian said the company is also working with the Department of Veterans Affairs on bringing the system to veterans, including in rural areas, with the option to run it on the VA’s own secure network.

Thessai has four employees in the U.S. and seven in Singapore. Nassirian is now looking to raise outside money, mainly to buy hardware in larger volumes and bring down per-unit costs.

Longer term, he wants to do away with the physical sensors altogether and detect movement from a home’s existing Wi-Fi signals, an approach researchers at Harvard and Carnegie Mellon are studying.

“I’m in technology,” he said. “I’m not going to sit still.”

#5480. Jumbo Series A Rounds Hiding The Real Squeeze On Seed Startups

Global startups have closed at least 114 Series A rounds of $100 million or more so far this year, Crunchbase reported in late September, and more than 70% of them went to AI companies. For most seed founders, that headline is a warning.

U.S. startups closed 272 Series A rounds in the third quarter, according to Crunchbase data, about 28% fewer than the 377 a year earlier. Seed held up better, at 984 rounds vs. 1,059. The megarounds hide how few A rounds are getting done.

Seed checks keep growing. The median U.S. seed round was about $3 million last year, 3x its 2018 level, according to Crunchbase. Yet only 24% of companies that raised a $1 million-plus seed in 2023 have moved past seed, and just 16% of the 2024 cohort, down from 55% or higher through 2020.

Uncork Capital‘s Andy McLoughlin told Crunchbase News that Series A investors now expect $2 million to $3 million in ARR, sometimes $4 million, and the time from seed to A has stretched past two years. If a seed won’t carry you to that bar with six months to spare, a smaller round is the better deal.

A bigger seed isn’t required. Take Atomic, a New York-based supply chain planning software company founded in 2023 (and not an MGV portfolio company). It raised a $3 million seed, right at the median, in April 2025, led by Madrona and DVx Ventures, then closed a $12.5 million Series A led by Madrona and Klass Capital about 17 months later.

Funds of $100 million to $500 million typically lead the Series A. Figure out which ones lead at your stage and when their current fund closes, then send the right partners updates for a year before you ask for anything.

The Series A bar is now a revenue bar, which makes it a go-to-market problem first. Most seed companies I meet have a stronger product than sales motion.

At MGV, our work starts with a first session we call Sales Jumpstart: we interview the founders and their team. We then score the company on our proprietary matrix: where it is today, where it should be, and what it needs to become a scalable go-to-market machine.

From there, founders work through workshops on outbound reach, qualification, profiling, the funnel, objection handling, hiring assessment, compensation plans, fundraising, deck building, storytelling and investor intros, with mentoring alongside.

A company at $2 million in ARR with a sales process a new hire can run is a better Series A candidate than one at $3 million built on founder-led deals nobody else can repeat. The founders who make it are already planning for the round after this one.

#5479. Sprout Ends at Block 3,543,405: What the ZIPs Say About ZEC in Orchard and Sapling

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

Zcash has three older shielded pools, and only one of them has a shutdown date. On November 5, NU7 will make the 22,263 ZEC left in Sprout unspendable.

The 346,000 ZEC still in Orchard and the 420,000 ZEC in Sapling face no deadline at all.

But the Zcash specifications include one conditional warning that covers all three pools, and it has been widely misquoted. Let's go through the ZIPs to set out exactly what each document says about each pool, and what it doesn't.

Together, the three older pools hold about 788,000 ZEC. Any full node reports these balances directly through the valuePools field of its getblockchaininfo RPC, so anyone running a node can check them.

The three pools are on very different paths. Sprout has a fixed end. Orchard is closed to new deposits, but no spec sets a closing date. Sapling remains a supported pool.

Sprout's end has been planned for years. ZIP 211, written in 2019, stopped new value from entering Sprout. It described that as "a step toward being able to remove the Sprout shielded protocol."

ZIP 2003 takes the final step. It doesn't target Sprout directly. Instead, it bans an entire transaction format: from NU7 onward, "the transaction version number MUST be 5 or 6." Sprout transfers can only be written as version 4 transactions, so Sprout funds can no longer be spent.

ZIP 259, the NU7 deployment spec, sets the activation height at block 3,543,405 on mainnet. It states the result directly: "funds remaining in the Sprout pool become unspendable."

The wording matters. ZIP 2003 says it does not "unissue, burn, or otherwise make Sprout funds permanently unavailable." The coins stay counted in Zcash's issued supply, and the ZIP leaves open "the theoretical possibility of re-enabling v4 transactions, or of adding another facility to retrieve these funds." It also cautions that this "may never be re-enabled."

Recovering Sprout funds was already hard before the deadline. According to ZIP 2003, the retirement of zcashd just before NU6.3 "removed the only maintained software that still provided wallet functionality for Sprout." The pool has barely changed in the last few weeks: the widely reported figure of 22,309 ZEC has fallen only to 22,263, so about 46 ZEC has moved out since.

Orchard's situation is newer and more unusual. ZIP 258 activated NU6.3 at block 3,428,143 and sealed Orchard after a soundness vulnerability was found and fixed. Since then, the consensus rules have enforced three restrictions:

ZIP 229 explains why: Orchard held "a substantial portion of ZEC" when the vulnerability was fixed, so moving those funds to a fresh pool was meant to restore confidence in Zcash's total supply.

The migration has largely worked. ZecStats counts 3,278,499 ZEC moved out of Orchard, about 90.5% of what was in the pool at NU6.3. That leaves about 346,000 ZEC, roughly 2% of the circulating supply.

Sapling has the fewest restrictions of the three. Version 6 transactions support it as one of the "supported shielded pools," alongside Orchard and Ironwood, and none of the NU6.3 or NU7 ZIPs restricts it.

There's one catch for Sapling users that many people are missing. ZIP 259 says the version 4 ban covers "all version 4 transactions, including transparent-only and Sapling transactions, not only Sprout transfers." Sapling funds stay spendable after NU7, but only through version 5 or version 6 transactions. Wallets still building version 4 transactions need to switch before the upgrade. Pending or offline-signed version 4 transactions won't confirm afterward, and "re-signing alone cannot make a version 4 transaction valid."

The sentence behind the "inaccessible funds" headlines appears in ZIP 2005, "Ironwood Quantum Recoverability," and is repeated in ZIP 229:

"Recovery would not be possible for funds still in the Sprout, Sapling, or Orchard pools; all such funds would be inaccessible after their respective protocols are disabled."

The sentence before it explains the context. Zcash's existing shielded protocols depend on discrete logarithms being hard to compute. If an attacker, using a quantum computer or another method, could break that, the protocols might have to be disabled "to prevent such attacks." Only funds in Ironwood would be recoverable, through a recovery protocol designed to stay secure against quantum attacks.

So this is a contingency, not a schedule. It describes what would happen to funds in the older pools if a future cryptographic emergency forced Zcash to shut them down. No ZIP proposes doing that on any date. The practical advice behind it is plain: funds in Sprout, Sapling or Orchard "should be migrated to the Ironwood pool" to be covered by recovery.

The software is ready. The Zcash Foundation released Zebra 7.0.0 on October 22. Its changelog says it "supports the NU7 network upgrade on Mainnet, which activates at height 3,543,405." The release moves Zebra's database from format v28 to v29. Zebra 6.x can't read the new format, so the Foundation recommends backing up the old state first. The zcashd compatibility sidecar must also be updated to zebra-compat-v1.3.0. Earlier builds can't follow mainnet past NU7.

This upgrade carries more risk than usual. ZIP 259 waives Zcash's usual rule that old software must shut itself down before an upgrade. The spec warns that "operators of unsupported software may therefore remain online at activation and follow a pre-NU7 consensus branch."

For holders, the guidance from each pool's spec comes down to this:

On November 5, Sprout closes. The 766,000 ZEC in Sapling and Orchard face no deadline, but the specs still recommend moving it to Ironwood.

#5478. Who gets your vote? What rumors should you spot? Election quiz and bingo offer guidance

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 2, 2026 at 10:28 amNovember 2, 2026 at 10:28 am

With Election Day tomorrow, a Seattle-area tech entrepreneur has a quiz to help voters sort through candidates and ballot measures, while University of Washington researchers have a bingo card for spotting familiar election-fraud rumors. Both offer some last-minute perspective — and a little levity.

Mike Dussault, a former SpaceX and Valve engineer and serial startup founder, built Voter Lifeboat, a free quiz designed to help Washington voters identify candidates and ballot-measure positions that align with their values.

“I’m not making money from it,” Dussault said via email. “I built it to help people vote.”

The app asks 17 questions about taxes, climate, housing, data centers and other issues, then generates a report card showing how closely candidates and initiatives align with a user’s answers. The site includes a detailed methodology and links to sources, and users answer the questions anonymously.

The quiz takes just a few minutes, offering another resource alongside traditional voter guides and endorsements from news outlets and other organizations.

Dussault put AI through its paces to build the tool.

“It was fun to task Claude with so much research and reasoning (to vet all the candidates and initiatives) that it maxed out a Claude Ultra subscription,” he said on LinkedIn.

The University of Washington’s Center for an Informed Public (CIP) has served as a watchdog of election-related misinformation for seven years, tracking where it originates and how it spreads online and in the media.

Its Election Rumor Research team this fall created “Rigged Election” Bingo to help people spot recurring conspiracy theories and misleading claims about election fraud.

“Allegedly hacked machines, dead voters, and statistical anomalies are some of the familiar tropes that supposedly ‘prove’ our election system is broken,” the team wrote in a recent post. “These aren’t new ideas.”

Some claims start with real issues, the researchers noted, but exaggerate their scope or omit the safeguards and remedies already in place. The bingo card is designed to help people recognize those patterns and distinguish isolated problems from misleading narratives about the election system.

In Washington, U.S. Attorney Charles Neil Floyd, the top federal prosecutor in Seattle, recently raised allegations of voter fraud. Floyd claimed last month that more than 400 noncitizens had been voting in the state and asked state officials to sequester their ballots.

Secretary of State Steve Hobbs said in a news release that his office was reviewing the allegations and that voter fraud in Washington is “incredibly rare.” He added that the timing of the announcement, a week before the election, “is no doubt intended to cast unfounded suspicion on the results.”

#5477. How a Starbucks drive-thru ‘fast pass’ could actually work

by Todd Bishop on Nov 2, 2026 at 10:46 amNovember 2, 2026 at 11:40 am

Starbucks’ idea to use technology to recognize regulars at the drive-thru is getting plenty of attention, but the actual implementation might not be as sci-fi as some of the headlines suggest.

CEO Brian Niccol said on the company’s earnings call last week that the coffee giant is “exploring experiences that recognize participating customers as they arrive, present personalized digital menus, and make payment more effortless.”

He didn’t say how that would work, and some reports quickly jumped to the conclusion that facial recognition could be coming to Starbucks — with one headline declaring that the company wants AI to know your face.

That may be a leap. Niccol’s own description of the idea, in an interview the next morning, centered on the Starbucks app: “When you pull up to the drive-thru, if you’re in our app, it will recognize you,” he told Yahoo Finance’s Brian Sozzi. “It’ll show the order that you’ve placed historically or the last time you ordered.”

From there, he said, “the barista will be like, ‘Brian, is it the usual?’ You’ll be like, ‘Yes, great. It’s paid.’ Now you’re off to the window to pick up your drink, and out you go.”

Niccol said it will be “the fastest drive-thru experience you can have,” adding, “We haven’t named it yet, but I feel like this is going to be a fast pass.” He acknowledged that it’s “a ways away.”

One way an app could recognize a customer without cameras is geofencing, in which the app uses a phone’s location to detect when a customer enters a zone around the store, as some restaurant chains already do for curbside pickup. Another is a small Bluetooth transmitter at the order board that detects a phone when the car pulls up.

Starbucks hasn’t said publicly how customers would be identified or where the idea would be tested. Responding to an inquiry from GeekWire, Starbucks said Niccol was speaking in the context of the company’s broader effort to make the drive-thru faster, more convenient and more personal, while preserving the interaction between baristas and customers.

“We’re early in this work, and we’ll test, learn, and scale what works,” Niccol said on the call.

Roughly half of Starbucks customers use the drive-thru, he said. Speed matters as Starbucks competes with drive-thru-focused chains such as Dutch Bros and 7 Brew, as Yahoo Finance noted.

Before any fast pass, Starbucks plans to begin testing “background AI models” in its current fiscal year, which began in late September, to help baristas enter orders more accurately and efficiently. The idea builds on a pilot that GeekWire reported on earlier this year, which listens as a customer orders and enters the items into the register automatically.

That approach keeps a person at the speaker, unlike chains that have tried letting AI take the order. McDonald’s ended its AI drive-thru ordering test with IBM in 2024, while Wendy’s has expanded AI ordering nationwide at its drive-thrus using Google Cloud technology.

Starbucks has had its own setbacks with AI in stores. In May, the company retired an AI-powered inventory counting tool built with Redmond, Wash.-based startup NomadGo, just nine months after unveiling it, after baristas reported miscounts and other glitches, as GeekWire reported in July.

“When it fell short, we listened to feedback and changed course,” Starbucks said at the time.

The drive-thru work is part of a broader tech push. Niccol said on the call that the current fiscal year will be “a major tech modernization year,” with new staffing, scheduling and point-of-sale systems rolling out to stores.

The company also plans to begin building delivery directly into the Starbucks app early next year, use AI to improve search in the app and eventually support ordering through AI assistants and from customers’ cars.

Starbucks’ business is picking up, with U.S. same-store sales up 7.7% in the quarter ended Sept. 27.
